Fed Court Denies
Injunction To C-P
NEW YORK—An injunction
filed by
Cameo-Parkway Records against Kama
Sutra
Productions
and Jerome
Kas-
enetz Ltd., over the release by Kama
Sutra of records by The Ohio Express
has been denied by a Federal Court.
Judge
Tyler
of the Federal Court
denied the injunction on Friday, April
5,
after being advised by Roemer &
Klein, Kama
Sutra’s
attorneys,
that
this was
the second such proceeding
which
Cameo-Parkway
had
brought
against
its clients.
On
Dec.
29,
1967, Judge Edelstein
of
the
Federal
Court
had
denied
Cameo-Parkway’s
attempt
to
enjoin
Kama
iSutra from
releasing
records
made by The Five Stairsteps & Cubie.
Judge Tyler, in denying the injunc-
tion,
indicated that Kama Sutra had
acted
properly
in
dealing
with The
Ohio Express, and indicated that there
was no binding contract between The
Ohio
Express
and
Cameo-Parkway
when
The
Ohio
Express
contracted
with Kama Sutra.
Judge
Tyler’s
decision was
made
after a day long trial and after testi-
mony was taken and briefs submitted
fro>m
employees
of
Cameo-Parkway
and Jerome Kasenetz and Jeffrey Katz.
Roemer & Klein argued that the same
issue that had been
litigated
in The
Five Stairsteps & Cubie suit was being
litigated
in The
Ohio
Express
Suit.
Both
Courts,
in
rendering
a
verdict
for Kama
Sutra,
found
that Kama
Sutra had acted properly.

King Requiem
NEW YORK—A jazz requiem in hon-

composed by Ronnie Roullier, director
of the New York Jazz Repertory Or-
chestra.
Based on
highlights
in
the
life of the late Dr. King, the requiem
is in the form of an eight part suite.
It will be performed by the 21
piece
Repertory Orchestra and a jazz choir
under
the
direction
of Jack Manno.
Plans
are being
set
for
a
recording
date,
and
all
proceeds
from
album
sales will be donated to the Southern
Christian
Leadership
Conference
to
help continue the work of Dr. King.

Creai Britain
Canaan
Following a boom year in disk sales, the first official figures on record sales
for
the
first month
of
the
current
year show
a continued
increase
in
total
volume business. All may change following the Budget but interest in records
has never been higher in the period immediately after the high-sale Christmas
period. Board
of Trade
statistics
reveal
that
total
record
sales
in
Januax’y,
normally
a
quiet
period,
reached
a new peak
for
the month
at
£2,845,000
($6,348,000). This compares with the £2,191,000 ($5,172,000) garnered from disk
sales
in January,
1967.
Increase in business was reflected both in the domestic and overseas markets.
Locally,
the
all-industry
turnover
last January was
£2,486,000
($5,966,400)
against £1,881,000
($4,322,400)
in the previous January. In the export market
turnover
increased from
the
£310,000
($744,000) made
in January,
1967,
to
£359,000
($861,600)
in
January,
1968.
Total
production
of
records,
too,
spiraled.
It was up
37
per
cent
overall on
the
previous comparable
period.
Singles and
E.P. production
rose by
21 per cent to
5,859,000
units. But the
real boom came in L.Ps which, compared to January, 1967, were up 65 per cent
to 4,635,000 units. With the exception of the best selling months of November
and December, this was higher than the total album production in any one month
last year.
With the conglomerate effects of the massively tough Budget
still far from
fully evident, the huge leap
in disk prices
is making those major companies
who have not entered the budget album field take a new look at the situation.
Of
all
lines
of
disk product the budgeter
is
the
only one
liable
to eke any
benefit
out
of the
increase
in purchase tax
and,
as
such, becomes an even
more
attractive product than
hitherto.
Most notable abstainer from the budget L.P. field is, of course, Decca Records
which has a healthy range of medium/low priced albums. Until now, the success
of these lines has tended to offset the urgency of Dacca’s penetration into the
budget
foray. Now, however,
the
increased
taxation has played havoc with
carefully
selected album
pricings
and
the
whole
of
the
non-regular album
market has. been put off balance. Decca’s Sales Manager, Colin Borland, admits
that his company
is now re-thinking
its position
in relation
to budget
lines.
He
stresses that no
decision
is imminent, but
if Decca
decides
to go ahead
in this new field the launch would not be before the Pall. If the full effect of
the new tax and the Budget generally
is to be taken into account, then Decca
may well wait until the New Year before unveiling a new range of product.
Robert Reisdorf, who heads up the British Liberty operation, is currently in
Germany for talks with Liberty’s German Managing Director Siegfried Loch
whilst Ron Kass,
in charge
of European
operations,
is
in Los Angeles
for
talks with Liberty Chief A1 Bennett. Liberty
is to absorb extra purchase tax
imposed by the Budget as far as the Blue Note label is concerned, and this will
continue
to
retail
at
45/lld.
Blue
Note
is
distributed
by
Liberty and
not
Philips as
is
all their other product. May
is to be a Slim Whitman month for
Liberty with poster and dealer campaigns. Whitman is a steady all-year-round
seller but a
boost
is
to
be
given
to
his new
single and album both
titled
“Cool Water.”
Following
the
rock
revival
mood,
Liberty
is
to
re-issue
an
Eddie Cochrane album “My Way” which
will also be issued on stereo as will
several other selected Liberty items.
Hal
Shaper
of
Sparta
Music
is
very
active
on
the
soundtrack
album
front. An L.P. containing music from the National Theatre Productions “Rosen-
crantz

Are

“The

“As You Like It” has just been issued in the U.K. on Decca and in the U.S.A.
on London. The album

debut

“What A Woman Does”; “I Can Guarantee You Love” by Tony Rivers
(Poly-
dor)
;

“Silly Boy
Blue” by

Shaper

Doors Manager Makes Music Think Young
NEW YORK — Bill Siddons, twenty-
year-old manager
of the
Doors,
per-
sonifies the trend towards youth in the
music
industry. One
of the youngest
managers
in
the
business,
Siddons
serves
as
spokesman
for
the
Doors,
and
pi-omotes
their
concerts. He
will
become heavily involved in the several
TV special and movie offers the group
has received.
Siddons explains that the Doors pre-
fer
to work
with young
people, and
that
their
business
relationships
be
based
on
friendship.
“Business,
yes,
but not cold, hard business.”
Because he spent so much time with
the Doors during his stint as their road
manager,
the
group
decided
that
he
was much more aware
of
the
direc-
tion
they
were
heading
as
artists.
“Management was management—not
friends,”
says
Siddons.
“The
Doors
and
I have found that as
five people
we
can work together as
one
united
force. We have found cohesiveness
in
excluding any outside force which al-
ways seems to work against our own
purposes in the end.”
The
youth-manaigement-friendship
trend
in major pop music groups
is
spreading’.
Jefferson Airplane
is now
being managed by Bill Thompson (an-
other ex-road-manager who found that
friendship and business do mix), and
so
far
the arrangement has
been
a
great success.
Siddons sums up the results as,
.
.
less animosity, and more organization
and productivity”.
A&M Pacts Pillory
HOLLYWOOD — A new group,
the
Pillory, has been signed to a recording
contract by A&M Records. The quintet
consists of Lindy Getz on drums, Greg-
ory Barton on bass guitar, Steve Pitts
on
rhythm
guitar,
Kerim
Capli
on
lead
guitar,
and
Suzannah
Jordon
doubling on electric twelve string and
vocals.
In
addition
to
signing
with
A&M, they have also been signed for
recurring
roles on the 20th Century-
Fox TV series, “Peyton Place,” which
airs on the ABC-TV network.

to
a
contract.

Capitol
release,

2,” received an

MAIN AnRACTION
(COMING NEXT WEEK)
AN ARTISTS RENDERING—One of
the many talents
to spring from
the
Liberty Records organization is Macey
Lipman, director of national sales and
promotion for World Pacific /Soul City
Records. Lipman has his original
oils
hanging in the homes and offices of his
friends in both H’wood and New York.
He has been painting since the age of
13 and, while he was studying photog-
raphy, put on a one man show at the
Philadelphia Museum College
of Art.
He refers to his style of rendering as
being that
“.
.
. my style of painting
is true to
life or in the same
field as
photography.” Lipman completes
ap-
prox. two paintings per year (two of
his latest efforts are displayed in the
H’wood
offices
of
Liberty.)
Lipman
entered
the
record
industry
in
1954
with
Philly’s
David
Rosen
Distribu-
torship. In 1960 he joined Kapp Rec-
ords as regional sales manager and in
1965 he
joined Liberty as
east
coast
district manager. In 1966 he was ap-
pointed
to
his
present
position
at
World Pacific.

GAZPACHO — Brass
Ring — Dunhill D/DS
50034
Gazpacho
is
defined
as “a
spicy blend
of
new and seasoned latin melodies.” This is an
apt
description of
this LP
of instrumentals
by the Brass Ring. Oldies like “Granada” and
“Yours” are juxtaposed with such contempo-
rary tunes as “Girl From Ipanema.” The pure,
bell-like sounds on the set make for a most
attractive
offering which
should
see
heavy
good music play.
JESSE JAMES—20th Century—Fox (S) 3197
iSinging
with
drive
and
intensity,
Jesse
James delivers a disk of soul songs calculated
to appeal to a large listenership. Included on
the
set are the
artist’s
latest single, “Green
Power,” “If You’re 'Lonely (Take My Hand),”
“Thank You
Darlin’,”
and
“Believe
In Me
Baby,” Parts
1 and
2. This LP could create
a good
deal
of excitement
saleswise.
OUR MAN IN WASHINGTON—Phil Flow-
ers—Dot DLP 25849
Phil
Flowers
has
been
packing
Rands’
nitery
in Washington
D.C.
for a long time
now. His music
is hard
driving, funky R&B
of
a highly
contagious
order. Some
of
the
stronger tracks on this
set are:
“I Saw Her
Standing There,” “Try A Little Tenderness,”
“Cry On My Shoulder,” and “The Great Pre-
tender.” There’s a ready made R&B market
for this powerhouse LP.

PRESENTING JOE WILLIAMS AND THAD

here

Ciassicai Picks
IVES: THE FOUR SYMPHONIES—Faber-
man/New Philharmonia Orchestra of London
—Cardinal VCS 10032/3/4
This
is the
first release of the four sym-
phonies of Charles Ives in one package. Ives
(1874-1954)
has come, in recent years, to be
recognized
as
one
of
the
most
important
American
composers, and
his
four sympho-
nies
are among
his most
important works.
Lovely
themes,
brilliant
orchestration,
pas-
sages of sheer power and moments of robust
humor
are
all
to be found
in
these works.
In
symphonies
2
and
4,
Ives
employs
the
themes of well-known tunes as “Yankee Doo-
dle” and “Columbia The Gem Of The Ocean.”
MORE HITS FROM TIN CAN ALLEY —
' ^
Eric
Andersen—Vanguard
VRS
9271/VSD
79271
Eric Andersen offers an album of folk-rock
ditties,

Shulman Named To
Dot Promotion Post
LOS ANGELES—Dot Records has ap-
pointed Moe Shulman, veteran record
promotion
executive,
to
the
post
of
east coast regional promotion director,
according to an announcement by Pete
Garris, national promotion director of
the
diskery. He replaces Lanny
Lee,
who has left the label.
“Dot
is entering the most produc-
tive period in the history of the firm,”
said Garris, “therefore our aim was to
bolster the east coast with a
‘heavy’
promotion man. We believe our goal
has been attained with the addition of
Moe Shulman.”
Shulman,
who
headquarters
at
World
Wide
Distributors
in
New
York,
first entered
the
field
in
1953
with the Edwin H. Morris publishing
firm. In 1958 he was tapped by ABC-
Paramount to helm east coast regional
promotion. A year later he accepted a
one year assignment from Roulette in
a similar capacity. Following his ten-
ure with Roulette, he was set as east
coast regional promo director of At-
lantic-Atco,
a
position he
held
until
1963 when he joined London Records,
resulting
in
his
being upped
to na-
tional promotion director a short time
later.
In August,
1967, Shulman
re-
turned to the publishing field and Ed-
win Morris as professional manager,
a
position
held
until
joining
Dot
Records.
In 1957, Sholes was appointed man-
ager
of
RCA’s
pop
singles
depart-
ment,
and
the
following
year
took
over the management of the pop
al-
bum
department
as
well.
He
was
named manager of West Coast opera-
tions
in
1961,
from
which
position
he
planned
and
directed
all A&R
functions and also coordinated
all ac-
tivities
and
policies
related
to West
Coast
marketing,
sales
custom,
re-
cording
and
administrative
opera-
tions. He
returned
to New York
in
1963, assuming the
title of vice pres-
ident
of
RCA’s
pop A&R
division,
which he held until death.
Held Industry Posts
Among
the many

he held with music business organiza-

Second Connie Awards
Ceremonies Set* For
May In Minneapolis
MINNEAPOLIS—The
Cotillion
Ball-
room
of
the
Sheraton-Ritz
Hotel
in
Minneapolis
will be
the
site
for
the
second
annual
Connie Awards
Cere-
monies, to be held May 27.
The Midwest Academy
of Contem-
porary Music, comprised of music re-
tailers,
clubs,
ballrooms
and
other
segments
of the music
industry
will
co-sponsor
the
awards
with
Connie
Hechter,
founder
of
the
event
and
publisher of Connie’s
“Insider,” a
bi-
weekly
music
trade
journal
of
the
Upper Midwest.
The Connie Awards are the Upper
Midwest’s
version
of
the
Grammy
Awards. Only members
of the music
industry in the Upper Midwest are eli-
gible. Talent will be recognized in two
dozen
categories
ranging from
indi-
vidual performers and bands to those
in all aspects of record production.
Five
finalists
from
each
category
will be determined by ballots cast by
“Insider” readers. The winner
of the
“Connie Award” of each category will
be
determined by
a
committee com-
prised of musicians and club and ball-
room operators.
“Best New Material,” is a new cate-
gory
added
to
the
ballot
this
year.
The winner
'will
receive
a
recording
contract with Mercury Records.
Mercury’s director of recorded prod-
uct, will give the keynote address at
the award
dinner.
Last
year’s
guest
speakers were executives from Colum-
bia, Mercury and RCA Victor Records.
Wilson Pickett has indicated that he
will attend the Connie Awards. Dick
Whitebeck and his 15-piece Blue Dia-
monds Band
will play for the event
again this year.
Connie
Hechter
established
the
awards to honor pop musicians of the
upper Midwest area as well as to focus
national attention on the
local music
industry. Another reason,
said Hech-
ter,
“is
to
bring
together
local
and
national
figures
of
the
industry,
to
exchange
ideas
and
to
create
unity
and strength within the industry.”
Some 115 pop musicians are finalists
on the 23 category ballot.

In 16th Prize Year
NEW YORK—Broadcast

This

the awards bring to 130 the number of

SCA
prizes
for
application
toward
their musical education.
Established
by BMI
in
1961,
the
project gives cash prizes annually to
encourage the creation of concert mu-
sic by
student composers
(under the
age
of 26)
to
aid them
in financing
their
musical
education.
All
awards
are
made
on
the
basis
of
creative
talent shown
in
original manuscripts
submitted and judged under pseudo-
nyms.
Prizes range from $250 to $2,000 at
the discretion of the judges.
Permanent chairman of the judging
panel
is William Schuman,

of the Lincoln Center for the Perform-
ing Arts. Others who served as judges

worth;

of

ald Harris, assistant to the president
for academic affairs at the New Eng-
land Conservatory of Music, and Oleg

of
the

Bay Symphony Orchestra.

Creat Briiain
The
British record business
is wall used
to matters
of contrasts—witness
the often incredible reversals of the public’s taste in music—but one contrast
which is likely to cause its share of comment is the instant success of a costly
album
pack
launched
by
Pye
Records.
This
pack,
featuring
two
LP’s
by
Donovan, plus poems, a booklet,
etc.,
is retailing at £3.
17.
6.
($9.30). Pye re-
ports an advance
of
15,000
on
the pack
titled
“Gift From A Flower To A
Garden.” This has been achieved in a climate of freeze and squeeze where the
big buying emphasis has been put on low-priced lined and budget properties.
But the hefty increase in purchase tax, which rocketed disk prices, seems not
to have
deterred
the customers from
this two-in-one package which
carries
a price tag above the new, inflated norm.
Don
Black,
Britain’s
Oscar-winning
lyricist,
currently
has
a
schedule
of
more than 20 numbers to pen for a variety of major feature films. More than
a dozen of them will be for a musical which Columbia
is to make tentatively
titled “Goodbye Summer”
and
which
will
star
Lulu,
the
singer who
took
Black’s “To
Sir With Love”
to the No.
1 spot
in America. At
this moment
Black
is
collaborating
with
Elmer
Bernstein
on
songs
for
Paramount’s
“Where’s
Jack”
starring Tommy
Steele
and
Stanley
Baker.
The
foremost
British
lyricist has
just completed “Sinful Davey” for
the
film
of the same
name which Ken Thorne scored. Number
is to be waxed by Esther Ofarim.
Constantly alert to any new wrinkle that will
sell records, EMI
is figuring
to tap the jet set market with a specially compiled range of albums under the
new banner, “Worldwide.” The diskery plans an
initial issue of nine albums.
LP’s will mirror the music of various countries, particularly the nations with
a high tourist trade. EMI has linked with a number of state tourist offices and
airlines for promotion purposes. Meantime, with the summer
traffic
in mind,
MGM
is launching a special Latin American month
in July. At least 10 new
albums and a half-dozen re-issues.
The well-tried theory of “making the headlines work for you” by rushing
out waxes with news value or likely to tap current interest in news events
is
being tried by Pye Records disk chief Les Cocks who has just cut a couple of
sides with one Frank Clarke. Clarke
is a Cambridge dustman
(trash collector)
who made the front page because Prince Charles, at present studying at Cam-
bridge University, was disturbed by his singing as he collected the garbage.
With commendable speed Pye had the newsworthy artisan
in
its
studios and
the result
is “Why Don’t They Buy Rubber Dustbins.”
Following a writ against Eurovision Song Contest winner “La La La”
al-
leging infringement of copyright on Ray
Davies’ “Death Of A
Clown,”
the
runner-up
in the contest “(Congratulations”
is now also
subject
to
legal pro-
ceedings. Irish writers Shay O’Donoghue and Aiden Magennis have
issued a
writ against writers
Phil
Coulter and
Bill Martin
alleging infringement
of
copyright. Through Segway Music
the Irishmen
say
that
“Congratulations”
has the same chord sequences
as
their composition “Far Away From
You.”
The latter number was recorded by Doc Carroll and the Royal Blues who took
it high in the Irish charts. Meantime,
it’s reported that 280 versions of “(Con-
gratulations” have now been recorded and more are in the pipeline.
MGM Records, which was swift to pick up top British deejays as vocalists,
has now swelled
its jockey ranks to four with the signing of Kenny
Everitt.
Unfortunately, Everitt has
just been axed by BBC Radio
for whom he has
been helming a prime time Sunday show. Deejays now
in the MGM fold are
Tony Blackburn, Jimmy Young, Tony Brandon and Everitt.
RCA, which has severed
its representation links with Decca Records to be-
come
the
eighth American company
to
go
independent,
has
scheduled
the
Monkees’ album “The Birds, The Bees, The Monkees” as
its
first LP
release.
Issue
is set for June.
Eurovision hit songwriters Phil Coulter and
Bill Martin have, in association
with
Larry
Page,
formed
a
production
company
called
“Different
Class”
whose product will be issued on the Page One label. The company will also act
as a talent agency for the discovery and recording of new
artists. The Page
One label
is currently registering good
sales with “Mexican Abanda” LP by
Pancho Gonzales not only in the British market but overseas as well. Released
originally on mono, a stereo version has now been issued.
Kassner Music have acquired the
British rights
to
the
17 songs from
the
American musical
“Cindy.” Words
and music by Johnny

“Cindy”
ran for

in

opens
out-of-town here May

for

its West End opening. Leading
role played by Hy Hazel.

===== PAGE 26 =====
Edison Cylinders Transferred To LP
SYRACUSE—Performances
by
ten-
ors Giovanni
Martinelli and Guiseppi
Anselmi,
never
before
released,
are
heard on the
first of
a
series
of LP
albums
issued
by
the Thomas
Alva
Edison Foundation.
The
technical
work
of
recovering
the
performances
from
the
grooves
of the original cylinders and disks was
done by Prof. Walter Welch, director
of the Foundation’s Re-recording La-
boratory
at
Syracuse
University.
Welch
is
also curator of the Univer-
sity’s Audio Archives.
Anselmi
sings
a
selection from Bi-
zet’s “The Pearl Fishers,” a previous-
ly unissued test pressing recorded
in
Europe in 1913. Martinelli sings “Vesti
la
giubba” from
“Pagliacci,”
record-
ed in 1929.
They are heard on “An Edison Mem-
orabilia:
Vol.
1.”
Vol.
2,
issued
at
the
same
time,
presents
ragtime
from
Edison
blue
Amberol
cylinders
of
1912 and
1913
and
dance
music from
discs
of
the
1920s. Among the artists on the cylin-
ders are banjoist Fred Van Eps play-
ing “Alexander’s Ragtime Band” and
soprano Anna Chandler singing “You
Made Me Love You,” a generation be-
fore Judy Garland repopularized
the
song
she
addressed
to
“Dear
Mr.
Gable.”
1920’s Music
The
disks
of
the
twenties
repro-
cessed
by
Welch
for
stereo-owning
moderns include Phil Napoleon and his
orchestra doing “Five Pennies” (1927),
the Red Nichols tune. The Golden Gate
Orchestra
and
the
California
Ram-
blers, both headed by Ed Kirkeby, are
represented
with
“Get
Out
and
Get
Under the Moon” and “Chinese Jum-
ble,”
from
September
and
October
of
1928
respectively.
Both
feature
Tommy Dorsey’s trombone. Personnel
on such recording dates varied accord-
ing to the availability of sidemen.
The
Edison
Memorabilia
stereo
LPs
sell for $5 each. New releases in
the series will be selected from among
the tens of thousands of Edison disks
and
cylinders
available
to Welch
for
re-recording.
Describing
the
techniques
he
uses
to
transfer
the
music from
the
old
cylinders and discs to tapes and then
to LP
stereo
grooves,
Welch
said:
“By
using
stereo
disk
cutting
tech-
niques it is possible to free the artists
of the early acoustical and
electrical
recording era from the effects of sing-
ing into a recording horn or an early
microphone.”
Welch
said
the
early
mikes were almost as “dead” as
the
horns.
Welch maintains that more quality
went
into
the
old Edison recordings
than
it was possible to bring out and
preserve
before
the
development
of
modern equipment. In his University
laboratory he has worked painstaking-
ly amid his
collection of old and new
equipment
to
recreate
historic voices
and sounds “with the primary purpose
of making the available early Edison
recordings a nearly indestructible and
permanent
part
of
civilization.” The
work
is being done with the coopera-
tion
of the Edison National
Historic
Site, West
Orange,
N.J.,
and
under

f. Power Biggs Month
NEW YORK—May has been declared
E. Power Biggs Month by Columbia
Masterworks, and the
label
is releas-
ing six albums by the renowned organ-
ist.
Highlighting May’s E. Power Biggs
release
is another product of the
or-
ganist’s international search for great
but forgotten instruments of the past,
“Historic
Organs
of
Spain.”
During
the summer
of
1967,
Biggs,
accom-
panied by Columbia Masterworks A&R
director John McClure, Columbia en-
gineers
and
several
tons
of
stereo
recording
equipment, embarked
on a
tour
of
Spain
to
track down
these
noble instruments
surviving over the
past two or three hundred years. They
traveled to such places as Toledo, the
Roman town of Segovia, the university
city of Salamanca, the walled city of
Avila,
Madrid,
Malaga,
Granada,
Valencia, Santiago de Compostela, and
Zaragoza. The result
is an important
addition to Biggs’ series of the historic
organs of Europe and a documentary
of authentic Spanish music.
Biggs
has
written an
introduction
for this recording, giving an account
of the
difficulties and
success
of this
arduous trip.
Handel’s
Sixteen Organ
Concertos
in two three-LP packages (Volume
1
contains Concertos Nos.
1-9 and Vol-
ume
2, Nos. 10-16) are another exam-
ple
of the long and tedious, yet
suc-
cessful,
detective work
accomplished
by Biggs. To find an authentic Handel
organ
took
several
years
of
inquiry
and travel in England. The search end-
ed in Sherwood Forest (of Robin Hood
fame), where an organ was found that
Handel not only had played himself,
but had actually helped design. Thus,
At CoL Masterworks
it was possible for Biggs to play the
Concertos on keys Handel played and
to
produce
the
very
sounds
that he
had heard.
Another
release
this
month
is
“Bach:
The
Six
Trio
Sonatas,” two
separate records of Biggs in his suc-
cessful new
role
as a
pedal
harpsi-
chordist.
Rounding out Columbia’s
offerings
of E. Power Biggs recordings is “Bach
Organ Favorites, Volume 3,” which is
packaged with a free bonus LP, “A
Biggs
Festival.”
The
“Bach
Organ
Favorites” recording continues Biggs’
successful
series of Bach’s most pop-
ular works
for the organ. “A Biggs
Festival”
features
organ
and
pedal-
harpsichord
compositions
of
Bach,
Handel,
Gabrieli,
Soler,
Mozart and
others played on instruments in eight
countries, and
it shows
Biggs’ many
facets
as
virtuoso,
scholar,
explorer
and champion
of the Baroque organ.
Biggs has
previously
explored
the
byways
of
the
organ
literature
in
such albums as “The Golden Age Of
The Organ,” “The Glory Of Gabrieli,”
“The Organ In America,” “A Festival
Of French Organ
Music,” and “The
Historic
Organs Of
Europe-Switzer-
land.”

FOCUS ojir jazz
nnimniiiMifliiiiiniiiuiiiuii
You might wonder, as did my editor,
Irv Lichtman, why
I would choose to
write about a comedy album in a jazz
column. Well, as
I remember, Lenny
Bruce’s most staunch supporters were
jazz
musicians, and
people who dug
jazz. They seemed to
find an
affinity
between their kind of music and what
Lenny
did.
To
them, Lenny
played,
only his horn was
his
facile wit and
his very forthright portrayal of things
as he saw them. This column, however,
is not about Lenny Bruce.
It’s about
Muri’ay Roman, who has picked
it up
where Lenny left
it
off, and his
first
big shot is an album titled, “You can’t
beat people up and have them say
I
LOVE YOU” (Tetragrammaton 101).
In my book GREAT
is a very spe-
cial word and I try to use it sparingly
so that when I feel sufficiently moved
to
do
so,
it
has
added
significance.
Murray’s
album
is GREAT
and
if
what few words
I put together here
will help bring
it to the attention of
people who might not otherwise know
about
it,
then mine must be
consid-
ered
a
public
service.
It’s
a comedy
album, and as the album title implies,
it’s also a social comment. Because of
the
incidence
of
some
four
letter
words
and
the
honest
conscience
of
the material
it’s not the kind
of
al-
bum that will receive a lot of airplay.
So,
it
seems
destined
to
become
a
“word of mouth” best
seller.
I might
have
said
“underground,”
but
that
word would be a disservice to Murray
and
his
colleagues
because
of what-
ever
implications
the
word
“under-
ground”
suggests.
This album
is
as
today
as
right now and
it’s
loaded
with the kind of talent that can stand
the scrutiny of anyone who considers
himself a valid judge of performance.
The only ones who would dissent are
those who
have
their
heads
in
the
sand or who have conscience monkeys
on their backs, because Murray Roman
says
it
just
the way
it
is and
that
can make a lot of people feel uptight.
First Comedy (LP In 8-Track)
Murray Roman has done something
that has never been done before in a
comedy album;
he has
utilized
eight
track stereo and, in so doing, has been
able to incorporate a multitude of spe-
cial
effects,
effects
which
are
com-
pletely interrelated to Murray’s spok-
en words.
Throughout the
entire album there
is a bridge of “down Soul music,” as
Roman
describes
it,
so
that there
is
never
a
void
between
tracks.
This
makes
for
a
complete
performance,
particularly as
all of the music, even
down to the lyrics,
is directly related
to the subject matter with which Mur-
ray
concerns
himself.
“A
beautiful
black man,”
is how Murray Roman
describes
Stu
Gardner,
who
plays
organ, sings, and leads the trio which
supplies
all
the
good
music
that
is
so
much
a
part
of
the
album.
I
shouldn’t be
surprised
if, as a result
of
this
exposure,
Stu
Gardner
gets
an
offer
to do an album
of
his own,
he’s that good.
Inevitably,
the most popular thing
on the album has to be a story Murray
tells about a tour he made with The
Baja Marimba Band.
It’s
one
of the
funniest, most beautifully told stories
I’ve ever heard, on record or
off, and
I’m
a
real
comedy
freak who
has
heard more than
his
share
of funny
stories. He
also
does a thing on the
riots which
is brilliant.
It’s from this
monolog
that
the album
derives
its
title. In
all, there are
sixteen things
that
comprise
the
album,
most
of
which
are
comedy
and
a
couple
of
which
are
pure
social comment, but
all steeped in honesty.
Major
Labels
Scared
Off
The sound on the album
is extraor-
dinary and
credit for
it goes
to two
very young men,
Bruce Dumas
and
David Briggs, who worked with Mur-
ray through the many nights that
it
took to get it done. Murray conceived,
produced, and paid for the album
so,
for
purposes
of
economy,
because
studio
time
is
much
cheaper
from
midnight to dawn,
all
the work was
done during those hours. When it was
completed
it was
offered
to many
of
the major labels, each of whom wanted
to buy
it but were scared
off by the
use
of the four
letter words.
Conse-
quently,
Murray
and
his
manager,
Roy Silver, released it and
it appears
that they will have made a good de-
cision in doing so.
I
find
it extremely
difficult,
in
the
space afforded to this column, to prop-
erly and adequately describe the man,
Murray Roman,
and
his
brain
child
which has become a reality in the form
of this long playing album. The best
possible way
I know to acquaint you
with him and
to whet your
appetite
to want to hear him, either in person
or on
this
recording,
is
to
set down
in
print some quotes from an
inter-
view I had with him last week in New
York:
“I love New York, but I was really
uptight with The Copacabana because
I was
doing
semi-hip Myron
Cohen,
Jewish
guilt,
newlywed,
bedroom
kinda junk Mother-In-Law jokes. For
a long time everybody had said, ‘Man,
you’re
really a
lot funnier when you
come
to my house cause you’re
rap-
pin’
about what you
believe
in
and
what you think is the truth and when
you
get on
the
stage
you’re ...
I
don’t
know.’
And
they
were
right
because when I got on the stage I was
doing my imitation of what I thought,
or
what my
managers
and
agents
thought,
a
comedian
should
sound
like.”
“I believe that this
is a comedy
al-
bum that is NOW!”
“Funny
is
honesty
that
is
exag-
gerated.”
“It’s what
I
relate
to.
I
relate
to
chicks.
I
relate
to bananas.
I
relate
to riots.
I relate to all the things that
are today
for me.
I do not relate
to
newlyweds
and
mother-in-laws.
If
I
had
a
mother-in-law
like
that
I’d
throw her out of the house
in thirty
seconds and
so would
all
the
people

live with us.”
“Somewhere
along
the
line
I
dis-
covered something pretty interesting.
I discovered fhat
it’s more important
to be interesting onstage than to be
funny. That if you’re interesting, and
likeable, people will listen.”
“I’m a rapper.
I really dig smokey
night
clubs and
concert
halls.
I
dig
talking to people.
I really dig making
people laugh,
or making them laugh
with me, or when they look at my life
and the confusion that
I go through
maybe identifying to the extent where
they can say, ‘Wow! That happens to
me,
too.
I
never
thought
anybody
thought of that.’ ”
“While we were promoting the
al-
bum we got to an area on the West
Coast where the program director of
a middle of the road station not only
refused
to
play
the album, which
is
his absolute right, but he negated the
possibility of any deejay or employee
of that station even listening to
it in
their home. A notice was put on the
bulletin board
of that station saying
that
if anyone even
listened
to
that
album in their home they were
fired,
which
is insane. And
I
told the man
that,
in some attempt to protect the
freedom
of
this
country,
or what he
thought was the freedom of this coun-
try, really what he should do, because
I
had
the
solution
for
him, was
to
make sure that we all wore blue cotton
outfits and had a fence around us, just
like China. Then we’d all know where
everybody
was,
because
in
China,
which
is supposedly what he opposed,
that kind of society, there’s never any
problem about what people
listen
to,
is there?”
“What’s
the value
of being Lenny
Bruce,
and
being BRILLIANT,
and
having an audience
of only two peo-
ple?
So
1
try
to
do what Mr. Tom
Smothers
does.
Forget
about where
his
head
is;
Mr.
Smothers
appears
with a short haircut and a red jacket
so that the frame of reference of the
overall public
is such that they’re not

Beatles' Apples Corps Expands
Their World-Wide Interests
NEW YORK—Two
of
the
Beatles,
John
Lennon
and
Paul
McCartney,
flew
to New York from London
last
week
to
announce
the
formation
of
Apple Corps Ltd., a world-wide group
of companies held equally by the four
Beatles, and to hold meetings regard-
ing the establishment of Apple Corps’
U.S.
operation. Lennon and McCart-
new were accompanied by six members
of their executive team: Neil Aspinall,
Brian Lewis, Denis O’Dell, Ron Kass,
Mai Evans and Derek Taylor.
At
a
press
reception
held
at
the
Americana
Hotel
on
Tuesday,
14,

world
markets
for
these
fine
per-
formers.
In 1965, Broderick was appointed to
head up the Country Music Associa-
tion’s International Committee, and in
1967 he was elected to CMA’s Board of
Directors. He
is also a member of the
National
Association
for
Recording
Arts and iSciences (NARAiS).
Prior to joining RCA, Broderick was
in the advertising business and moved
into
sports promotion
as
a National
Advertising and Publicity Director for
athletic and entertainment spectacles.
During this period, he edited and pub-
lished an 8-page newspaper on sports
as well as assisting in network TV as
color commentator.
Leaving the
sports
arena
in
1953,
he published a group of trade papers
for a brief period before joining RCA
in late 1954.

Pop Picks
HONEY—Andy Williams—Columbia CS 9662
Andy
Williams
should
have
no
difficulty
pleasing his large following with his new LP.
Comprised mostly of current and recent hits,
the
set showcases the chanter in one
of his
best
disk performances
to
date.
Highlights
include
the
title
track,
“The
Impossible
Dream,” “Love
Is Blue” and “Up, Up And
Away.” Williams’ warm, romantic renderings
should carry
this
set
to
a high
position on
the charts.
THE ROMANTIC WORLD OF EDDY
ARNOLD—RCA
Victor LPM/LSP
4009
The nickname
“Tennessee
Ploughboy”
no
longer really applies to Eddy Arnold, for his
style and
the
songs he
sings
are nowadays
as frequently in the pop as in the country bag.
Many of the numbers he does appeal to both
markets.
“It’s Over,” the
first track on this
set and Arnold’s latest single, is a pop-country
song,
and
three
of
the
other
outstanding
tracks, “By The
Time
I
Get To
Phoenix,”
“Honey” and “Gentle On My Mind” have hit
both
pop
and
country.
Whatever
changes
Arnold has made, he’s
still a highly popular
artist, and this LP should be a big
one.
Pop Best Bets
JOHN GARY SINGS/JOHN GARY SWINGS
—RCA Victor LPM/LSP 3992
Four members of songster John Gary’s own
family
selected
the
songs
for
this
album.
Judging by Gary’s performance, his relatives
did some
pretty good
choosing. Gary
is
at
home
in
all of the numbers, both the ballads
and the swingers. Top tracks include “A Fog-
gy Day,” “Portrait Of My Love,” “You’re My
Everything” and “I Don’t Want To Set The
World On Fire.” A nice pop-good music
set,
this one
should do
well
in the marketplace.
PARIS BY NIGHT — Paul Mauriat & His
Orchestra — Fantasy 8380
Conductor-arranger Paul Mauriat recorded
this
album
of
songs
associated
with
Paris
before he hit the number 1 spots on the
sin-
gles and album charts with “Love
Is Blue”
and “Blooming
Hits,”
respectively.
Here,
in
lush, lightly swinging
style, are such stand-
ards as “Under Paris Skies,” “April In Paris,”
“Autumn
Leaves,”
and
“Poor
People
Of
Paris.” This LP should generate considerable
sales excitement.
SWEET BEAT— Caterina
Valente— London
PS 536
A legendary figure in the nightclub world,
songstress Caterina Valente always turns
in
an exciting performance. On her latest album,
the
lark lends her
rich contralto
voice
to
a
host of pop
tunes, including songs
of fairly
recent vintage such as the Beatles’ “We Can
Work It Out” and Peter, Paul & Mary’s
hit,
“I Dig Rock ’N’ Roll Music” and old standards
like “OP Man
River”
and
“C’est
Si
Bon.”
Should do nicely saleswise.
HIT TRIP—Charlie Byrd—Columbia CS 9627
Guitarist Charlie Byrd renders
a package
of pop
ditties,
coaxing
a
clear,
clean
tone
from
his
instrument. Among
the
tunes
are
“Love Is Blue,” “Talk To The Animals,” from
the
film
“Doctor
Dolittle,”

This melodious LP figures to score solid sales

JOHHNY CASH AT FOLSOM PRISON —
Columbia CS 9639
This album was recorded at Folsom Prison
in California, and never has Johnny Cash had
more
eager
listeners
than
the
convicts
for
whom he sang and played and
to whom his
music was
like a transfusion. Cash has been
“behind bars a few times” himself
(he gives
an excellent description of prison
life
in the
liner notes), and his rapport with the prison-
ers was
close
and
unaffected. Many
of
the
numbers on the album have to do with prison
and crime: “Folsom Prison Blues,” “Cocaine
Blues,” “Greystone Chapel,”
etc. A powerful
and moving album.
THE TOM JONES FEVER ZONE—Parrot
PAS 71019
There
should be
feverish
sales
activity
in
store for this aptly titled LP by Tom Jones.
The artist sings twelve pop tunes, his power-
ful,
dynamic
voice
creating
the
excitement
for which he
is noted. Included on the set are
“Delilah,”
currently
on
the
charts, “Danny
Boy,” “I Was Made To Love Her,” and “You
Keep Me Hanging On.” Watch this one soar
up the charts.

Leka And Pirn: Hit Writers For
Kama Sutra And The Lemon Pipers
NEW YORK—When
Paul Leka and
Shelley Pinz wrote “Green Tambour-
ine,” they created a song that was to
become Kama
iSutra
Music’s
biggest
item and establish the Lemon Pipers,
who had the hit version of the song on
the Kama
Sutra
organization’s Bud-
dah label, as one of the hottest groups
in the country.
All
this
did not happen
overnight,
however.
Bob
Reno,
general
profes-
sional manager of Kama Sutra Music,
tried
to
place
“Green
Tambourine”
with
a number
of
artists
and
labels
before
it
finally
got
to
the
Lemon
Pipers. At that time, the
Pipers had
already had one single out on Buddah
and were producing themselves. Leka,
whose talents are not limited to song-
writing, produced the
Pipers’ “Green
Tambourine” session himself and has
been their producer ever since.
The
Lemon
Pipers’
waxing
of
“Green
Tambourine” became
an
RI-
AA-certified
million-seller,
and,
to
date, the song has appeared
in seven
additional
single versions and on ap-
proximately two dozen albums. Among
the artists who have recorded “Green
Tambourine” are Lawrence Welk, Les
Brown,
Mrs.
Miller,
the Lennon
Sis-
ters,
Julian
Gold and
the Do Re Mi
Children’s Chorus.
Paul Leka, who writes the melodies,
and Shelley Pinz, who contributes the
words, have been working together for
almost a
year, and during that time
they have
turned
out about twenty-
four songs, including
several for the
Lemon
Pipers’
“Green
Tambourine”
album (among which was the follow-
up to the “Green Tambourine” single,
“Rice
Is
Nice”)
the
Pipers’
current
chart
item,
“Jelly
Jungle,” and ma-
terial
for
the
group’s
second
album,
“Jungle Marmalade”
(not yet
in
re-
lease). Vikki Carr
is scheduled to re-
cord a new Leka-Pinz song in the near
future.
Leka
is currently producing a new
group called the Brooklyn Bridge for
Buddah. First single is due out shortly.

HOLLYWOOD — The soundtrack

the
United
iStates.

(book
type album with three surfaces of full

ers

to

for

sumer use. In addition, giant one sheet

are
also
available
to
dealers for
dis-
play purposes.

Great Britain's Best Sellers
Great Britain
With confusing
regularity the launch
of new
labels continues
in the U.K.
almost on
a weekly
basis and
the mere
fact that the summer
(usually
dull
saleswise)
is approaching
is having no deterrent effect. Just on the market
is
the new Gem label, marketed by Philips, which
is a vehicle specially developed
for Geoff Stephens and John Carter. Formed into a writing/production team,
these two
talents, who together have had several big successes, have penned
and produced
the
first two
releases on the
label—“Conversations” waxed by
A. P. Dangerfield and “Peace” by the Carter-Stephens Chorale. The company’s
policy, however,
is to seek out and foster new recording and composing talent.
Meantime the
first release on Les Reed’s own label, Chapter One,
is set for
May 17th issue. Pressed and distributed through IDecca, Chapter One makes its
bow with “Cry My Heart” by the March Hare. CBS which is rapidly developing
on this front
is pressing and distributing SNB, a new logo being launched by
Simon Napier
Bell, manager of the Yardbirds.
First release
is “No Need
to
Explain” by Flamma Sherman. A little further ahead Liberty Records is setting
the
launch
of
the
Sunset
logo,
a
low-price album range
retailing
at
17/6d
($2.10).
Initial
release, inked
in for August,
will comprise 25 LP’s including
works by Jan and Dean, Slim Whitman, Johnny Burnett, Rick Nelson, Johnnie
Ray and Fats Domino.
Having started with one record retail outlet some
five years ago, Beat and
Commercial Records Ltd. have now expanded into a growing concern embracing-
manufacture, production, retailing and publishing. Their three labels, Coxsone,
Amalgamated Records (GB)
Ltd. and Blue Cat, are specialist labels with ma-
terial taken from Jamaican masters and directed at the West Indian population
in the U.K.
In June they are turning
their
attention
to a more
pop-slanted
label
(Action) which will be
r & b
oriented.
Distribution
is handled through
Island and Philips Records. A music publishing outlet, B & C Music, will also
start operations
in June.
Adrian Rudge (formerly of Page One Records) and Tony Palmer (ex EMI)
have joined forces to form Finito—a promotion/management/production com-
pany.
They have got off to a good start with Jacky (for whom they act as managers
and producers) who is currently in the Top Ten with “White Horses” on Philips.
They have
also
taken
on
the
U.K.
promotion
of Buddy
Greco. Rudge
and
Palmer will be visiting the States later in the month for talks with major and
indie record manufacturers with a view to setting up lease tape deals.
Peter Phillips of KPM Music
is delighted with his company’s chart success
at the moment having got
5
in the Top
20. Peter, accompanied by his father
Jimmy Phillips, plans a Stateside visit at the end of May to seek and acquire
new material.
The independent Transatlantic Records, headed here by Nathan Joseph,
is to
issue a sample album Audio
Fidelity Stereo Showcase featuring some
of the
best tracks from Audio Fidelity albums available
in the U.K. Advance orders
in excess of 15,000 were received three weeks before release date (May 31st).
The newly-formed
the Pentangle—a
five member group
including celebrated
Bert Jansch and John Renbourn make
their debut on
Transatlantic’s Big T
label with “Travellin’ Song” and an album “The Pentangle,” both produced by
indie Shel Talmy. The group have a tight schedule of TV and concert dates in
the U.K. and plane to Oslo May 30th for TV. John Renbourn’s solo album—-wait
for
it—“SirJohnA LotOfMerrieEnglandsMusikThyngeAndYeGreneKnyghte”
pheew!—is selling at a terrific rate and
is already in Top 50 folk charts.
“One
of the most elegant receptions
of the year”
is how the Welcome
to
Britain party hosted by
Jeff Kruger of Ember Records at the Carlton Tower
Hotel was described. Voted “Top Male Singer”
in the country & western cate-
gory in the recent Grammy Awards, Campbell packed numerous radio, TV and
personal appearances
into
his two week stay including
a
spot
in the Bobbie
Gentry TV Spectacular. His current single on Ember
is
“I Wanna Live” and
an album
is being rush-released.
Mike Vernon of Blue Horizon currently in America visiting Chicago and New
Y
Tork
seeking and
recording
potential
artists
for
release
in
the
U.K.
Also
finalizing plans for the month-long tour of clubs by the Fleetwood Mac in June.
“Fleetwood Mac” has been a consistent best seller in the British LP charts and
is now issued in the U.'S. on Epic. Vernon will also have discussions with Gene
Goodman re Goody Two Shoes Music—a subsidiary of the Chappell Organiza-
tion—which publishes most of the material on Blue Horizon.
Ben Nisbett just back from ten days
in New York and Hollywood visiting
the Francis Day & Hunter offices. He also negotiated a deal with Artie Mogull
of the newly-formed Tetragrammaton Company which gives Feldmans complete
involvement in the diversification of the whole Tetag-rammaton empire.
Frank Fenter, who recently left the post of A & R chief at Polydor Records
in order to take up full time representation of Atlantic Records in Europe, has
set up his own independent Zip Code Productions. He will continue to operate
from the Polydor HQ as Atlantic label manager but will now also undertake
publishing, artists’ management and indie production.
Quickies:
Cliff Richard opened a season at the Talk Of The Town May 13th
.
.
. Decca issue Frankie Davidson’s “Hector The Trash Collector,” a
hit for
Davidson
in Australia
.
.
. After a whirlwind tour of Europe, Aretha Franklin
flew into London for two concerts and a reception hosted by Atlantic Records
.
.
. The Association, also in London, were guests of Pye Records who issue new
single “Time For Livin’ ”... Another American visitor Erroll Garner here for
concerts and TV
.
.
. French singer Sacha
Distel
in London coincidental with
first MCA release “Writing On The Wall,” an English adaptation of his French
hit “Monsieur Cannibale”
.
.
. “What A Wonderful World” topping Best Selling
Sheet Music Lists for Valando Music
.
.
. The Music Trades Association reveal
that
last year combined music industry
sold instruments and
records
to the
value of around £70,000 ($168,000,000). Half of the total was exported
.
.
. The
Foundations currently on four-week tour of American cities followed by Tahiti,
Australia, Japan, Manila, Hong Kong, Singapore, Ceylon,
Beirut, Cyprus and
Israel.

International News Report
A&M Expands Logo Identity In Latin Area
HOLLYWOOD—The A&M
logo
will
appear in 24 countries in Latin Amer-
ica
as
the
result
of the appointment
of four new international
affiliates
in
the area. Further production and pro-
motion
are
seen,
according
to David
Hubert, A&M’s international director,
through this Latin expansion.
The
new
affiliates
are
Industria
Electricas E. Musicais, Fabrica Odeon
(EMI)
for Brazil: RCA Victor Mexi-
cana
for
Mexico,
Central
America,
Colombia, Ecuador,
Peru:
El
Palacio
De La Musica, S.A. for Venezuela and
EMI Suppliers (Sud America)
S.A.C.
el for Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay,
Bolivia and Chile. Announcement was
made by David Hubert,
international
director for A&M.
Artist Promo
Planned
Hubert stated that many A&M
re-
cording artists are already established
in the Latin American countries, they
include
Herb
Alpert &
the
Tijuana
Brass, The Sandpipers, Chris Montez,
Sergio Mendes and Brasil ’66 and An-
tonio
Carlos
Jobim.
Hubert
is
also
planning
promotional
campaigns
to
enhance
the
popularity
of
these
ar-
tists, but
in
addition
to
this he
will
begin concentrated promotion on Tom-
my
Boyce
and
Bobby
Hart,
Julius
Wechter and the Baja Marimba Band,
Wes Montgomery,
Liza
Minnelli and
other A&M artists in due time. Addi-
tional
artists from the
Creed Taylor
package which includes, Herbie Mann,
The
Soul
Flutes,
Artie
Butler, Tam-
ba
4 and Paul Desmond
will
also be
included
in
this promotion campaign
and
expansion.
To
begin
this
promotion,
Sergio
Mendes
and
Brasil
’66
will make
a
concert tour appearance
in
Brazil
in
the later part of June as well as The
Sandpipers making a concert tour ap-
pearance
in Caracas, Rio De Janeiro,
San Paulo, Venezuela and Argentina.
Charles Lloyd Group To
Far East For State Dept.
Monument Sets Teichiku
As Licensee In Japan
NEW YORK — The
Charles
Lloyd
Quartet,
fresh
from
its
first
prime
time TV appearance
(Bell Telephone
Hour,
April
26)
left
last week
for
the Far
East under
the
auspices
of
the Offices of Cultural Presentations of
the
U.S.
State
Department.
Seven
week tour opens in Okinawa, May 15,
and
continues
through
Hong
Kong,
Bangkok,
Vientiane,
Kuala
Lumpur,
Penang,
Singapore and
Manila.
The
group
is
already
in
Japan,
where manager George Avakian has
set
concerts
in
Tokyo,
Nagoya
and
Osaka. Following the
final
State De-
partment concert June
28, the group
will
probably
play
in
Australia and
Honolulu before returning to the U.S.
for the Philadelphia Musical Festival
at JFK
Stadium.
During
its
Far
Eastern
tour,
the
Quartet will appear on radio and tele-
vision as well as play concerts in local
halls
and
outdoor
arenas.
Visits
to
universities,
music
schools,
and
ex-
change performances with
local mu-
sicians are also planned.
Lloyd, who made
history with
six
European tours in 1966-1967 including
the breakthrough
at the
Soviet Jazz
Festival, has crossed the line for jazz
to pop without any change in the mu-
sic which made him “Jazzman of the
Year”—in last year’s Down Beat Read-
ers’
Poll. So great
is
Lloyd’s appeal
to
college, auditorium and light-show
audiences
that
the
group
has
not
played a jazz club in over a year. The
Quartet’s
last
American
appearance
before
leaving
for
the
Pacific
was
typical of
its offbeat engagement: the
finale
of
Hunter
College’s
longhair
“New Images of Sound”
series, shar-
ing
a program
with
films
featuring
the music
of John
Cage, Edgar Va-
rese
and
Harry
Partch.

Evans
Trio At Jazz Fest
NEW YORK—The Bill Evans Trio has
been
selected
as
the
only American
jazz
instrumental group
to
play
the
Montreux Jazz
Festival. The
festival
is considered to be one of the biggest,
most
important
jazz
festivals
to
be
presented
in
Europe
this
year.
His
performance, on June 15 in Montreux,
Switzerland,
will be recorded for
re-
lease later this year by Verve Records.
Evans’ manager, Helen Keane, will ac-
company
the
artist

RCA Stereo 8 Campaign In Italy w/
Gas Stations,, Cartridge Player Co.
MILAN—RCA
Italiana
is
preparing
a big promotion and exploitation cam-
paign on the
Stereo
8 cartridge.
In an interview with Giuseppe Or-
nato, Cash Box has learned that RCA
has
tied-in
with
Agip,
the
gasoline
company, and Voxson, manufacturers
of tape cartridge machines to introduce
the Stereo 8 cartridge system through-
out
the
entire
chain
of Agip
filling
stations in Italy.
Agip
is the Italian National Petrol
Company,
associated
with
the
state
firm ENI. They
are
the
only
Italian
gasoline producers, and
for
this
rea-
son Agip owns a large chain of filling
stations. According
to the agreement
just signed, as a first step 1,000 filling
stations
on
all
the
most
important
routes will be equipped with a Stereo 8
cartridges self service system; as sec-
ond
step
all other Agip
stations
will
also be authorized to sell Stereo 8 mu-
sic cartridges.
Voxson has manufactured a special
Stereo 8 tape recorder; the
series in-
cludes different models; some of them
are radio sets and tape-recorder. They
are
sold
at a competitive
price. The
lowest
retail
price
for a Voxson
set
has been fixed at Liras 45.000
(about
$72)
while
the
highest
price reaches
Liras
115.000
($185).
Voxson
sets
are
considered among
the best
car tape recorders available
on
the
Italian market
either for the
very high fidelity sound reproduction,
as well for the
simplicity of use and
for the small
size of the
set.
Together with the cartridge display,
Voxson
has
equipped
Agip
stations
with a special cartridge tape recorder,
in order to give customers the oppor-
tunity to listen to the cartridges they
are buying.
The RCA
Stereo
8
cartridges
are
sold at a price of 4.980 Liras
(about
$8). An interesting point
is that Ste-
reo 8 customers can exchange in every
Agip station their old cartridges with
new
ones,
paying
only
Liras
500
(about
82!tf')
in
return
for
their
old
cartridges.
The deal was conceived by Giuseppe
Ornato
and
the
contract
has
been
signed by him with
Danilo
Accivile,
Agip general manager, and with Ar-
naldo
Piccinini,
president
of Voxson.
A strong promotional campaign un-
der
the
logo
“Give Me
Music And
Petrol”
has
been
planned
by
Agip.
Advertising
campaign
includes
all
Italian daily papers and magazines.
The Agip
filling
stations
equipped
with the “Stereo 8” cartridges service
will have a special identification plate:
a black musical note on a yellow field
and the words “Stereo 8.”
The number
of
Stereo
8
tape
re-
corder
sets already
sold
in Italy
are
estimated at 50,000 units, but Voxson,
thanks to this special service and the
promotional campaign involved
in
it,
predicts for the first year of the agree-
ment a production of at least 200,000
sets.
Aretha Triumphs On 1st Euro Concerts
NEW YORK—Aretha Franklin’s
first
European
concert
tour, which wound
up in London May
11, was a big suc-
cess. The
Atlantic
Records’ hitmaker
played
to turnaway crowds
at every
performance
in the
six
countries she
visited on the
tour, and cracked
rec-
ords in some of the houses she played.
In Rotterdam, where she gave two
concerts
at
the
Concertgebouw,
she
played to standees at both shows. In
Montreaux,
Switzerland,
she
topped
the
bill at the Casino for the Golden
Rose Festival
(Eurovision). She drew
thousands of fans to the Jahrundert-
halle in Frankfurt, Germany, and set
a new
house
record.
The
artist’s
two
performances
at
the
Olympia
Theater
in
Paris
were
among
the
high
spots
of
her
tour.
She
filled
the
huge
auditorium
for
both
shows,
playing
to
over
15,000
Parisian
soul
fans.
Two
days
later
she packed Bene’s Solanger in Stock-
holm,
performing
before
more
than
12,000
cheering
followers.
She wound up
her
tour with two
concerts in London; one at the Astoria
in
that
city
and
the
other
at
the
Odeon-Hammersmith.
At
both
con-
certs
Aretha
received
standing
ova-
tions that lasted for 15 minutes. Ac-
cording
to
Frank
Fenter,
Atlantic’s
European rep, her appearance in Lon-
don was among the most exciting mu-
sicals
event
to
occur
there
in
over
a year.

Pepsi's Contribution Waters 'Roots Of Jazz
imiiniiniiiiiniiiuiinnniiniiiniiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii^^
FOCUS ON JAZZ
giiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiimniiiniimininiiiiniRUiiiiiniiiiiiiniiiiiiiiiiiiiiuiinffl
ffp.a
HAMPTON, VA.—A program entitled
“The Roots
of Jazz” has been made
possible by
a
contribution by
Pepsi-
Cola
to
the Hampton
Institute
Jazz
Festival. This program, which will be
held on Thursday, June
27,
in Ogden
Hall on the Hampton Institute campus
will trace the background and roots of
jazz.
It will feature the Original Tuxedo
Jazz Band,
direct from New Orleans
and one of the legendary exponents of
New Orleans
jazz. The country blues
will be represented by blues guitarist
and
singer
Skip
James.
The
urban
blues of Chicago will be demonstrated
by Muddy Waters and his Blues Band.
The
great
“stride” and
“rent-party”
pianist
Willie “the Lion” Smith
will
also perform.
The climax of the program will be
the
appearance
of
the
great
Earl
“Fatha” Hines and his Quintet. Hines
is
one
of
the
greatest
pianists
that
jazz has produced and has been an im-
portant
figure
in the history
of jazz
since
the
1920’s
when
he
was
co-
leader
of
the
famous
Louis
Arm-
strong-Earl “Fatha” Hines Hot Seven.
Many of the greatest personalities of
jazz got their start with the big bands
that “Fatha”
led
in the
thirties and
forties. Included in the Hines alumni
are
Billy
Eckstine,
Charlie
Parker,
Dizzy
Gillespie,
J.
J. Johnson, Sarah
Vaughan and a host of others.
This program
could not have been
possible without the above mentioned
contribution of Pepsi-Cola.
“The Roots of Jazz” on June 27
is
the first of the three evening concerts
that constitute the first Hampton Jazz
Festival, which is produced by Hamp-
ton
Institute
in
association with the
famed Newport Jazz Festival of New-
port, Rhode Island. The Friday even-
ing,
June
28
concert
will
feature
Dionne Warwick, Herbie Mann, Wes
Montgomery,
Cannonball
Adderley,
Archie Bhepp, and Thelonious Monk.
The Saturday evening, June
29,
con-
cert will feature Jimmy Smith, Ram-
sey
Lewis,
Dizzy
Gillespie,
Count
Basie, Gary Burton, and Nina Simone.
The
Friday
and
Saturday
evening
concerts will be held under the stars in
Armstrong Stadium on the Hampton
Institute campus in a musical amphi-
theater
specially
constructed
for the
festival.
For
information,
write
Hampton
Jazz
Festival,
Box
6289,
Hampton,
Virginia 23368.

Nat'I Promo Mgr.
For Blue Note
LOS ANGELES—Blue Note Records
has appointed A1 Riley
to the newly
created
post
of
national
promotion
manager.
Riley’s appointment
is part
of what the
label
calls a “major
ex-
pansion of jazz product emphasis.”
Riley, who attended New York Uni-
versity, went to work for Liberty Rec-
ords Inc. five years ago in the shipping
department of the New York Branch.
He advanced through the sales and
promotion departments and,
until
his
appointment
to
the
Blue
Note
post,
was
regional
promotion man
for
all
Liberty
Records
Inc.
jazz
and R&B
product.
Riley will headquarter
at the Blue
Note offices at 1776 Broadway in New
York.
He will report directly to Blue Note
general manager Fuhrman.

Looking over last week’s Cash Box
list
of
the
top
one
hundred
albums,
it
became
apparent
that
there
was
a comparative absence of jazz albums
on that
list. Actually, of the top one
hundred,
only two
could
be
honestly
classified
as
jazz albums.
It depress-
ed me
and
it
posed
the
question
in
my
mind, “What
has become
of
all
the heros in jazz?”
No More Big Jazz Record
Sellers
Until
very
recently
there
has
al-
ways
been more
than
a
handful
of
jazz
albums
numbered
among
the
best
sellers,
a
Brubeck,
a
Basie,
a
Miles
Davis,
a
Stan
Getz, a Ramsey
Lewis,
a Horace
Silver.
I
reflect
on
the
excitement
that
was
generated
by people
like Lester Young, Charlie
Parker,
Dizzy
Gillespie, Bud
Powell,
Thelonius Monk, and
so many
others
of
that
ilk.
True,
they were
all
in-
novators
and,
as
such,
they
merited
that kind
of
adulation, but
the
sud-
den
realization
that
among
today’s
jazz
players
there
is
no
one
who
towers above
the
others, as
reflected

sales,
makes

wonder
where
the
responsibility
lies.
Have
the
record
companies
forsaken
their
jazz
artists
for
the
more
lucrative
fields of pop and folk? Have the jazz
musicians
played
themselves
into
a
corner, whence
the buying public be-
comes smaller and smaller? Have
to-
day’s
young
pop
artists,
borrowing
from
jazz
and
incorporating
jazz
in
their
music,
lured away what would
have become
the new
corps
of
jazz
devotee ?
Assuming
that
some
of
this
conjecture
is
fact, how can
the
situation
be remedied ? How can
the
outstanding
jazz
artist
be
restored
to that elevated
position where more
than mediocre album sales
is the best
he can hope for?
Rock Groups Now
Playing
Jazz
It’s my
feeling
that
the
fusion
of
jazz
into
today’s
pop
music
is
the
main
reason
that much
of
the new
jazz audience has been usurped. Pre-
viously,
after
serving
his
listening
apprenticeship with
rock
’n
roll,
the
natural gravitation was to jazz. Rock
’n roll graduates were the most likely
prospects
for
recruitment
into
the
world
of
jazz
and
college
kids,
as
well as all kids of that age, represent-
ed the most fertile area for new jazz
market.
This
is
not
to
suggest
that
today’s
young
people
are
no
longer
embracing
jazz,
but
certainly
not
in
the numbers that they have in the not
too distant past. The transition from
pop
music
to
jazz
has
been
made
much
easier
for
the
young
listener
by
the
presence
of
such
groups
as
The Jefferson Airplane, Blood, Sweat
&
Tears,
The
Rascals,
The
Electric
Flag,
and many
other
such
groups
that number among their members ex-
cellent musicians with an imaginative
flair
for
jazz.
Consequently,
another
plateau of listening has been inserted
in
the
evolution from
pop
music
to
jazz, a more gradual
rate
of growth
which,
for
the
most
part,
is
more
comprehendible
and
more
easily
di-
gested.
Coupled
with
this
is
the
fact that such as the above-mention-
ed groups concern themselves, by use
^
of lyrics, with the matters of the day,
to which young people can easily re-
i
late.
i

Christopher Crist

HIGH PRESSURE BLUES — Freddie Hub-
bard—Atlantic SC 1501
Here’s an exciting set that should help to
increase Freddie Hubbard’s reputation. Hub-
bard plays trumpet
(and fluegelhorn on one
number), and four
of the
six compositions,
including the potent title track, are his own.
His playing is lyrical, often poignantly sweet.
As a composer, he can convey strong emotions
effectively
and
“swing”
in

carefree manner. Could be big jazz
sales
in
store for
this LP. Watch
it.

EVELYNE CROCHET PLAYS ERIK SATIE
—Philips PHS 900—179
During his lifetime, French composer Erik
Satie
(1866-1925) was
criticized for his lack
of form and regarded as an eccentric of little
significance. Today, he fares somewhat better,
and the charm and power of his dry, straight-
forward works are becoming increasingly re-
cognized.
On
this
album,
Evelyne
Crochet
gives
an
excellent
performance
of
thirteen
of Satie’s piano pieces. Some of the titles are
strange
(“New
Cold
Cuts,”
“Canine
Pre-
lude”),
but
the music
is
not.
Should
be
of
interest
to many
classical
listeners.

Bovema started an enormous action promoting the French chansons. Label
manager Theo Roos released a.o. albums of Charles Aznavour, Mireille Mathieu,

_ “Chante

“Lookin’ Ahead”
is the
title of the new album of the Dutch top group the
Buffoons. No less than fourteen tracks adorn this wonderful album which will be
a massive seller! The latest single “Sunday Will Never Be The Same” reached
the Dutch Top 20 in two weeks. The American soul singer Lou Rawls was wel-
comed
in Holland by Bovema’s General Label Manager Mr. Roel Kruize and
Capitol label manager Mr. Joop Visser. He taped a half hour color television
' show, accompanied by a Dutch

will be Bovema’s
Jazz
month. A wonderful campaign has been
de-
signed by Joop
Visser. Highlights are the promotion albums featuring John

The songs and artists have been finally chosen for the preliminary rounds of
the new “German Pop Music Contest” with the finals being held in Berlin on
July 4th. The three juries choose 26 songs from the hundreds of entries and, of
course, 26
artists have been chosen as well. The artists are Anna-Lena from
Metronome, France
Gall,
Teldec; Marc
Bertrand,
Liberty;
Nilseii
Brothers,
Richter GmbH; Jacqueline Boyer, Cornet; Mary Roos, Electrola; Gisela Marell,
Metronome; Peter Orloff, Cornet; Siw Malmkvist, Metronome; Jurgen Herbst,
CBS; Christiane, Teldec; Corry Brokken, Deutsche Grammophon; Renate Kem,
Deutsche Grammophon;
the Jacob
Sisters, CBS; Graham Bonney,
Electrola;
the Leismanns, Ariola; Inga, Teldec; Cryin’ Strings, Vogue; Sigi Hoppe, Ariola;
Dorthe, Phonogram; Tonia, Teldec; Rex Gildo, Ariola; Helmut Schmidt, Vogue
and Howard Carpendale, Electrola.
12 songs and artists will be chosen for the finals and you’ll get a first hand
report on the event as
it happens in this column in Cash Box.
Rock and roll seems to be making headway in Germany as the discotheques
and dealers report heavy action on old rock disks. Teldec is leading the way right
now with “Peggy Sue” by Buddy Holly and “Rock Around The Clock” from
Bill Haley. The firm has also released LPs by Buddy Holly, Bill Haley, Little
Richard, Elvis Presley and Jerry Lee Lewis featuring the
old rock and
roll
goodies.
Teldec is now celebrating the opening of their new pressing plant in Nortorf.
The plant can turn out 100,000 records
in one
shift and
is the most modem
pressing facility in Europe at this time.
Both
Peter
Meisel
of Hansa Productions and
Teldec
are beaming
at
the
prospect
of the upcoming
celebration on June
5th
in
Berlin. On that
date,
recording ace Manuela (who Hansa produces and Teldec distributes)
will re-
ceive a golden record for 4 million sold records during her career. The young
star has never made a disc that has sold less than 100,000. Whew!
Teldec also announces the
sale
of over 300,000 records
sold on Tom Jones’
version of “Delilah” with France Gall racking up 60,000 sales for her “A Banda.”
“Fiddler On The Roof”
in German has passed the 30,000 LP
sales mark and
“Stereo A La Carte” featuring
the
English Decca Phase
4
Stereo sound
is
over the 40,000 mark in LP sales.
Liberty Records has obtained the services of well known Heinz Lukas as head
of the promotion division. Heinz will head up the press, public relations,
etc.,
for the firm. He formerly worked in a similar capacity at Philips Records and
has for the last few years written one of Germany’s most popular pop music
columns for a Berlin newspaper.
The
last
trip
of Phonogram’s teenage
star Vicky
to Japan was
a smash
success. Vicky traveled there
to personally pick up her “Pop Music
Statue”
award and followed the ceremony with 14 TV shots and 22 radio interviews. The
18-year-old
talented miss
is
really
on
her way
to
a fabulous
international
career.
Aberbach Music put out a special listing of the top “Oldies But Goodies” that
they publish
in the wave of the new rock and
roll craze which
is also being
heavily felt here
in Germany.
Deutsche Vogue
is giving the big push to Swiss Miss Arlette Zola who has
now recorded her first German language record and will follow
it up doing a
major discotheque tour.
Alfred Schacht is really going to town with push platters “Ain’t Nothing But
A Houseparty” from the Show Stoppers and “Elevator/ “Yes” by the Grapefruit
leading the way. The Hamburg publisher
is
pulling out
all promotion stops
for the two disks.
The new Maris Records out of Berlin seems to have a hit on their hands as
the first recording by the label of Norman Ascot has been in the local hit parade
now for
five weeks running. The young
star
will have
his TV
start as well
with the popular “Studio B” show this week.
Hans Gerig Music has a double hit on its hands as the Cliff Richard Eurovision
smash “Congratulations” enters the top ten twice this week. The English and
the German versions of the song are now in the chart.
Larry Yaskiel, managing director of Stigwood-Yaskiel International, dropped
us a
line to say that this
is the m.ost successful month
in the history of the
young company with 10 records under the top 40. The records are spread over
several American
firms
as
well
as
the German
ones. The
hits
are “Simon
Says” and “Green Tambourine” on Buddah. “A Banda” with Herb Alpert on
A&M, “Der Graf Von Luxemburg” with Dorthe on
Philips, as well as “Cin-
derella
Rockefella”
with
Esther &
Abi
Ofarim
and
“Mighty
Quinn”
with
Manfred Mann.
Polydor
is represented with “Jumbo” by the Bee Gees, along with “World”
and “Words” and the Move with “Fire Brigade.” The only promotion firm
in
Germany has also acquired the Chess /Checker/Cadet labels for D.G.G. and the
“Horizontal” LP from the Bee Gees leads the LP hit parade in Germany. The
other Bee Gees album
is also
still under the top 10.
Larry’s two
latest
projects
are Bobby
Goldsboro whom
Stigwood-Yaskiel
could swing into Germany for a quick TV shot with his song “Honey” and a new
group being launched by Polydor called the Wonderland.
That’s
it for this week
in Germany.

3uddah Sets
1st Confab; Rock Ork There
NEW YORK—June 7-9 is the time set
t'or the nine month-old Buddah label’s
ni’st convention, to be held at the City
Squire Motor Inn here in N.Y.
Billed as “Buddah’s
Little Conven-
tion”, the conclave will be a gathering
of distributors, promotional and sales
personnel for three days
of business
and sport.
Buddah
will
fill the three-day con-
clave
with
presentations
of
product,
announcements
of
artist
signings,
guest speakers and entertainment. The
convention
presentation
will
be
con-
ducted by general manager Neil Bog-
art,
director of R & B
activity
Cecil
Holmes, and
director
of pop
activity
Marty Thau.
Bogart said the convention will kick
off
Friday
night
at
Carnegie
Hall
where
the
46-man
Kasenetz-Katz
Singing
Orchestral
Circus —
the
world’s
first rock symphony orchestra
—will premiere in a Buddah promotion
for an audience of distributors, promo
reps, sales personnel, radio delegates,
the
consumer,
fan
and
trade
press,
talent buyers and industry leaders.
New LP’s
Saturday morning will see the pre-
sentation
of Buddah’s new album re-
leases, headlined by the “Orginal cast
Album” of the Kasenetz-Katz Singing
Orchestral
Circus.
“Jungle
Marme-
lade” by the Lemon Pipers, “Yummy,
Yummy, Yummy”
by
the
Ohio
Ex-
press,
“Finders
Keepers”
by
Salt
Water
Taffy,
“Classmates”
and
“Checkmates”,
two
anthology
LPs
featuring Buddah’s hottest artists, and
“Zalman Yanovsky Is Alive And Well
In Argentina”, the album debut of the
former Lovin’ Spoonful lead guitarist.
Previewed at the convention will be
Team Records, the new
label
distrib-
uted by Buddah for the product of in-
dependent
producers
Jerry
Kasenetz
and Jeffrey Katz. Buddah recently in-
troduced the new Cobblestone Records,
with debuts by Alohe Burke, sister of
the
Five
Stairsteps,
and
the
Boss
Blues.
Saturday evening Buddah will host
the conventioneers
to an all-expense-
paid “night at the races” at Roosevelt
Raceway,
followed by a
blast-out
at
the
Rolling
Stone
discotheque where
Buddah
will
introduce
the
14-piece
Brooklyn Bridge.
Guest
speakers
at
the
convention
will
include
Kal
Rudman,
George
Lorenze
of “Behind The
Scenes”, A1
Herscowitz
of WPRO
radio.
Provi-
dence,
and
Dick
Starr
from KYA
radio, San Francisco.
Art
Kass,
executive
vice
president
of Kama Sutra and Buddah Records,
reported that sales for the
first nine
months
of
Buddah’s
operation
have
passed
7,000,000
singles
and
500,000
LPs.
Hits
So far, Buddah has racked up three
top
ten
hits,
“Green
Tambourine”
(Lemon
Pipers),
“Yummy, Yummy,
Yummy”
(Ohio Express) and “iSimon
Says”
(1910
Fruitgum
Company).
The Pipers and Fruitgum singles have
been certified as million-sellers by the
RIAA but their total sales are closer
to
the
2,000,000
mark.
Other
chart
singles for Buddah have included three
by
the
Five
Stairsteps
&
Cubie
(“iSomething’s
Missing”,
“A
Million
To
One”,
“The
Shadow
of
Your
Love”), the 1910 Fruitgum Company
(“May
I Take A
Giant
Step”),
the
Lemon Pipers
(“Rice
Is Nice”, “Jelly
Jungle”),
and
Zally Yanovsky
(“As
Long As You’re Here”). Buddah has
also scored
in the LP charts with
al-
bums by
the Lemon
Pipers
(“Green
Tambourine”),
the
1910
Fruitgum
Company
(“Simon
Says”)
and
the
Five Stairsteps & Cubie (“Our Family
Portrait”).

Humperdinck new

Neckar Upped At Liberty
LOS ANGELES—Liberty Records has
named David Neckar general manager
of
the
diskery’s
production
depart-
ment, it was announced by Irv Kessler,
vice president of the label.
Neckar was
in the production con-
trol departments
of RCA Victor Rec-
ords and was production control man-
ager
and
distribution
manager
for
Mercury Records
in Richmond, Ind.
He received his education at Indiana
State
University, majoring
in math-
ematics and physical science and also
attended Earlham
College,
Executive
Training
Institute.
Neckar will report to Kessler.

carried in last week’s review.

Allan Dale To Green-Stone
As Eastern Rep, GPM
NEW
YORK—Charles
Greene
and
Brian
Stone have named Allan Dale
as head
of
east
coast operations
for
their
York-Pala
and
Greene /Stone
production
outfit
as
well
as
general
professional
manager
of
their
Ten-
East,
Five-West
(both
BMI,)
and
Fifth
Avenue
(ASCAP)
publishing
firms. In addition to his being eastern
liaison man
for
Greene
and
Stone,
Dale will supervise press coverage to
the
trades,
the consumer
press,
and
the
underground
press
on
the
East
Coast for
all acts under the Greene/
Stone banner.
Greene and Stone are
currently
in
New York for confabs with Dale, re-
lating
to
the
selection
of temporary
office space for the interim period re-
quired for the restoration and refurb-
ishing of their proposed mid-Manhat-
tan, Brownstone
office complex. Dale
will be based in New York, reporting
directly
to
Greene and
Stone
at the
Los Angeles headquarters of the com-
panies.
The Greene /iStone pubberies include
catalog by such writers
as:
Geolfrey
Stevens,
iSonny
Bono,
and
Charles
Marawood,
in addition
to
substantial
catalog by the Iron Butterfly and the
Buffalo
Springfield.
Included
among
the acts currently under the Greene/
Stone
aegis,
are:
the Cake
(Decca);
the
Rose
Garden
(Atco)
;
Geoffrey
Stevens (Decca)
: Two Guitars, Piano,
Drum & Daryll
(Atlantic);
the Poor
(Decca);
and
the
Iron
Butterfly
(Atco.) The Greene /Stone duo
is par-
ticularly well known for having been
influential
in
the
initial
rise
to
na-
tional prominence
of: Sonny &
Cher,
the Troggs, Bob Lind, and the Buffalo
Springfield.
Dale, who has most recently been a
writer on the
editorial
staff
of Cash
Box
Magazine,
was
previously
em-
ployed by Grove Press
and,
prior
to
that, spent several years engaged
in
folk music
research,
having
concen-
trated
his
efforts
primarily
in
the
Southern
Appalachin
regions. He
is
married
and
the
father
of two
chil-
dren.

have

will
also
attend.
Mansfield, Smith
Promoted By CROC
NEW YORK—Capitol
Records
Dis-
tributing Corp. has promoted Kenneth
F.
Mansfield
to
the
post
of
national
promotion
manager,
according
to an
announcement
by
Robert
L.
Yorke,
vice president and general manager of
the firm. At the same time, the com-
pany
has
promoted
Bobby
Smith
to
chain store coordinator in New York.
In
his new capacity Mansfield
will
be
responsible
for
all CRDC promo-
tional
services
and
the
coordination
thereof.
Reporting
directly
to Mans-
field
will be the east and west coast-
based artist relations departments, ra-
dio and TV
services department, and
the field promotion department, which
supervises
Capitol’s
complete
promo-
tional staff.
Since
joining
Capitol
in
January,
1964,
as
district promotion manager,
Mansfield
has
held
positions
of mer-
chandising
project
manager,
single
records merchandising manager, and
A&R producer
for
specially
assigned
acts.
Prior to his association with Capitol,
Mansfield
was
affiliated
with
Cubic
Corp.
in
San
Diego. He owned
and
managed “The Land
of Oden”
night
club there and was
a member of the
Town Criers, an Ava Records record-
ing group.
Mansfield
graduated
with
a
B.S.
degree
in marketing from San Diego
State in June,
1961.
Reporting directly to Ralph Schecht-
man, CRDC’s New York district sales
manager,
Smith
will
implement
the
promotion
of
upcoming
product
for
maximum
exposure
in
chain
stores
and multi-outlet retail operations.
Smith came to Capitol
in 1966 and
has served in New York as the label’s
singles promotion man.

3 Special Concerts Set For Newport
NEW YORK—Festival Field, a thirty
acre plot on the outskirts of Newport,
Rhode Island that seats 18,000 people,
will again be the cite of the Newport
Jazz Festival (July 4-7) and the New-
port Folk
Festival
(July
23-28)
and
also,
this year,
of three
special
one-
night
performances
by
Harry
Bela-
fonte
(July
20),
Andy
Williams
(August 3) and Herb Alpert and the
Tijuana
Brass
(August
10).
George
Wein
is the producer of the festivals
and of the three special concerts.
Jazz Festival
Highlight of the Jazz Festival
will
be the “Schlitz Salute To Big Bands”
Friday evening, July
5. The evening
will encompass
over
thirty
years
of
big band
history
and
will
bring
to-
gether Count
Basie, Duke
Ellington,
and Woody Herman and
their
ever-
green orchestras. Dizzy
Gillespie will
reassemble
his
big band
for
the
oc-
casion.
Special
guests
will
include
Charlie
Barnet,
Tex
Beneke,
Benny
Carter,
Erskine
Hawkins,
and
Jack
Leonard. Also, producer Wein has in-
vited
the winners
of
big band
com-
petitions
at Notre Dame and
M.I.T.
to participate. The afternoon sessions
will have the accent on big bands as
well.
Trumpeter
Clark
Terry
will
showcase
his
aggregation
Friday
afternoon, and
Sunday, July
7, Ray
Charles
will
have
an
afternoon
all
to himself.

ODE TO 52nd STREET—KENNY
BURRELL (Cadet 798)-^ This
is an
album of high
level music, much be-
yond the average
release. On
it, the
guitar of Burrell
is heard to
its best
advantage and much of the success of
the album should
also be
credited
to
Richard
Evans, who
collaborated on
most
of
the
compositions,
arranged
the music, and conducted the orchestra
that accompanied Kenny’ guitar. One
side
of
the album
is
devoted
to
an
extended
work,
“Suite
For
Guitar
And
Orchestra”,
a
four
part
inte-
grated work that is much less formal
than the
title suggests. The
flip
side
is made
up
of
five
selections,
three
of
which
are
originals.
Dizzy
Gil-
lespie’s “Con Alma”, and Dmitri Tiom-
kin’s
beautiful “Wild
Is The Wind”.
Each successive Kenny Burrell album
gives evidence
of
his continuing ma-
turity as a complete musician and on
this new Cadet album, in the company
of
a
large
orchestra
using
brass,
strings and woodwinds, he gives a very
impressive performance.

GEORGE
VAN
EPS’
SEVEN-
STRING GUITAR
(Capitol
2783)—,
About a dozen years ago, George Van
Eps recorded an album for Columbia
titled,
“Mellow
Guitar”.
It was
the
kind
of album that
sold
quietly, but
steadily, and, to the best of my knowl-
edge,
is
still
available.
It was
the
kind
of album
that
all
of Van
Eps’
fellow guitarists knew about and own-
ed, as one would own a primer. Then
there was a hiatus of nine years when
George
practically
stopped
playing,
let
alone
recording.
In
1966
he
did
an
album
for
Capitol
called,
“My
Guitar”,
which
drew
great
acclaim
from
the
critics. This new Van Eps
album, played on a seven-string guitar,
the
kind
of
instrument
that he
has
been playing since 1940, is an absolute i
joy to the ear and
it epitomizes
the
essence of taste in music. In the com-
pany of marimba and drums, Van Eps
explores twelve
selections, practically
all
from
the
standard
bag
and
all
played with consummate artistry. His
lean attack makes him the master of
understatement,
and
in
his economy
what good notes he plays! Playing ind
company of a marimba, the voicing is!
beautiful and shows Van Eps
cif
to/
his best advantage. This
is the kind
of rare album that, unless one listens
attentively,
could
be
regarded
as
a
moderately
ordinary
one.
But
with
great things, isn’t it often thus ?
