Crest of a Wave
As
a matter
of
fact,
looking back
at the
‘false alarms’ that
signalled a
big boom
in blues instrumentals with
more than r&b market showings they
now look
like breaking surf
showing-
rising tide for the ork single. Now the
pop
beachhead
is
being
hit
with
a
crested
wave
of
r&b
instrumentals,
and
whether
the
big wave
has
just
crashed or the “surf’s up” situation
is
just beginning remains to be seen. But
the crux
is that singles with a body of
blues,
soul and
jazz
are bigger than
ever with a wider market appeal and
far stronger
sales.
Each
of
the
successive waves that
hit
in
the
last few
years
might
be
pavers
laying a
foundation
that has
made the new rush
possible; opening
the
pop
public’s
eyes
to
soul
sound,
and
breaking
in
the
pop
ear
to
the
difference
that
is
the
very
heart
of
soul.
Going back to the “Soul Sauce” and
Ramsey Lewis hits which are the first
off-the-pop-center majors to bring non-
pop
instr-umentals
into
the
spotlight
since
the
early
rock
days,
the
slow
shift
is
visible
that
has
established
an audience capable of picking up on
blues
sides. From
there,
it was
the
growth of super star instrumentalists
like
Booker
T,
Jr. Walker and King
Curtis who showed up consistently on
the
pop
charts
(albeit
at
the
lower
end) with an occasional major hit that
kept the appetite whetted and inched
the pop awareness
further
off-center
toward a blues area.
Last year, the drive toward instru-
mental covers
of pop
hits
raised the
attention
level
to
a peak
that,
until
last month has been
unequalled. Tied
in
with
the
success
of
records
like
“Soul
Finger”
from
the
Bar-Kays,
Cannonball Adderley’s Grammy winner
“Mercy,
Mercy,
Mercy,”
“Hip-Hug-
Her”
by
Booker
T,
Jr.
Walker’s
“Pucker
Up,
Butter Cup”
and
King
Curtis’
“Memphis
Soul
Stew”
along
with “Groovin’ ” and a growth in blues

Great Britain
Following
one
of
their
sudden
and
startling
snap
decisions,
the
Beatles
have decided
to close their Apple Clothes Boutique
in London’s Baker
Street.
The
staff arrived one morning recently to
find three weeks’ salary
in
lieu
of
notice and instructions
to give away the thousands of pounds worth of stock
to passers by and anyone prepared
to take
it away free. Various
conflicting
reasons have circulated
to explain the closure, the two most prevalent being
that the Beatles were
dissatisfied because
the boutique had turned
into
just
another clothes shop and that they wished
to concentrate without distraction
on
their recording and
film
projects now underway beneath
the main Apple
Corps banner. The boutique bombshell has done nothing to reveal exactly how
serious and long term the Beatles are about the rest of their Apple empire.
Britain’s Clodagh Rodgers came third in the recent Greek Song Festival
in
Athens with the Jack Fishman-Roy Budd song “Ask Anyone.” She
collected
£500
as
the
prize.
Louis Neess
finished
first
for
Belgium
with
“Iris,”
and
Italy was
second
with
“Se Tu
Soffrisse Quando
Soffro
Io” sung
by Jimmy
Fontana.
Ron Randall, professional manager at Acuff-Rose Music for the past seven
months, has resigned to join the Bron Associated Music companies as general
manager. The appointment took
effect August
5th. Other industry moves
in-
clude
the naming
of
Vic
Ridgewell
as
Pye’s
distribution
manager
shortly
after
leaving
the
Philips/Polydor
job
of
national
planning
and
fulfillment
manager;
the resignation
of EMI Records
advertising
liaison manager Nevil
Skrimshire to join the new Morgan Music enterprise as marketing and promo-
tion manager; and
jazz
specialist Charles
Collett being named as promotion
manager for Liberty’s Blue Note
line.
The Western Orchestral Society, which administers the well-known Bourne-
mouth Symphony Orchestra, has formed a new ensemble to be known as the
Bournemouth
Sinfonietta which
will
play
small town
concerts
in
the West
Country areas which help to subsidize the main symphonic unit. George Hurst
will be principal conductor, and the
first concert
is set for September 18th at
Ringwood
in Hampshire.
Visits by American stars during the
fall are building
rapidly. Expected
in
September are the Doors and Jefferson Airplane, with Peaches
’n’ Herb and
the Canned Heat due in October. The Box Tops are slated for November, and
the Beach
Boys
will
be
back
for
concert engagements
in
December.
Bruce
Channel, who’s scored with
his “Keep On” deck and
recent personal appear-
ances, hopes
to return for a more extensive series
of dates before Christmas.
Top Dutch blues group Cuby and the Blizzards
will
be playing here October
3rd through 13th.
The Bee
Gees’ American
stint was
delayed by
the
collapse
of Robin Gibb
suffering from
nervous
exhaustion.
Gibb was
hospitalized
briefly, and
then
transferred
to a Sussex health farm for two weeks of rest and recuperation.
The Bee Gees hope to pick up their tour schedule in Michigan on August 24th.
Tom
Springfield,
hit songwriting brother
of Dusty,
is
cutting an LP and
single for Decca under Marcel Stellman’s supervision. The album
will feature
several
of his own numbers, and
the
sessions
will be
Springfield’s
first vocal
ones since the Springfields disbanded.
CBS
will now
call
its new LP sessions devoted
to
Scottish and
Irish music
Inheritance
instead
of
Heritage.
It was
discovered
that Saga
has
the
right
to
the use
of Heritage as a
label name
in
this country.
Mercury
is
releasing
a
sampler LP
as an
appetizer
for
its new Mercury
International
series devoted to country and western repertoire planned for an
October
launch.
Entitled “Country and Western Winners,”
the
sampler
fea-
tures
stars
like Roy Drusky, Roger
Miller, Faron Young, Rusty Draper and
Flatt and Scruggs.
Len Beadle
of Lawrence Wright Music concluded a
deal
with Larry Page
of Page
One Records whereby Page One
will distribute independent product
cut by
Beadle for the Wright company.
First
release under the new
deal
is
“Sweet Lorraine” by Billy Budd on August 23rd.
Quickies: Patsy MacLean will represent Britain as the BBC entrant at the
international
song
fest
in
Sopot,
Poland,
August
22nd
through
24th
.
.
.
Anita Harris
is
in competition with Mama Cass on “Dream A
Little Dream
Of Me”
.
.
. Sonet has released Bruce Channel’s new recording of “Hey Baby”
.
.
. Julie
Driscoll and Brian Auger featured on new Music For Pleasure LP
.
.
. London premiere
of “Hair” now
set for September 26th
at Shaftesbury
Theater.

^ f. Af. Scott Exits Capitol For Time Disks
NEW YORK—Francis
M.
Scott
III
has been appointed managing director
of Time-Life Records, effective Oct.
1,
1968,
reports
James
Linen,
presi-
'
dent of Time, Inc. In this newly-crea-
ted position, Scott will report to Rhett
•
Austell, publisher of Time-Life Books.
'
Scott
is
presently
vice
president
of
^
business
affairs
at
Capitol
Records,
where for the past
19 years he has
i
served in virtually every field of record
production,
being
credited
with
200
pop and 75
classical albums.
^
As
head
of
Time-Life
Records,
a
division of Time-Life Books, Scott con-
j
tinues a relationship that began with
the inception
of Time
Inc.’s domestic
^
record
enterprise.
Time-Life Records
was
specifically organized
in 1965
to
%
create
and
market
“The
Story
of
Great Music,” a classical record series
covering
the
last
four
centuries
of
outstanding music. Besides
his
other
executive duties at Capitol, Scott was
responsible
for
managing
Capitol’s
part in the “Great Music”
series.
*’
Each volume
in the “Great Music”
series
combines Time
Inc.’s
editorial
»
and graphic resources with an album
of recorded music from the
catalogs
of Angel
Records,
Capitol’s
classical
label, and
the
affiliated
resources
of
EMI
of
London.
More
than
eleven
volumes, each
consisting
of four LP
recordings, plus a rich illustrated book
^
describing
the
context
in which
the
music was composed, and a guide
to
t
the
recordings,
have
been
marketed
in
the
United
States
exclusively by
mail order. Another five volumes, each
containing
five
long
playing
records
plus
a
listener’s
guide,
have
been
1
marketed
under
the
title
“Concerts
of
Great
Music”
as
supplements
to
*
the
initial
series.
^
Recent T-L
Expansions
Building on the success of
its
first
series, Time-Life Records has recently
undertaken the development of several
series,
including
both
classical
and
(
pop music. These series will also draw
^ on
the
repertoires
of American and
European
record
producers
and
will
^
be sold by mail order here and abroad.
In addition, Time-Life International
Recordings
has
collaborated
with
Deutsche Grammophone since 1964 in
the mail order
sales
of
classical and
semi-classical albums in ten countries
throughout the world.
Scott
will
be
responsible
for
the
development of these expansion plans,
(
as well as for the on-going business of
'
the record
division. His
office will be
in the Time &
Life Building
in New
"
York.
Capitol
Records
president
Stan
I
Gortikov
accepted
iScott’s
resigna-
tion with “great regret.” Capitol
In-
dustries
president
Glenn
Wallichs
said that “in nearly twenty years
of
service Scotty has made many import-
ant contributions to Capitol’s growth.
We are sorry to
see him
go, but we
wish him well
in his new association
and
hope
that
the
work
Time
and
Capitol
do
together
will
continue
to
keep us in touch.”
Scott’s outside interests include sail-
ing, gardening, and the National Acad-
emy of Recording Arts and Sciences,
which
he
has
served
over
the
years
as
a
national
trustee,
treasurer and
president.

Mercury Family Sets Largest Release Ever,
76 IP's To Be Supported By Mammoth Promo
CHICAGO—Mercury Records is ready-
ing
its
largest
and
most
powerful
cumulative album release in the label’s
23-year history. In support of the re-
lease,
all
corporate
labels’
sales and
promo brass began a 10-day nationwide
itinerary
last week
(14).
Executives
are demonstrating 76 new LP’s for the
fall
in
color,
sound
film
showings,
and parties for accounts
in 29
differ-
ent
cities
are
being
held
through
August
24.
“We
decided
to
take
the
Mercury
show
on
the
road
because we
wish
to bring to the attention of everyone
in
the
personnel
of
our
distribution
and their accounts the importance
of
the
product
in
our
fall
releases,”
Irving
Green,
corporation
president
stated. “This exhaustive personal trav-
eling by our key people to distributors
and
record merchandisers avoids
the
lost time which might result
if they
had
to attend normal national meet-
ings. And, we know that more
inter-
ested people within the ranks of the
wholesale
and
retail
record
business
will
now,
more
personally,
feel
the
enthusiasm
of our own
staff,” Green
concluded.
Smothers Bros. Packages

ers

Al Silver To Direct
Expanded R&B Division
For Roulette Label
NEW YORK—Al
Silver, absent from
the
disk
for the
past four
years,
is
returning
to the wax wars
to
direct
expansion of the Roulette label’s R&B
division.
Silver,
who
formed
the
Herald-
Amber disk operation in 1953, offering
a long
string
of R&B-type
hits,
will
head the
label’s R&B department,
di-
recting the acquisition of new talent,
masters and planned entry
into
pro-
duction.
Among
Silver’s Herald-Amber
hits
were “Shake a Hand” by Faye Adams,
“Tonight
Tonight”
by
the
Mellow
Kings,
“Story
Untold”
by
the
Nut-
megs,
“I
Love You
Madly”
by
the
Charlie &
Ray,
“Still
of the Night”
by
the
Five
Satins, “Get
a Job” by
the Silhouettes and “Stay” by Maurice
Williams.
Silver
started
in
the
disk
business
in
1947 when
he
opened
a
pressing plant. He
also owned Angel
Music Publishing.
Al
Silver

THE CLOWN DIED IN MARVIN GARDENS
—Beacon Street Union—MGM SE 4568
The Beacon Street Union made the charts
with
their
first album, and they should
see
even better action with their new set. Imagi-
native
lyrics and
sophisticated rock combine
to make the LP a
listening experience that
the group’s fans will surely not want to miss.
The
inventive
title tune and a long
(16:24),
mind-blowing track called “Baby Please Don’t
Go” are two of the album’s highlights. Keep
close tabs on this one.

MGM SE
4526
Sam the Sham could have quite a sizeable

funky vocalizing has earned him a large and
faithful

of
admirers,
all
of whom
should welcome
his
latest
effort. “Old Mac-
Donald Had A Boogaloo Farm,” “The Down
Home

“Stagger

“Yakety
Yak” are just four of the treats on an album
filled with
goodies.

SHOSTAKOVICH: SYMPHONIES NOS. 2 &
3—Gould/Royal Philharmonic Orchestra and
Chorus—RCA Victor LSC 3044
Russian
composer
Dmitri
Shostakovich’s
Symphonies Nos. 2 and 3 receive their world
premier
recordings
on
this
LP.
Composed
in
the
1920’s, both symphonies
are
socialist
programmatic
works
(Symphony
No.
2
is
dedicated to the October Revolution of 1917,
Symphony
No.
3
to
the
first
of May,
the
international
holiday
of the working
class).
The symphonies were condemned by
Stalin’s
regime
for
their
dissonance
and have been
largely ignored
in
the West.
Interest
could
well be generated in the works by this album.
F^TS IS BACK—Fats Domino—Reprise 6304
Fats Domino, the great rock and roll singer
and
pianist who had a long
string
of
gold
records
in
the
1950’s,
is back with a bang.
Though his style hasn’t changed a great deal,
he
doesn’t sound
in
the
least out
of
date,
and
his
readings
of
such
tunes
as “Lady
Madonna”
(his
latest
single, now
on
the
charts),
and
“Lovely
Rita”—both
Beatles
numbers—are right
in the groove. Could be
heavy action on this
one.
LOOK AHEAD—Pat Boone—Dot DLP 25876
His
brief sojourn in Nashville’s invigorat-
ing
climate may prove
highly
beneficial
to
Pat Boone, whose latest album, produced there
by Anita Kerr, takes the veteran chanter into
new,
green
pastures.
The
smooth-as-silk
Boone voice sounds thoroughly at home with
such
outstanding
country
songs
as “Gonna
Find Me A Bluebird,” “Love Of The Common
People,” “Take These Chains From My Heart,”
and
‘“roo Soon To Know.” Good change
of
pace for the
artist.
DAYS OF PEARLY SPENCER — WHO
KILLED EZRA BRYMAY—David

liams—Kapp KS
3547
The debut

of underground exposure and created a
cer-
tain void that this album

The Irish-born singer/writer runs through 11

his current “Who Killed Ezra Brymay”

Could happen
big.
WINE AND SONG—Sergio
Franchi—RCA
LPM/LSP—4018
The latest album from this feelingful Italian
tenor is one that all Sergio Franchi fans will

to have. Franchi’s voice

a

This

Liberty Heats Up For
LOS ANGELES—Liberty Records has
launched
one
of
the
most
extensive
group promotions in the label’s history
for Canned Heat,
it has been reported
by Dennis Ganim, national promotion
manager for the diskery.
The $100,000 promotion campaign is
directly tied in with the group’s latest
single, “On The Road
Again,’’ which
is
currently
on
the
chai-ts,
and
the
group’s
latest
LP,
“Boogie
With
Canned Heat,” which is moving up the
Top 100 Albums.
Distributors and branches are being
provided with pre-recorded commercial
spots advertising both of the Canned
Heat
LPs
and
with
color
films
of
Canned
Heat
performing
“On
The
Road Again” for television use in their
respective areas.
In
addition
Liberty
is
purchasing
spots on key Top 40 and underground
stations
in every major market area
and in key secondary markets.
Canned Heat
Ads
are
being
purchased
in
trade
publications and major consumer and
underground publications.
The
merchandising
program
in-
cludes distribution to retail outlets of
10,000
copies
of
the
issue
of World
Countdown which featured the group
and 50,000 copies of a special Canned
Heat issue of the Liberty Record which
includes a Canned Heat poster. Distri-
butors and retailers are also being pro-
vided
with bumper
stickers,
buttons,
and individual posters.

CaABoK Platter Spinner Patter
Two
recent
protests
against
radio
stations came to naught with the pro-
testers struggling mightily before go-
ing down
to
defeat. One
protest was
a one-man effort, the other was a group
attempt, but the results of both bore
no fruit. Dick Booth, a 27-year-old dee-
jay at WTXL-West Springfield, Mass.,
was informed that he was going to be
laid
off in two weeks due to economic
reasons. He went
on
the
air,
asking
listeners to protest the
firing.
In the
15
hours and
40
minutes
of
Booth’s
appeal, over 1,000 calls came in on his
behalf,
according
to
the
deejay.
But
another precinct was yet to be heard
from—Booth’s
boss.
'The
deejay was
fired, and he ruefully recalled the old
saw: “You can always tell the boss
,
.
.
but he never listens.”
On another front, the massed forces
of
1-2-3
Records
in
Atlanta
blunted
their swords, or at
least their picket
signs,
against
the
citadel
of WQXI-
Atlanta. The outlet had not been airing
the label’s new release, “Birmingham,”
by the Movers, so the diskery
set up
a picket
line
in front
of the building
housing the station. The protest began
during
the
noon
hour
on
Peachtree
Street,
knotting
Atlanta’s
always
heavy
traffic.
1-2-3 promo man Mike
Clark handed out free records
to mo-
torists, and
busses
stopped
to
allow
passengers
to
read
the
signs.
The
label’s protest was extremely “heated”
in
that
the
picketers were
parading
on the hottest day of the year in At-
lanta. Moved by the sight of the per-
spiring
pickets,
the WQXI
staffers
sent out ice cold drinks to the march-
ers. As
of this writing, however,
the
outlet’s response to
1-2-3’s record has
also been
ice
cold. The
disk
has
not
been receiving airplay on WQXI.

'Hang 'Em High'
NEW YORK—United
Artists
Music
is currently conducting an all-out drive
for single and album recordings of the
Dominic
Frontiere-composed
theme
and background score for the United
Artists
flick, “Hang ’Em High.”
“Hang ’Em High”
is
the fourth
in
a series of UA westerns starring Clint
Eastwood. The music from the
other
flicks, “A Fistful Of Dollars,” “For A
Few
Dollars
For
More”
and
“The
Good, The Bad And The Ugly”
pro-
duced
lots of disk action.
Frontiere composed the themes for
the
successful
television
series
“The
Invaders,”
“The
Flying
Nun,”
and
“That Girl.” He
is also associate pro-
ducer and composer
of the theme for
“The Name
Of
The
Game,”
a
new
television
series.
Frontiere
is
sched-
uled to be
in New York soon to com-
mence scoring background and theme
material
for
“Popi,”
a new UA
pic-
ture which will
star Alan Arkin.
Among the new recordings of “Hang
’Em High”
is Hugo Montenegro’s sin-
gle on RCA. Montenegro is just coming
off his smash
single of “Theme From
‘The Good, The Bad, And The Ugly’.”
A new album by the maestro-arranger
titled “Hang ’Em High”
is currently
on the charts.
United
Artists
Records
has
the
original
soundtrack, which
is
on
the
the
charts,
as
well
as
a
single
by
composer
Frontiere.
Veteran
music
man and sound specialist Enoch Light
has already cut an album version on
his
Project
3
label, and
a
single by
him
is due out immediately.
An
upcoming
single
by
Booker T
on the Stax label
is also due. In addi-
tion the
artist
is recording an album
which will contain “Hang ’Em High.”

NEW YORK
Ken Schaffer hosted a “hear-in” for
Douglas International last week. Pur-
pose of the gathering, which was com-
posed of a small number of music biz
people, was
to
collect comments
(on
tape)
to be edited into radio commer-
cial form about
several new Douglas
album
projectors.
Along
with
wine,
tequila
and
imported
food from
the
House Of Yemin, guests were treated
to excerpts from an unusual album by
the late Malcolm X, the last disk from
jazzman Eric Dolphy and some tunes
out of the
label’s
Richie Havens
set.
One
of the more enjoyable events
so
far this year.

HOLLYWOOD
A
Bat-ty
Idea
For The Music
Biz
Did you ever wonder how the trades
would read
if the record biz was regu-
lated like big league professional base-
ball?
It it was you might (perish for-
bid)
be reading items such
as
this
Columbia’s
first division record club
has announced one
of the big trades
of
the
season—“Bo Bo”
Bennett
has
been
sold
to A&M’s House
of David
team for an undisclosed sum of money,
two
utility
singers
(Claudine “Crazy
Legs”
Minelli,
“Shoeless”
Joe
Ochs)
and a vocal group. The Sandlotters.
Marv Heifer
Bob Levinson
“Bennett has a couple of good years
left
in him,” said Columbia manager
Casey Lieberson, “and he can
still belt
a long ballad. But we
felt we needed
some
speed
in
the
form
of
“Crazy
Legs”
Minelli.
She has
several
star-
tling curves and holds the league rec-
ord for the longest note ever held
at
the Coconut Grove park.”
Bennett, reached at his home in Man-
hattan, blamed a soil- right larynx for
his inability to come up with more hits
this
season. He
said
he was
looking
forward to being on the same team as
“Pee Wee” Alpert and “Daffy” Mendez.
“I’m
a few years away from
retire-
ment and
the A&M
front
office
has
promised me
an A&R
slot when
I
finally hang up my tonsils.”
In the meantime it’s understood that
Columbia
will
be
cutting
its
roster
down
to
the
player
limit
within
the
week, optioning

Williams

act

of

JIMI HENDRIX EXPERIENCE
SINGER BOWL, N.Y. — The second
show
of the N.Y. Rock
Festival was
a
major improvement
over
the
first,
both
in music quality and crowd con-
trol. However,
traffic
control has not
yet been solved
(that, at least,
is one
thing
producers
Shelly
Finkel
and
Gary Kurfirst have nothing to do with)
and we missed the Soft Machine, who
opened the show.
The
next two
acts,
both from
Co-
lumbia,
the
Chambers
Brothers
and
Big Brother & the Holding Co.
(fea-
turing
Janis
Joplin)
have
both been
reviewed
in
recent weeks and
suffice
it
to
say
that
both
lived up
to
the
earlier
(very
favorable)
reviews and
put the
sell-out crowd
of
18,000
in a
high-pitched mood.
Jimi
Hendrix
is
a
showman,
but
unlike some of the other theatrically-
minded performers around, he
is also
a first rate guitarist. Familiar Hendrix
material
(from
his
first two albums)
included “Hey Joe,” “Purple Haze” &
“Let Me Sit Next To Your Fire!” New
to the majority of the audience were
his
renditions
of
“Wild
Thing”
and
“Like
A
Rolling
Stone.”
Although
Hendrix’ showmanship makes him the
focal point of the group, the other two
members of the Experience, Noel Red-
ding and Mitch Mitchell, are both first-
rate
musicians.
Hendrix’
rousing
fi-
nale, which saw him batter his guitar
into the fabric of his loudspeaker, left
both singer and audience emotionally
moved. Score one for the Jimi Hendrix
Experience.

MORT FFOA
iiimin
This is the story of The Garden State
Arts Center, a jazz event that is to be
held
there,
and
the man who
is
the
guiding light of this magnificent am-
phitheatre. At the time of this writing
The
First Annual Garden
State Arts
Center Jazz Festival is two days hence;
when
this comes
out
in
print
it
will
have already taken
place. Because
of
my personal involvement in The Festi-
val, as
its producer,
I have planned
it
thus.
I
particularly want this column
to serve as a tribute to The Arts Cen-
ter, not as a billboard for the two day
jazz concert, or as a review of the two
night’s music.
Located
in
Holmdel, New
Jersey,
just thirty miles south of Newark on
The Garden State Parkway and at the
beginning
of
the New
Jersey
shore
area, The Arts Center
is a
six and a
half million dollar site, including a five
thousand
seat
domed
amphitheatre
with ample parking facilities to accom-
modate a capacity crowd. This amphi-
theatre was designed by Edward Durell
Stone and affords every patron the best
possible opportunity to see and to hear,
no matter where
he
is
seated. There
are no columns to obstruct one’s view
and the accoustics are incredibly good.
In addition, there is a lawn area on the
periphery
of
the amphitheatre which
can accommodate another three thou-
sand patrons. Happily, there have been
many
nights
this past summer when
every available seat
in the house has
been occupied and every inch of lawn
space has been, too.
This past summer was the inaugu-
ral
season
for The Arts
Center, and
a
very
successful
one,
I
might
add.
Why not when
it offered such attrac-
tions
as Judy
Garland,
Harry
Bela-
fonte, Andy
Williams,
Victor
Borge,
Liberace,
Diana
Ross
and
The
Sup-
remes,
Peter,
Paul
and
Mary,
Judy
Collins, Arlo Guthrie, The Rascals, The
Philadelphia
Orchestra under Eugene
Ormandy and featuring Van
Cliburn,
The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra of
London conducted by Antal Dorati, Jan
Peerce,
Roberta
Peters,
The
Jeffrey
Ballet and others. Anyone, no matter
how uninformed about the performing
ai'ts, would concede that such an array
of
talent
is
absolutely
first-rate
and
sufficiently
varied
to
offer something
for everyone.
Further,
each
of
these
top performers has remarked that The
Arts Center
is one of the
finest
sites
of its kind in the world.
Of course, in any undertaking of this
proportion
there
are many
areas
in
which confusion and error can present
themselves.
It’s a great tribute to the

can

Rockflow Plans Fall Open;
Nears Capitalization Goal
NEW YORK—Rockflow, a pop music-
dance-environment-public party, which
received
praise
from
such
national
magazines
as
Life and
the Saturday
Evening Post during
its
several
per-
formances in late 1966 and early 1967,
has taken
over an
entire building
in
downtown New York for
its perman-
ent revival during the
fall.
Emphasizing
that
it’s
not
a
“psy-
chedelic
discotheque”
by
any
means,
Rockflow
director
Harvey
Kramer
called
his “show” the “product
of
le-
gitimate,
well-known
and
respected
members
of
the
art
community;
a
shattering, inhibition annihilating ex-
perience run on a
script that changes
from day
to
day, making each Rock-
flow a new excursion.”
The
capitalization
of
Rockflow,
de-
scribed
as
being
somewhere
on
the
continuum between a club and a
the-
atre, is being handled by Ken Schaffer.
It calls for sponsorship from corpora-
tions
whose
products
are
integral
There
is
one man who, more than
anyone
else, has been responsible for
the existence of this magnificent
site.
His name is D. Louis Tonti and his offi-
cial
title
is Executive
Director, New
Jersey Highway Authority, The Arts
Center is his dream and he has seen it
come to fruition. Even at this stage of
the game, Tonti is inextricably involved
in everything that concerns itself with
the operation of the
site. Considering
that his position as Executive Director
of The New Jersey Highway Authority
is enough to keep three men completely
busy, the fact that he can find the time,
the energy, and the
interest that the
Arts Center demands is a tip-off to his
enthusiasm for the performing arts. If
there were a Lou Tonti in a position of
authority in each community the world
of the performing arts would be much
richer.
As
a
consequence
of
his
catholic
tastes, the fact that Tonti felt that all
segments of the performing arts should
be represented at The Arts Center, The
First Annual Garden State Arts Center
Jazz Festival came to be. The sugges-
tion
for a jazz offering was proposed
at what must be considered a late date,
the end of July, a time when less im-
aginative
and
less
daring men
than
Tonti would have declined because of
the
element
of
time.
But Lou
Tonti
jumped into the project with limitless
energy and
enthusiasm.
I was
called
in to co-ordinate and produce the two
nights
of
music,
in
association
with
The New Jersey Highway Authority,
and here we are just two days away
from curtain time, with the assurance
of
a
sell-out
for
both
nights.
With
someone
less devoted than Lou Tonti
at the helm, this probably would never
have come to pass. In my time
I have
worked with many people, but few who
have
been
as
energetic,
efficient,
de-
voted to the arts and as warm as is Lou
Tonti.
It should be a matter of record
that
the
world
of
performers
has
a
good friend in him.
About the Jazz
Festival, there will
be two shows, Friday, September 6th
and Saturday, September 7th. The Fri-
day program
will feature
Stan
Getz,
Herbie Mann, Arthur Prysock, Jimmy
Smith and Ahmad Jamal.
Saturday’s
performance will highlight Dave Bru-
beck with Gerry Mulligan and
Louis
Armstrong and His All Stars. There is
every reason to believe that both nights
will be very successful, both artistically
' and financially,
so
that,
in
truth,
this
will be The FIRST ANNUAL Garden
[ State Arts Center Jazz Festival.
If
I
know Lou Tonti, and
I think
I
do, not
I long after the Saturday night perform-
ance
he
and
I
will
be
getting
busy
formulating next year’s SECOND AN-
NUAL Garden State Center Jazz Fes-
!
tival.
parts of Rockflow and its scripts, such
as musical equipment manufacturers,
cosmetic
firms, beverage
outlets,
rec-
ord
companies,
etc.
According
to
Schaffer, the past credentials of Rock-
flow
itself,
and
the
credentials
of
Rockflow personnel as trend-setters in

in

at

and NBC. He
established and

of The New York

merstein begins

October
1. Locations are being screen-

has
also
announced
that

Association Ends Tour
NEW YORK—Bringing SRO
crowds

the

just
ended

week summer tour.
Highlighted by an appearance in the

Illi-
nois State Fair and a

Current

a
fall

(19)
in Canada

of

their
fifth.

1

will

Productions’

TRO's Raskin Drive
Opens With Push On
"Those Were The Days'
NEW YORK—A big push is being put
on the new Gene Raskin song, “These
Were The Days” by the Richmond Or-
ganization (TRO).
Recorded by the new British singer,
Mary Hopkin, the song has just been
released
here
on
the
Beatles-associ-
ated
Apple
label
through
Capitol
Records.
The song
itself marks
the opening
of a long-term TRO push on Raskin’s
works.
Eighteen-year-old
Miss
Hop-
kin,
who
was
discovered
by
famed
model Twiggy and whose Apple single
was produced by Beatle Paul McCart-
ney,
is the subject of a current mass
media press campaign.
TRO production chief Judy Bell has
readied a special edition of the sheet
music for “Those Were The Days,” in
which
front
and
back
covers
are
adorned with glamour photos
of the
blonde Miss Hopkin. In addition, TRO
is
plugging
Miss
Hopkin’s
with
a
series
of
saturation
postcard
teaser
mailings
to
press,
deejays,
and
pro-
gram
directors. These
efforts
are
all
being coordinated with those of Apple
and
its American
distributor, Capitol
Records.
The
song,
TRO’s
number
one
plug,
is
also being pushed
in Europe
through
the
Essex
International
operation
in
London
and
through
Editions
Essex,
TRO’s
Paris-based
French-associated
company.
Accord-
ing
to David
Platz,
international
di-
rector of Essex International, French
and Russian versions of the song are
already
in the works.
It is understood that another British
singer,
Sandie
Shaw,
has
also
cut
“Those Were The
Davs.”
Operations
in London and New York are expected
to focus on obtaining maximum album
coverage on the song in both vocal and
instrumental versions. Broad exposure
is also envisioned on a
flock
of other
tunes penned by Raskin.

FOCUS ON JAZZ
FEGAI
Prestige inks Jefferson
BEGENFIELD,
N.
J.—Prestige
Rec-
cords has signed veteran jazz
singer
Eddie
Jefferson
to
a
recording
con-
tract,
it
was
announced
by
Don
Schlitten, A&R director for the label.
Jefferson
is one
of the originators of
the vocalized
jazz
solo
first popular-
ized by King Pleasure and later by the
Lambert, Hendricks and Ross group.
Much of his work has been devoted to
putting
lyrics
to
the
solos
of
saxo-
phonist James Moody, a longtime as-
sociate.
Jefferson
has
also
written
lyrics for material from
such
artists
as Charlie Parker, Coleman Hawkins,
Horace Silver, and Lester Young. The
first album by Jefferson
is scheduled
for winter
release.

things
went
down
in
a
very
orderly
manner.
There
were
minor
difficulties like insufficient microphones
to
capture
the
sound
of
the
many
talented
soloists,
and
someone
less
affable than Mann might have been
uptight
about
it,
but
Herbie’s
easy,
informal manner overcame whatever
hassles
were
evident
and
made
the
audience willing participants
in what
was happening onstage.
Accustomed
as
we
are
to
seeing
Herbie Mann
in
his
quintet
setting,
it was something of an awsome
con-
templation
to
await
his
music
in
a
showcase that included
a twelve man
string section, three reeds, two trum-
pets, an extra guitarist, an extra per-
cussionist,
and
a
pianist,
all
under
the direction of a conductor. From
a
previous
conversation
with
him,
I
learned that Herbie wants to showcase
new young
talents
that he
feels
are
deserving.
Consequently, “The
Music
World
Of
Herbie
Mann,”
with
its
multiple
settings,
affords
him
the
opportunity
to
do
so.
Among
the
featured
soloists
this
evening
were
guitarist
Larry
Corryel,
trumpeter
Charles
Tolliver,
David
“Fathead”
Newman
on

and
flute,
Bobby
Capers
on
baritone
sax,
Bob Yancy
on trumpet and
flute, Sam Corwin on
piano,
and
Steve
Marcus
on
tenor.
All of these young players in addition
to Herbie’s regular
quintet members,
vibist
Roy
Ayers,
guitarist
Sonny
Sherrock, drummer
Bruno Carr and
bassist Miroslav Vitous. Much of the
success of the big band offerings should
go
to
conductor,
arranger
William
Fisher,
whose
presence
onstage was
that necessary
link
for
the cohesive-
ness that showed. Alternately the pro-
gram featured big band settings, small
group
settings,
solo
excursions,
and,
as a
finale, something reminiscent
of
a
jam
session
on
“Hold
On,
I’m
Cornin’,” with everyone wailing.
Expect Bigger Things
Forearmed with the knowledge that
the
ensemble
had
only
the
briefest
rehearsal
time,
I was
astonished
to
hear
“The
Music
World
Of
Herbie
Mann” come
off with

even two

three
nights
of playing
on the job, with the calibre of musi-
cians that Mann is using it, will sound
as though
they’ve
been
doing
it
for
months instead of days.
Herbie Mann
is
to
be
praised
for
his attitude about offering a voice
to
the many young and talented players
in
his “World.”
Similarly, Art D’Lu-
goff,
the
genial
and
adventuresome
owner
of
The
Village
Gate,
should
be singled out for his sense of daring
in undertaking a presentation of this
proportion.
Most
of
D’Lugoff’s
col-
leagues in the night club business get
cold
feet when

to
hiring
a
group
larger

a
quartet
or
a
quintet. When

Herbie where
else he thought he could present this
package
he
shrugged
an
unknowing
I
shrug.
NARM Board Meet
PHILADELPHIA—On
September 26
and
27,

Association
of
Record Merchandisers’ (NARM) board
of directors
will convene for

Los Angeles.
The

was

by

Geldbart,
president
of NARM
and of L and F Record Service in At-
lanta,
Georgia.
In
making
the
an-
nouncement, Geldbart stated that the
prime business of the meeting will be
a
complete

and
planning
session
for
the
Eleventh
Annual
NARM Convention, which will be held
February 28 through March
5,
1969,
at the Century Plaza Hotel.
The format
will be
established for
,
the
business

and
seminar
sessions, as well as for the social ac-
tivities and
the NARM Awards Ban-
quet.
In
addition,
plans
will
be
dis-
cussed for the person to person set-up
and the possibility of an exhibit area.
Initial planning was instituted at the
NARM Tape Convention held recently
in

1969 NARM
?
Convention Committee met under the

of Jack Grossman,
conven-
tion chairman. A complete review will

of
hotel

gard to the setting up of the program
and format.
In addition to convention planning,
the NARM board of directors will also
review policies of convention registra-
tion, company membership, and
vari-
ous
problems
generated
by
industry

; Stan-

CnshBon Record Rumblings
NEW YORK—Singles Take Up Foster Child
Policy
Add
another
length
to
the
reper-
cussions
of a
hit LP: the foster-child
single.
In addition to renewing sales on en-
tire
catalogs,
a
series
of
hit albums
have
created demands
for
reissue
of
stillborn
hits. Most
successful
of the
reborn children have been “Sunshine of
Your Love” and “You Keep Me Hang-
in’ On” from
the Cream and
Vanilla
Fudge respectively; but this week’s re-
release package includes “Sookie Soo-
kie” the preceding and now follow-up
single from
Steppenwolf
and
a new
year-old “Not So Sweet Martha Lor-
raine” from Country Joe & the Fish.
The two latest demonstrate the ma-
jor effects of “time a’changin.” Either
of the newest is an example of a “hit”
that was “born before
its time”; and
both point up the new era which allows
an in-the-grooves track to become re-
incarnated.
With the Steppenwolf track, the side
was one
of the nearest hits that hap-
pened
(almost)
for
the team
before
“Born
to
Be
Wild”
took
the
team’s
name
out
of
the
literary
tradition
alone. For Country Joe, the not-quite-
enough
status
has
been changed
not
because
the
group
has
grown
big
enough to break the
side, but because
the market has grown to expose “pro-
gressive” singles
in more than under-
ground quantity.
In a sense both of these not-so-oldie,
and formerly not-quite-goodie enough
outings
are
foster
children
of
either
album or later singles parentage. With
this
development,
the
total
catalog
picture
becomes
a
Cinemascope
pro-
duction with a supporting cast
in the
singles
field as well as LP’s.

New NARAS Governors 
NEW YORK-The New York chapter 
of NARAS, the record academy, has 
elected Peter Yarrow, Esmond Ed- 
wards and Ben Tucker to their board 
of governors. 
Yarrow, one third of the Peter, 
Paul and Mary team, replaces Ray 
Charles, the choral conductor, who 
has moved to the West Coast. Ed- 
wards, record producer for MGM- 
Verve, comes in for Joe Harnell, who 
moved to Philadelphia to work on the 
Mike Douglas TV series. Tucker, vet- 
eran bassist and composer, recently 
turned producer, takes over John 
Simon's spot. 
In another move, the Board of Gov- 
ernors elected three alternate trustees 
who will function when any of the 
chapter's six regular national trustees 
are unavailable. Chosen were Milt 
Gabler, Decca Records a. and r. ex- 
ecutive; Mickey Kapp, president of 
Compass Records, and Jim Lyons, edi- 
tor and publisher of the American 
Record Guide. Both Kapp and Gabler 
have served previous terms as na- 
tional trustees.

tir,

president 
of 
NARAIS, the disk awards society, chats 
with Pete King, (left) Nasatir's pred- 
ecessor following Nasatir's election to 
the society's top post.

Tape News Report 
Once Over Lightly 
Cassette Booklet 
NEW YORK - A new, colorfully - 
illustrated consumer booklet describ- 
ing the versatile uses of the Audiopak 
Compact Cassette in school, business 
or at home has just been published 
by Audio Devices Inc. 
Titled "the Everything Thing," the 
booklet is designed to stimulate con- 
sumer interest in cassettes as an all- 
purpose, convenient and easy -to -use 
recording tool for memory or com- 
munications purposes. It is offered to 
retailers, without charge, as an ad- 
junct to in-store merchandising ac- 
tivities. 
The booklet's pop-art illustrations 
highlight the varied roles the Audio- 
pak Compact Cassette plays as "The 
Everything Thing" for different users, 
from student to businessman. 
Among the uses featured are: as a 
"memory bank" to help students re- 
view lectures on the eve of examina- 
tions; as a fast and simple method 
for recording broadcasts that permits 
easy tuning out of unwanted portions; 
as a personalized letter that can be 
mailed anywhere in the United States 
or to servicemen overseas for 20 cents, 
while providing for a longer message 
than the average letter; as an aid to 
the businesman in recording meetings 
or "jotting down" notes that can be 
easily transcribed later by the secre- 
The booklet points out that pre- 
sion engineering of the Audiopak 
Compact Cassette eliminates wow and 
flutter and that its specially designed 
Audiotape prevents tape jam-ups. 
The booklets are available from 
Audio Devices Inc., 235 East 42nd 
Street, New York, N.Y. 10017. 
3M Tape Sweepstakes 
ST. PAUL, MINN. - A combined 
dealer -consumer magnetic recording 
tape sales promotion program, includ- 
ing more than 3,000 prizes, has been 
announced by the Magnetic Products 
division of 3M Company. 
To be launched immediately, the 
sweepstakes promotion features two 
grand prizes of trips for two, any- 
where in the world, for both a con- 
sumer and dealer. Other prizes range 
from consumer and dealer trips to 
Jamaica and Puerto Vallerte to cam- 
eras, luggage and travel alarm clocks. 
In all consumers will win 3,001 prizes 
and dealers 83. 
To participate dealers must sell and 
display "Sctoch" recording tape and 
also display 3M's 3 new point -of -pur- 
chase items: a full color mobile, a 
sweepstakes window/wall banner and 
a sweepstakes counter card with con- 
sumer entry forms. 
Consumers obtain entry forms from 
a participating dealer, fill out and mail 
as instructed attaching either an end 
of roll plaid tab or a 3 x 5" paper con- 
taining the words "Scotch" recording 
tape. 
Contest ends November 30. Winners 
will be selected by an independent or- 
ganization and notified in December. 
Dealers may obtain information and 
contest materials free from their local 
3M Magnetic Products division repre- 
sentative or: 3M Company, Magnetic 
Products Division, Market Services 
Department, 3M Center, St. Paul, 
Minn. 55101. 
Kornbrodt Chairs 
EIA Unit Again 
NEW YORK - Herman Kornbrodt, 
vice president of Audio Devices Inc., 
has been reappointed chairman of the 
recording and reproducing system 
components committee of the Elec- 
tronics Industries Association. 
Kornbrodt is in charge of sales and 
marketing for Audio Devices, the pro- 
ducer of precision magnetic tapes for 
sound recording, cartridges and cas- 
settes and the special tapes they re- 
quire, computer tape and disk packs, 
instrumentation tape and videotape. 
Liberty Response To Consumer 
Tape Returns: Standard Warranty 
HOLLYWOOD-Liberty hopes to do 
something about one of the major 
problems confronting tape manufac- 
turers: the increase in percentage of 
tapes being returned as defective, a 
conclusion reached at the NARM ses- 
sion on the subject several weeks ago. 
Earl Horwitz, general manager of 
the Liberty Records stereo tape divi- 
sion, outlined Liberty's plans: 
"Since nearly 50% of the tapes re- 
turned are actually found not to be 
defective from the standpoint of man- 
ufacture when they are examined," 
Horwitz said, "we do not feel that the 
manufacturer should accept complete 
responsibility." 
Standard Warranty 
"Therefore, starting November 1, 
Liberty will put a standard warranty 
into effect. Terms of the warranty will 
be explained in an insert which will 
be placed in each cartridge."

ASCAP Awards Hit New High; 
$658,450 To 1,813 Writers 
NEW YORK-A new record will be 
set by ASCAP when it distributes 
$658,450 in awards to 1,813 writer 
members, ASCAP president Stanley 
Adams has announced. These awards 
for 1968-69 are the highest of any 
during the nine years that the Society 
has been making these special grants, 
and they boost the cumulative total 
to more than $5,000,000. 
Some $321,800 is going to 1,221 
writers in the "popular" field which 
encompasses contemporary pop -rock, 
country music, R&B, jazz, motion pic- 
tures, and musical theatre. The re- 
maining $336,650 is being distributed 
to 592 composers and authors of sym- 
phonic and concert works, reflecting 
ASCAP's continuing commitment to 
foster the cultural growth and en- 
richment of America's musical heri- 
tage. 
Awards To Writers of Chart Songs 
Writers of chart songs again re- 
ceived special recognition in this new 
group of ASCAP awards. These writ- 
ers include many top new talents in 
the music world, such important crea- 
tors of today's "now" sounds as Bobby 
Russell ("Honey" and "Little Green 
Apples") 
and Jim 
Webb 
("Mac 
Arthur Park"). Other award -winning 
writers whose works have blossomed 
on tradepaper popularity charts since 
March 1st include Hamilton Camp, 
writer of "Here's To You"; Sheila 
Davis, author of the English lyric of 
"Who Will Answer"; Gary Geld and 
Peter Udell, creators of "Sealed With 
a Kiss"; Guy Marks, who wrote "Lov- 
ing You Has Made Me Bananas"; 
Tom Paxton, writer of "Bottle of 
Wine" and "The Last Thing On My 
Mind"; and Stuart Scharf, who pen- 
ned "Like To Get To Know You." 
In keeping with its new policy (be- 
gun at its last meeting) of granting 
awards to ASCAP writers whose 
compositions have appeared on the 
charts the Popular Awards Panel re- 
iterated that "the listing of a mem- 
ber's work on a tradepaper popularity 
chart has a bearing on its prestige 
value," and again set up guidelines 
for determining the amount of the 
award to a writer with a chart song. 
Points were assigned to each compo- 
sition based on composite tradepaper 
chart listings. All ASCAP writers 
who had songs listed on one of the 
charts used (and was otherwise elig- 
ible for awards under the procedures 
followed by the Panel) received an 
award. The charts of Cash Box, Bill- 
board, Record World, and Variety 
were used in making the awards. 
Leading Talents Honored 
Among the exceptional talents who 
also received awards are jazz men 
Ornette 
Coleman, 
Kenny 
Burrell, 
Dizzy Gillespie, Horace Silver, Billy 
Taylor, and the new ASCAP members 
Chic Corea, Chuck Israels and Mike 
Maineri; country writers Hal Blair, 
Cy Coben, Don Robertson, Billy Edd 
Wheeler, and Sheb Wooley; Major 
pop -folk 
writer -performers 
Joan 
Baez, Judy Collins, Bobbie Gentry, 
and Arlo Guthrie; R&B writer Jimmy 
Holiday; and multi -talented Herb Al- 
pert, creative leader of the world 
famous Tijuana Brass. 
Awards To Writing -Performing 
Groups 
Awards were made to writer mem- 
bers of some of the most exciting 
groups on the current rock scene: the 
Doors (John Densmore, Robby Krieg-

Musical Theatre Grants 
ASCAP honored outstanding musi- 
cal theatre writers with shows cur- 
rently on the boards, men such as

Grants To Classical Composers 
1968-1969 awards are going to many 
outstanding ASCAP composers and 
authors in all phases of classical or 
"standard" music-symphonic, con- 
cert, recital, religious, and educa- 
tional. Award winners include George 
Crumb recipient of a 1968 Pulitzer

Awards to Writers On Campus 
The awards list includes more than

Marchand MRC Prof. Mgr. 
NEW YORK-MRC Music, the new- 
ly -formed Mercury subsid, has named 
Donny 
Marchand 
as 
professional 
manager, reporting directly to Bob 
Reno, MRC general professional man- 
ager. 
According to Reno, Marchand will 
be looking for both new and experi- 
enced writers and has already signed 
his first tunesmith, Danny Green, to 
an exclusive MRC pact. Marchand 
will work closely with the writers in 
the development of material and will 
also be active in placing upcoming, as 
well as existing, MRC songs. 
Marchand joins the firm from the 
professional staff of Famous Music. 
Prior to that, he was on the staff of 
Sunbeam Music. He will be headquar- 
tered at MRC's 110 West 57th St. 
offices.

The ASCAP awards are made by 
two panels of distinguished men who 
are not members of the Society: the 
Popular Awards Panel and the Stand- 
ard Awards Panel. 
Awards Rules 
The Standard Panel limits its 
awards to members of the Society 
receiving less than $20,000 in regular 
performance royalties, and the cut- 
off for the Popular Awards Panel is 
$15,000. The grants are given to 
writers whose works have a unique 
prestige value for which adequate 
compensation would not otherwise be 
received by such writers, as well as 
to writers whose works are performed 
substantially in media not covered by 
ASCAP's coast to coast survey of per- 
formances. 
Mancini To Conduct Music; 
1969 Oscar Awards Show 
HOLLYWOOD-The music director 
and conductor for the 41st annual 
awards presentation of the Academy 
of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences 
will be Henry Mancini, three -time 
Oscar 
winner. 
The 
announcement 
came from producer -director Gower 
Champion. 
The noted conductor, who has writ- 
ten the music scores and songs for 
numerous Hollywood films, won two 
Oscars in 1961. The first was for best 
scoring of a dramatic or comedy pic- 
ture, "Breakfast At Tiffany's", and 
the second for writing the music for 
the best song, "Moon River", from the 
same picture. 
He also won an Academy Award the 
following year, for writing the music 
for the best song, "Days Of Wine And 
Roses", from the film of the same title. 
In addition to his three awards, 
Mancini has 
been nominated for 
Academy Music Awards on six other ,_ 
occasions, between 1954 and 1965. 
In 1954, he was nominated for best 
music scoring of a musical, "The 
Glenn Miller Story"; in 1961, for 
writing the music for the song, "Bach- 
elor In Paradise"; and in 1963, for 
the song "Charade". In 1964 he took 
two nominations: for a substantially 
original music score, "The Pink Pan- 
ther", and for writing the music for 
the song, "The Sweetheart Tree", in 
1965. 
The 41st Academy Awards will be 
color telecast nationally by the Ameri- 
can Broadcasting Company, on April 
14, 1969. 
Columbia Issues Single Of 
Tribute To Robert Kennedy 
NEW YORK-A single of "Battle 
Hymn Of The Republic/Ave Maria" 
as sung by Andy Williams at St. 
Patrick's Cathedral during memorial 
services for the late Senator Robert 
F. Kennedy on June 7 and 8, 1968, is 
being released by Columbia Records. 
The single release is being made 
available by Columbia in response to 
the many phone and letter requests 
received by the label from consumers, 
- 
wishing to obtain a recording of 
Williams' tribute to the late Senator. 
Royalties from the sale of this re- 
cording will be donated to the Senator 
Robert F. Kennedy Memorial Founda- 
tion.

One McGuire Stands Alone 
NEW YORK-Phyllis McGuire, who's 
made several solo appearances on the 
Ed Sullivan, Johnny Carson, Perry 
Como and Mike Douglas TV'ers, made 
her solo nightclub debut at the Riviera 
Hotel, Las Vegas last week (24), 
opening a four week stand. Since the 
professional retirement of her two 
sisters, Phyllis has been touring the 
leading summer theaters, starring in 
various musicals, getting ready for 
her club debut. Murray Kane wrote 
and staged her act, and her musical 
conductor is Tony Riposo.

Capitol Launches Promo 
Drive For Fred Neil 
HOLLYWOOD - Capitol Records is 
launching a promotion push for Fred 
Neil and the song he wrote, "Every- 
body's Talking," in order to introduce 
both the artist and the tune to record 
buyers who may not yet know them. 
Nillson's rendition of "Everybody's 
Talking" was on the charts recently. 
Besides heavy advertising in the 
"underground" press and shipments of 
Neil's albums to radio stations now 
programming "progressive rock," Cap- 
itol is making this offer to record buy- 
ers: Buy either one of Neil's two Capi- 
tol albums from any record dealer, 
send Capitol the receipt for that pur- 
chase, and get the other Neil album 
free. According to an official at Capi- 
tol, this is the first time that any rec- 
ord company has employed this pro- 
motion device. Capitol expects to give 
away several thousand Fred Neil al- 
bums-a cost the company thinks will 
be justified by the amount of publicity 
the campaign will generate. The offer 
will be advertised in the "under- 
ground" press. 
Songs written by Neil have been 
recorded by more than 75 artists and 
groups, including Peter, Paul and 
Mary, the Serendipity Singers, John- 
ny Rivers, the Lovin' Spoonful, Nill- 
son, Spanky and our Gang, MC -2, 
Kenny Rankin, and Harry Belafonte. 
Others, such as Jefferson Airplane, 
have written songs about Neil. 
Neil has been a part of the music 
scene for about ten years, appearing 
at clubs in New York and "holding 
court" for visiting singers, musicians 
and songwriters at his home in Coco- 
nut Grove, Florida.

New York operation.

Klein, a major stockholder in MGM 
and Paramount Pictures and also 
owner of Cameo -Parkway Records. 
Miss Leigh will begin her duties 
October 1st.

President of Tetragrammaton, has ap- 
pointed Ron Krietzman to the post of 
coordinator of artist relations and all 
related media. Krietzman, former as- 
sistant to Roy Silver, starts his duties 
immediately.

Bios for 
Dee Jays 
Arthur Brown 
To say that Arthur Brown's stage 
routine is dynamic would be the under- 
statement of the age. He appears on 
stage in flowing multi -colored robes, 
his face streaked with colorful make- 
up, a helmet on his head, and his hair 
on fire. While his band backs him in 
a mixture of rock, R&B, jazz, and pop, 
he shrieks, jumps, yells, growls, and 
sings. Arthur Brown was born on June 
24, 1944, in Whitby, Yorkshire. His 
father invented the first fully auto- 
matic toothbrush, and has completed 
a pneumatic car. He now plays bar 
piano in the London area. Arthur 
studied law at London University but 
was expelled at the end of the first 
year for failing his exams and for re- 
peatedly making grand Zen gestures 
in lectures. Later, he studied philos- 
ophy at Reading University, where he 
formed a college group which worked 
in the Reading area. 
Now as 
a 
reading artist for Atlantic, Arthur 
is at the number 3 spot this week on 
the Top 100 with "Fire," and his LP, 
"Crazy World Of Arthur Brown," is 
slotted at number 20 on the album 
charts. 
Patti Drew 
Patti Drew was born on December 
29, 1944, in Charleston, South Caro- 
lina. She and her five sisters, who 
were raised in Evanston, Illinois, be- 
gan singing in church choirs and at 
local events. Out of this sextet emerged 
a pop trio, the Drew-Vels, which con- 
sisted of Patti and two sisters, Lor- 
raine and Erma. After being signed to 
Capitol Records, the threesome hit the 
R&B charts with a single entitled 
"Tell Him." When Patti's sisters be- 
came occupied with housewifely duties, 
Patti went out on her own as a single. 
She cut a few disks for a Chicago 
label, but sales were slow. Then Patti. 
recorded her own rendition of "Tell 
Me." Capitol heard the new treatment, 
and signed her to a contract. Her cur- 
rent single, "Working On A Groovy 
Thing," is number 88 on the charts 
this week.

Decca Records and Chappells hosted reception for Tom Springfield celebrat- 
ing his first recording as a singer since the break-up of the Springfields five 
years ago. The album is entitled "Sun Songs" and three tracks are Springfield 
compositions published by Springfield Music via Chappells. A single track, 
"Signora Steinway," (a Springfield composition) is released simultaneously. 
Springfield has, of course, been active on the songwriting front and gave 
the Seekers a No. 1 American hit with "Georgy Girl." 
Blues specialist Mike Vernon has signed a long term contract with Decca 
Records for the production of records. He already records John Mayall, Ten 
Years After, the Webb, Savoy Brown and Nigel Denver and will continue to 
work with these artists and seek new talent. With his brother Richard, Vernon 
runs the Blue Horizon label which is distributed by CBS and this arrangement 
will continue. The label achieved enormous success recently with the "Fleetwood 
Mac" album which was resident for several weeks in the album charts. 
Ray Stevens in town with manager Don Williams (brother of Andy) promot- 
ing his latest American hit "Mr. Business Man" on Monument published by 
KPM Music. During his ten day stay, Stevens taped three TV shows. Another 
Monument artist, Jo Simon, due in October 20th promoting "Message From 
Maria"; to take part in the "Festival Of Soul" concert sponsored by Harold 
Davison; and tape a color TV show for BBC 2. He will fulfill continental dates 
before returning to the States. 
Chris Matthews, President of Memnon Amusement Company, in Britain 
recently to set up a British operation, acquire office accommodation and staff. 
The plan is to run the British company on the same lines as the American 
set up i.e. music publishing, artist management, promotion and production. 
Aim is to seek and develop British talent both here and in the States and 
American artists in Britain. 
Don Partridge is planning a trip to America in January, 1969, for a promo- 
tional link with the Columbia picture "Otley" starring Tom Courtenay and 
Romy Schneider to be premiered in New York that month. Partridge wrote the 
theme song and sings it on the soundtrack. His new Columbia single "Top 
Man" features Partridge's new all -electric one -man -band technique. 
The new RIM label (a subsidiary of the Rediffusion Organisation) made its 
debut with three singles and two albums. The albums "Silhouettes Of Success" 
by the Howard Blaikley Orchestra features instrumental versions by the 
prolific songwriting team Ken Howard and Alan Blaikley of the hits by the 
Herd, the Honeycombs, Dave Dee, Dozy, Beaky, Mick and Tich., etc. RIM 
is distributed by Phillips and deals have been signed in Holland, New Zealand, 
Australia, Japan, France, Spain, Germany, Italy, Belgium and the Scandinavian 
countries. 
Alex Perucchini of Zenza Fine Music Milan in London recording the 
Grapefruit's latest release "Come On Marianne" in Italian for that market. 
Perucchini penned Italian lyrics as he did for their previous release "Dear 
Delilah." During his trip Perucchini visited publishers placing and acquiring 
material. He is interested in recording more British artists for release in 
Italian and is planning a visit to America at the end of October with the same 
object in mind. 
Peter Blake, designer of the Beatles "Sgt. Pepper" L.P. cover, has designed 
the sleeve for the Pentangle's new double album "Sweet Child." The album 
is released by Transatlantic Records coincidental with the group's nationwide 
tour which kicks off at the Royal Albert Hall on November 5th. 
A lavish party was thrown by Lionel Bart at his "weird but welcoming" 
Chelsea home to celebrate his "Isn't This Where We Came In" album just 
issued on Deram. No ordinary album this as it involved some 200 people and 
took nine months in the making, the end result of which is a new concept in 
L.P. format. A selection of catchy songs is woven into a reflective look at life, 
or as Bart describes it, "A musican autobiography with yours truly making 
the mouth music." 
David Mirisch, in town with the 5th Dimension to tape a Tom Jones special, 
advises that the group will be returning for a six week tour taking in the 
U.K., Germany, Italy and France commencing January 3rd. They will also 
appear at the San Remo Festival and MIDEM followed by a season at London's 
Talk Of The Town. 
Cliff Richard (currently playing a season at the London Palladium) was 
special guest of honor with the Shadows at a party hosted by EMI Records to 
celebrate Cliff's ten years in show business. Cliff, the Shadows, Manager Peter 
Gormley and Producer Norrie Paramor were each presented with a decanter 
by EMI Records Managing Director Ken East, and Cliff and the Shadows 
were presented with copies of all their Silver Disks (21) and Gold Disks (5). 
All guests were given a copy of their latest album "Established 58" (Columbia) 
packaged in a special double fold sleeve. All 14 tracks were penned by the 
Shadows.

1st Euro Tour For 
James & Shondells 
NEW YORK - Tommy. James & Tho 
Shondells fly to London October 1 for 
a month long tour of the British Isles. 
The group will play special concert 
dates in addition to performances on 
several national theatre chains such 
as the Odeon, ABC and Gaumont cir- 
cuits. The tour opens October 4 with 
a concert at the Astoria Theatre, Fins- 
bury Park, London, followed by the 
Odeon, Manchester (5), the Gaumont, 
Bradford (6), a jaunt into Scotland 
where they play the ABC Theatre, 
Edinburgh (9), then a trip to City 
Hall, Newcastle (10), followed by per- 
formances at the Odeon, Birmingham 
(12), and the ABC, Chesterfield (12). 
On October 13 the group plays at 
the Empire Theatre, Liverpool, fol- 
lowed by dates at Colston Hall, Bristol 
(14), the Odeon, Cardiff (16), the 
Adelphi, Slough (17), the Gaumont, 
Ipswich (18), the Granada, Testing 
(19) and the Coventry Theatre, Cov- 
entry (20).

Announced by Phonogram, a new single by top French artist Johnny Halli- 
day entitled "Queste mie mani, the Italian version of his French hit "Entre 
mes mains." Also from Phonogram comes word that the opening tune of the 
new TV series "7 Voci" entitled "Stasera si" has been assigned to Armando 
Savini. 
Flamenco has recently been discovered by the Italian public due to the 
initiative of Ri.Fi Records. The label, under the Variety logo, has released two 
albums by world-renowned Spanish guitarist Manitas de Plata: "Manitas Et Les 
Siens" and "Hommages." The artist is currently in Italy making his debut 
at the Teatro Manzoni, which show will also be televised. 
The popularity of Adamo here is once again confirmed in that he won the 
recent juke box referendum "Festival Bar." The EMI Italiana artist is due in 
Milan the end of this month to take part in the first show of the new series of 
"Settevoici" when he will present his new Italian recording "La tua storia 
e' una favola." 
The "Festival Bar" also confirmed the strong popularity of CBS Italiana 
group I Camaleonti who received first prize for the best coupling presented at 
the contest-"Io per lei" b/w "Non ti scordar di me." They also were awarded 
a special prize as being the most successful Italian group in 1968. 
Strong reaction here for the American hit "Hush" recorded for EMI Italiana 
by the Deep Purple. An Italian cover by Giuliano Girardi (PDU) has also been 
very favorably received. 
The top Brazilian talent of Chico Buarque de Hollanda is currently in Rome 
for a series of recordings for RCA Italiana. Chico will make his debut in Italian 
via an LP (`The World Of Chico Buarque de Hollanda") and two singles, first 
of which is a self -penned number entitled "Quem to viu' quem to ve." 
Cerned Carosello has released under the United Artists banner the top Ameri- 
can hit `Harper Valley P.T.A." as performed by Bobby Martin. Also from 
Cemed Carosello comes word that their Renata Pacini has been declared 
winner of the "Festival di Vasto," a special contest for songstress/composers. 
The two titles penned by her and Gianni Meccia are "Goodbye My Love" and 
"Troppo presto, troppo tardi."

MARSHALL CHESS is shown (right) at a meeting with Durium's top execu- 
tive Giampero Scussel during his recent visit to Europe. Chess, president of 
America's Chess, Checker and Cadet label complex, conducted similar policy

çashsox Germany 
Tours take the spotlight in Germany this week with the big Sammy Davis, 
Jr., tour leading up the list of goodies. Sammy covered Nurnberg, Karlsruhe, 
Essen, Hannover, Berlin, Bremen and Hamburg working in large auditoriums 
to packed houses, but the most original appearance took place in Munich 
at the underground night spot "Blow -Up." Tickets went for $25 a crack 
and people who wanted to stand downstairs under the stage were able to 
be on the spot for just $11.25. Some prices. Sammy was doing his first tour 
of Germany and it was a tremendous success. 
The second major event of the next weeks will be the Tom Jones tour. Tom 
is also expected to draw top box offices during his visit with the Ted Heath 
Band. Teldec will be working hard to glean publicity from both events. 
Metronome has had its hands full with visits too. King Curtis & his King- 
pins together with the Sweet Inspirations and Deon Jackson visited Germany 
for a tour with a 3 -day stint in Munich's "Big Apple" discoteque topping 
the trip. The Doors visited Frankfurt for a sold -out visit and their first 
shot on German TV in color, and Ben E. King headed down this way to do a 
shot for the "Beat Club" TVer with his new Atlantic waxing "It's Amazing." 
He'll then do a tour kicking off in Hamburg's "Star Club." Off the soul and 
psychedelic kick, Siw Malmkvist from Sweden and Belgium's best Sir Henry 
and his Butlers visit Germany for the "Star Parade" TVer on the 2nd 
channel. 
Electrola has their hands full with the Ray Charles tour from the 27th 
of September until the 4th of October, while CBS will host Donovan in 
December. On the local side of the picture, Ariola has their top artist Udo 
Jurgens touring Germany to packed houses for his one-man show and the 
"Show Express" is now on tour with Manuela, Dorthe, Graham Bonney and 
Horst Jankowski's Orchestra. Jacqueline Boyer, Beauty Milton, the Lords, 
Joy and the Hit Kids, Neil Christian, Peter Orloff, Howard Carpendale and 
Eric Sylvester are also on the bill. It's the first try at presenting an all-star 
pop show in several seasons. 
Gaby Richt of Metric Music tells us that "Walking To New Orleans" from 
Fats Domino is getting the big push on Liberty, while Liberty Records 
itself is giving the gun to promotion for the Canned Heat and their top 
smash "On The Road Again." 
Phonogram Records had reason to crow recently as their top stars Abi 
and Esther Ofarim did a 45 -minute color spectacular on German TV that 
was the best musical show of the entire season. The show jolted the record 
sales of the already best-selling group to new highs. 
D.G.G. reports that Rafael Kubelik and his Bavarian Radio Symphony 
Orchestra will tour the U.S.A. and Canada from October 16th until November 
13th this year. Hans Gerig Music is going all out to see that "Those Were 
The Days" from Mary Hopkin gets the promotion that it deserves. Along 
with the English hit version, Sandie Shaw is making the race hot as the 
popular songstress has not only released the song in English but has also 
done a German version of the tune. 
The 10th anniversary of Warner Bros. -Reprise -Seven Arts records is 
getting the big play at Teldec these days with special promotion on the 
product of the firm and special releases for the big event getting the big push. 
Joel Hochdorf of MCA dropped bios of Neil Diamond, Hugh Masekela, the 
Forum Quorum and the Peppermint Rainbow to start off his contact as 
International Publicity and Promotion chief of the firm. 
Cornet Records has a special entree into Paris through the appearance 
of Roland W. at the Olympia with his special smash "Monja." 
Speaking of festivals, and who doesn't. The radio -TV bosses met recently 
with representatives of the record indipstry to decide how the German entry 
for the "Song For Europe" Grand Prix Eurovision de la Chanson will be 
chosen. The results of this talk should be announced in the next few days. 
That's it for this week from Germany.

Well, the Monkees have been and gone. 
The tour was a fine success and proved that the four boys have ability 
above and beyond what we had come to appreciate from their records and 
television programs. RCA rush -released their new single before it had ap- 
peared in some overseas areas; the titles are "Mary, Mary" and "What Am 
I Doin' Hangin' 'Round." 
Australian Record Company, through their CBS banner, have issued a 
very interesting locally -produced album called "Source" featuring the talents 
of Adelaide (South Australia) artist Doug Ashdown. The set is best described 
as a progressive rock and is one of the best attempts at this modern trend 
in this country. 
Chappell & Co. have released the sheet copy to the instrumental click 
"Soul Limbo" which is out here by Booker T. & the M.G.s through the Festival 
people. 
Reportedly one of the most expensive albums ever produced in this country 
is the new one for local group the Twilights. The set is known as "Once 
Upon A Twilight" and is scheduled for release about the time this goes to 
print. From what we can gather, the cover is quite a feature of the whole 
thing, which was produced for EMI by David Mackay, who is presently with 
EMl in London. 
New local singles through Festival Records include Maggie Joddrell with 
"Morning Dew" & "Broken Blossoms"; the Wild Cherries with "I Don't Care" 
c/w "Theme For A Merry -Go -Round"; Noeleen Batley with "You Made 
Me Love You" & The Trolley Song"; Tex Croft has "I've Walked A Long' 
Long Way" c/w "Round Hole Guitar"; the Campact has "Good Good Feelin" 
and "It Won't Be Long"; the Dave Miller Set are out with "Let's Get 
Together" and "A Bread And Butter Day"; the Same Day Twins have 
"Walking And Talking" c/w "Little Bit Afraid." This latter release was - 
produced by Pat Aulton for the Robert Stigwood Organization and is issued 
here on the Festival label. 
Australian Record Company have started a big promo drive in support 
of the new release by Big Brother & the Holding Company with "Piece Of, 
My Heart" which is rating on the Cash Box Top 100 in the States.

Webb, Audio Arts 
In Catalog Deal 
HOLLYWOOD - Audio Arts has 
signed a two-year deal with Jim 
Webb's Canopy Music for exclusive, 
world-wide sales rights to the Ja -Ma 
catalog, which includes more than fifty 
Webb compositions. Audio Arts presi- 
dent Madelon Baker, who gave Webb 
his first long-term contract and later 
sold it to Johnny Rivers in the inter- 
est of Webb's career, will supervise 
the catalog, to be co -administered 
with Canopy by ABC -Dunhill, under 
the direction of Jay Lasker. 
Webb will have the last word as to 
who first records his tunes in Ja -Ma. 
Among the several in production or al- 
ready recorded are "Whatever Hap- 
pened To Christmas," cut by Frank 
Sinatra as a single and a cut on the 
Sinatra Family Christmas album.

NEW YORK-"Our clients want their 
commercials to become hit songs," says 
Herman Edel, a leading producer of 
commercial music, "and we have to tell 
them that if we could produce hits, 
we'd be in the record business. But the 
fact is that the two industries are mov- 
ing closer together than ever and even 
if we can't make the hits a regular 
practice, we are creating hit `sounds.' " 
Edel pointed out that because of the 
wide exposure given to many commer- 
cials, a special sound such as a mexi- 
cali beat, or a heavy brass sound, will 
quickly work its way into the public's 
mind and create faster acceptance for 
recorded product in the same vein. 
"We've started to work closer with rec- 
ord producers and execs so that we can 
obtain test pressings and pre-release 
copies of major new product. This will 
let us plan our commercial productions 
so that we will be on top of, and some- 
times in advance of, a new pop music 
trend. The commercials would there- 
fore remain timely for longer periods 
and would also provide the record in- 
dustry with a means of subliminal sup- 
port for their new musical directions." 
Affecting Radio 
Edel believes that commercials have 
already had a strong effect on the 
sound of middle road stations. "Ad 
agencies are more in tune with the 
times than most radio stations. They're 
aiming their commercials at the young 
and are using modern sounds. A radio 
station that has confined its program- 
ming to the Percy Faith -Mantovani 
sound will find that it has to start 
playing more `contemporary' (not to be 
read as `rock') material to lead into 
and out of the commercials." 
Edel, whose firm won a batch of 
Clio's in this year's Commercial Fes- 
Delvy Pleads MGM's A&R 
On Coast; Stays At Big 3 
NEW YORK-Richard Delvy, who has 
been handling record production deals 
for Big 3 Music (Robbins -Feist -Miller 
and its subsidiaries), will take on 
added duties as West Coast A&R di- 
rector for MGM Records. Delvy will 
be working closely with veteran exe- 
cutive Jesse Kaye, who, for many 
years, has successfully coordinated 
major film music product for the label. 
According to Arnold Maxim, who 
heads both firms, the tandem efforts 
of Kaye and Delvy will be aimed at 
"reestablishing the company's creative 
machinery and talent contacts in the 
prime West Coast area." Delvy will 
be cutting MGM artists based on the 
West Coast and is also expected to set 
up sessions for the label's other art- 
ists when they are available in his 
area. He has already initiated con- 
siderable West Coast action for the 
publishing company, including recent 
success with Colours on Dot Records. 
In his direction of the publishing 
company's production activities, Del- 
vy indicated that he will continue to 
maintain the broadest possible base 
with a working representation on all 
major labels. His prior experience 
runs the gamut of contemporary mu- 
sic with strong credits in the top 40 
field as promotion man, publisher and 
record producer, with a long line of 
past production successes on Dot, 
Crescendo, Vault, Challenge and At- 
lantic. He will operate from his office 
at 7033 Sunset Blvd. in Hollywood.

The first Apple LP by the Beatles will be a double album. The group com- 
pleted 24 titles the end of last month and decided to release them in double 
album form simultaneously in the U.K. and America mid -November. The sleeve 
design is likely to be less elaborate than that for their "Sergeant Pepper" 
LP in order to keep the retail price of the double pack within feasible limits. 
The first LP by Apple hit parader and Paul McCartney protegee Mary Hopkin 
will also be released in mid -November. 
Nems Managing Director Vic Lewis has named Roy Guest as Concert Promo- 
tion Executive and Cyril Black as Senior Music Publishing Executive with the 
company. Guest brings with him top folk acts like Al Stewart, the Johnstons, 
Dominic Behan, Jackson C. Frank and "Hair" star Sonja. Guest's first assign- 
ments involve London and provincial concerts for Johnny Mathis in November; 
the same for Donovan in January and February plus a six -city provincial tour 
for the Incredible String Band. Lewis has been finalizing details in California 
for the Mathis visit as well as discussing possible London and provincial book- 
ings for the Monkees. Black, older brother of Oscar -winning songwriter Don 
Black, joins Nems after four years as Professional Manager of Screen Gems in 
London. He will seek new songwriting talent for the company and undertake 
co-ordination with the Nems record label, distributed by CBS. 
Bob Barrett, producer of Vince Hill recordings including his mammoth "Eidel- 
weiss" hit, advises that Hill is to make concert appearances in Australia 
throughout October, via the States and the Far East where his "Why Can't I 
Remember To Forget You" is currently in the Philippines Hit Parade. His 
current Columbia single is "You Forgot to Remember" and a new album is 
planned for December. Barrett spends much time outside the EMI studios pro- 
ducing specialized product such as "Cutler Of The West" by Adge Cutler 
featuring West Country drinking songs and comedy, and is responsible for the 
first "drag" album: "Presenting Lee Sutton" recorded in a Camberwell pub. 
Jazz, brass bands, choral and light orchestral music also come within his orbit 
and he records many ablums for EMI's Studio 2 Stereo series. 
Morris Diamond, International Musical Co-Ordinator of United Artists in 
California, in London augmenting the release of disks from the forthcoming 
movie "Chitty Chitty Bang Bang" to be premiered in December. Title song has 
recordings by New Christy Minstrels (CBS); Paul Mauriat (Philips) and the 
Button Down Brass Band (Philips). "Hush -a -bye Mountain" has disks by 
Wendy Craig (Philips); Jean Livingstone (Fontana); Bobbie Gentry (Capitol). 
More are expected shortly. Albums of the score will include New Christy 
Minstrels (CBS) and Walter Ridley Orchestra (EMI). 
Johnny Cash flies in October 25th for an eight day visit. He plays six venues 
one of which is the London Palladium and his act will be recorded live by Bob 
Johns for release in album form on CBS. Promoter Mervyn Conn is negotiating 
a Johnny Cash tour for May, 1969, taking in Sweden, Holland, Israel, France, 
Germany and the U.K. 
United Artists Records is rush -releasing a Leroy Holmes album, one side of 
which contains music from "A Few Dollars More." Unlike "A Fistful Of 
Dollars" and "The Good, The Bad And The Ugly" there was no soundtrack LP 
for this movie, and the Holmes issue results from many requests and enquiries 
from the U.K. retail trade. The same composer, Ennio Morricone, has penned 
the score for "The Big Gun Down" starring Lee Van Cleef who appeared in 
"The Good, The Bad And The Ugly" and the film and soundtrack albums are 
scheduled for December. 
Johnny Keating, who returned here in April after three years in the States, 
is writing the score for the next Walter Shenson movie, "A Talent For Loving" 
starring Richard Widmark, Topol and Cesar Romero. The film was originally 
intended as a vehicle for the Beatles. Keating has plans to compose a symphony 
in the near future.

in which Holland, Belgium, Germany, Yugoslavia, Czechoslovakia, Austria,

Polydor to Release 
Debut Nazz Single 
NEW YORK - SGS Records has an- 
nounced that Polydor Records, Ltd. 
will release the debut Nazz single, 
"Open My Eyes" and "Hello Its Me" 
in Great Britain on Oct. 20. The LP, 
`Nazz,' will also be released in Eng- 
land as soon after the Oct. 20th date 
as possible. Packaging for the album 
will closely follow the LP created by 
SGC for domestic markets-in which 
case, the Nazz album will be one of 
the first Sur -Pak prototypes for the 
English market. 
On Oct. 28, the Nazz will arrive 
in London for a week of promotion on 
the new recordings, followed by a 
month -long series of sessions at Tri- 
dent Studios where they'll record their 
second album. The new LP will be re- 
leased by Atco and Screen Gems in 
the United States early in 1969. 
Introduction of the Nazz product 
overseas will be marked by the same 
kind of launching program which in- 
troduced them to U.S. consumers. 
Extensive trade ads as well as na- 
tional consumer ads are prepared 
in conjunction with John Kurland 
Associates, the firm which manages 
the group. In addition to the use of a 
color promo film for TV, in -person per- 
formance and TV appearances, there 
will also be a heavy radio advertising 
campaign utilizing the same radio 
spots, created by the Nazz themselves, 
that SGC is now featuring in such 
markets as New York, Boston, Phila- 
delphia, Los Angeles, Detroit, Denver, 
Seattle, San Francisco, Buffalo and 
other key markets where the Nazz al- 
bum has registered important album 
sales.

Transamerica Buying Metromedia In $300 Mil Stock Deal 
NEW YORK-Metromedia, the giant 
communications, marketing and enter- 
tainment complex, will merge into 
Transamerica Corp. in an exchange -of - 
stock deal that amounts to $300,000,- 
000. 
As announced by John W. Kluge, 
board chairman 
and president of 
Metromedia, and John Beckett, presi- 
dent and chief executive officer of 
Transamerica, Transamerica will ex- 
change three-quarters of a share of 
its common stock for each outstanding 
share of Metromedia. Once Metro- 
media shareholders and the Federal 
Communications Commission (FCC) 
approve this preliminary agreement, 
Metromedia would operate as an in- 
dependent subsidiary of Transamerica. 
Music -Disk Interests 
With regard to Metromedia's hold- 
ings in the music business, move 
comes at a time when the company is 
busily expanding into music publish- 
ing and records. Former interest is 
well underway via the recent purchase 
of Tommy Valando's music publishing 
operation. Disk -wise, Metromedia is 
nearing the market with Metromedia 
Records, an affiliate helmed by Len 
Levy (see separate story on appoint- 
ment of Manny Kellern to head A&R). 
Transamerica, of course, has substan- 
tial music business entities in United 
Artists Records and Liberty Records 
and their music publishing operations. 
The Transamerica -Metromedia devel- 
opment is probably too embryonic for 
an evaluation as to whether or not 
both music -disk units will themselves 
encounter of merger of their own. UA 
Music, under Mike Stewart and Mur- 
ray Deutch, did absorb Liberty's mu- 
sic publishing operation, Metric, and 
Al Bennett became head of both UA 
Records and Liberty, with separate 
exec staffs for both labels. But, it was 
emphasized that Metromedia would 
be an autonomous division of Trans- 
america.

going from here, president 
E. R.

For the past three years since the
