Denmark 
New at the charts here this week are Johnny Reimar at Philips with "Lemon 
Tree" in Danish, debuting at seventh spot, and Gitte Haenning at HMV with 
the Italian tune "Azzurro," also in Danish, debuting at eighth spot. 
Ann Tholsted, 20, Triola recording songstress, just had her first LP album 
at the market last week. The album was released all over Scandinavia as well 
as England, Germany and Holland. Miss Tholsted has also just appeared in a 
popular Dutch TV show as a part of the promotion of the album. Teenmakers, 
also a local Triola recording group, just had their first LP album at the market 
last week. One of their singles, including "Mo'reen" and "Dreamworld," has 
just been released by Jamie Records in the U.S., reports Morks Musikforlag. 
EMI recording group, Ulla, Ulrik & Mikael Neumann, had a local TV show 
here the beginning of Nov. As a trio, they are recording for the Columbia 
label, but there is also a single at HMV with Ulla and Mikael Neumann. A 
German EMI group, Lords, are contracted for a tour in Denmark during Nov. 
New name at CBS here is local songbird Eva just having her first single 
at the market. She might be a new name on records, but in Germany, she has 
just completed her fifth TV show, and in Denmark she has done very well as 
restaurant entertainer, among others at the Kystens Perle. 
EMI just rushed out the Stateside soundtrack LP album from the film 
"Barbarella," now a hit at the Scandinavian cinemas. 
Recent releases from Nordisk Polyphon Akts. (NPA) include "A Day With- 
out Love" with Love Affair at CBS, "Kentucky Child" with Georgie Fame, 
and "Wait For Me Mary -Anne" with Marmalade, also CBS. Releases also 
include six CBS LP albums. 
Diana Ross & Supremes, Tamla Motown group, will also appear in Denmark 
in connection with their planned Swedish concerts the middle of Nov. 
Hede Nielsens Fabriker A/S has three new local RCA Victor singles with 
Eugen Tajmer, Poul Rudi and Synne Rifbjerg. Other releases include "It 
Crawled Into My Hand, Honest" with Fugs, a Reprise LP album. 
Tono A/S has a new Christmas LP album among its recent releases. 
Bertrand Bech & Orchestra has done a number of well-known season songs 
under the title "Julesne" (Christmas Snow). 
Metronome releases include "Light My Fire" with Doors, "Josefine" with 
Tommy P., both at Metronome, "Komm and bedien dich" with Peter Alexander 
and "Ein seltsames Paar" with Jo Ment Ork., both at Ariola. Releases also 
include a number of LP albums at Ariola, Baccarola and Hansa. 
Sweden 
New sheet music from the Stig Anderson publishing house includes "Cette 
Nuit La" with Swedish lyrics ("Den första sommaren") by Anderson who also 
has done the Swedish lyrics to the German tune "Arrivederci Frans," here 
titled "Arrivederci Hans." "Harper Valley P.T.A." has the title "Fröken 
Fredriksson" with lyrics by Stig Anderson, who also signed the lyrics to 
"Mycket kär," originally an Italian tune "Non illuderti mai" but also known 
under its English title "My Little Lady." Finally, Anderson has written the 
Swedish lyrics to the Italian "La bambola" here titled "Dockan," but also 
known under its English title "The Love Alarm." All here listed tunes are 
published by Sweden Music AB. Polar Music AB has a folio with 12 local 
songs, and also has the local tune "Var egen sang" (Our Own Song) with 
words and music by Björn Ulvaeus. Screen Gems Musikförlag AB is out with 
the sheet music of "Angelica" and "The Look Of Love," the latter with 
Swedish lyrics ("Just nu 
. 
. 
. just här") by Bengt Haslum. Finally, United 
Artists Musikförlag AB is out with the theme music from the movie "The 
Good, The Bad And The Ugly" by Ennio Morricone. 
Long John, a local group from the city of Skövde in western Sweden, has 
their EMI debut record at Parlophone at the market. Titles include "Sitting 
Here Baby" and "Don't Want You No More." Last summer, the group was 
voted "best Swedish pop group" by the radio listeners. The group has so far 
been on a tour in Norway and is planning a tour in Denmark next December. 
Also a tour in Holland is scheduled. 
Tommy Blom has debuted as soloist with a Metronome single including "A 
Little Bit Of This ..." in Swedish b.w. a local tune. 
Recent releases from AB Knäppupp include Rune Larsen, a Norwegian 
singer, with a couple of Swedish folk songs at Triola. Danish group Teen - 
makers and their "Mo'reen" and "Dream World" at Triola was also released 
last week. 
RADA Epands Operation 
VANCOUVER: Ralph Harding, gen- 
eral manager of RADA Record Press- 
ings has announced an expansion pro- 
gram to establish the recently formed 
firm 
as 
an international 
agency. 
RADA will also step up its bid for 
business from Canada's three western 
provinces. 
Harding is currently on a cross 
country promotion trip drumming up 
business for his west coast operation. 
He has found eastern reaction warm 
to his proposal of pressing for the 
British Columbia and Alberta mar- 
kets. The present rate for pressings 
works out to anywhere from 7¢ to 
10¢ with up to five days for crossing 
the country. Harding claims that 
RADA can reduce this price signifi- 
cantly as well as effecting a saving 
in time. 
RADA has also had soundings from 
the U.S., particularly from the north 
western states. Firmed deals have al- 
ready guaranteed RADA the shipment 
of up to 200,000 pressings for this 
year. A major factor in garnering 
sales from the U.S. has to do with the 
Kennedy round of tariffs whereby the 
rate of duty is being lowered from 
10% in 1967 at the rate of 1% each 
January 1st., until 1972 when it will 
become stabilized at 5%. 
On completion of his trip across 
Canada, Mr. Harding will spend some 
time in New York, negotiating the 
purchase of more equipment. 
As well as record pressings, RADA 
offers complete production and dis- 
tribution facilities, album design and 
fabrication.

ITCC Sales Figures Revised 
NEW YORK-Net sales for the fiscal 
six months ended Sept. 30, 1968 at 
International Tape Cartridge Corp. 
were $3,508,500 instead of the pre- 
viously reported (Oct. 25) $4,148,947. 
The corrected sales figure compares 
with $2,819,720 for the first half in 
the prior year. 
According to James J. Elkins, pres- 
ident incorrect net sales resulted from 
inter -company sales upon consolida- 
tion. 
Audio Devices Expands 
Floor Display Program 
NEW YORK-Audio Devices has ex- 
panded 
its 
"Audiotape 
Recording 
Center" floor display merchandising 
program, according to an announce- 
ment by Herman Kornbrodt, vice pres- 
ident of the company. 
"Dealer response to the program 
has been good and we are planning 
to make additional units available to 
broaden the scope of the program," 
Kornbrodt said. 
Designed to assist retailers in their 
in-store merchandising efforts, the 
floor display provides a coordinated 
selling unit for different types of tape 
recording products. 
"In addition to providing convenient 
one -stop shopping for consumers, the 
display makes possible more efficient 
service during the fall and holiday 
buying seasons," Kornbrodt said. 
The "Audiotape Recording Center" 
is available in two designs and is of- 
fered with a bonus of free merchan- 
dise to dealers who order a minimum 
of 300 reels of Audiotape. The bonus 
includes 15 Audiopak AC -60 cassettes 
and 12 copies of the guide, "How To 
Make Good Tape Recordings," with 
a total retail value of $60. 
The 
sturdily -constructed 
"Audio - 
tape Recording Centers" features fine- 
ly -finished steel supports, wire racks 
and shelves. and solid-nanel storage 
cabinets with mar -proof surfaces.

CASH BOX 
2 New Lear Patents 
& Japanese Victor Deal 
DETROIT-Lear Jet Stereo has been 
issued seven patents involving play- 
ers and stereo 8 tape cartridges. Ed 
G. Campbell, vice president -general 
manager, said the most significant 
patent is No. 3,403,868, which was 
issued on October 1, 1968. The patent 
involves both stereo type players and 
stereo type cartridges. 
Lear Jet Stereo, Inc. pioneered the 
development of the 8 -track stereo tape 
cartridge player and 8 -track stereo 8 
cartridges beginning in May, 1964. 
Campbell also stated that Lear Jet 
Stereo, Inc. and Victor Company of 
Japan, Ltd. entered into an agreement 
granting the Victor Company of Japan 
exclusive manufacturing rights and 
sub -licensing rights in Japan. This 
agreement, the company said, rep- 
resents a major breakthrough in in- 
ternational electronics marketing, and 
will "demonstrate the world-wide ac- 
ceptance of the Lear 8 -track concept." 
Ampex Cites Top 
Sales, Earnings 
NEW YORK-Record sales and earn- 
ings for any second quarter or first 
half were achieved by Ampex Corp. 
in the period ending October 26, 1968, 
reports William E. Roberts, president 
and chief exec officer. 
Sales for the second quarter of 
fiscal year 1969 totaled $73.900,000, up 
25 percent from $59,332,000 a year 
ago. Net income after taxes was 
$3,501,000 or 36 cents per share, up 17 
percent from $3,002,000 or 31 cents 
per share. 
For the first half, sales totaled 
$132,876,000, un 19 percent from $112.- 
081,000. Net income was $5.986,000. 
or 62 cents per share on 9,642,593 
average shares outstanding. up 
18 
percent from $5.074.000 or 53 cents 
per share on 9,574,055 shares. 
Roberts said incoming product or- 
ders for the first half were up 26 per- 
cent, providing a solid basis for con- 
tinued gains in the second half of 
the year. 
James Smith Joins GRT 
SUNNYVALE, CALIF.-James 
H. 
Smith has joined General Recorded 
Tape, Inc. as senior mechanical engi- 
neer. His responsibilities include the 
mechanical design and development 
of production equipment and profes- 
sional tape handling equipment. 
He was previously affiliated with 
NCR, Ampex and General Electric. 
Smith received his B. S. in mechan- 
ical engineering from San Jose State 
College. He is a member of the Cali- 
fornia Society for Professional Engi- 
neers. 
GRT is an independent producer of 
pre-recorded stereo tapes for the en- 
tertainment, educational, government 
and industrial markets.

UNIVERSAL CITY RECORDS 
CashBox Record Ramblings 
NEW YORK 
Soul Moves 
There are a lot of ways that pro- 
ducer Gerard Purcell could have gained 
exposure for his soul acts, but we 
think that the one he picked will 
benefit the entire black music com- 
munity. Purcell has launched a weekly 
Monday night soul showcase at the 
Village Gate, which will give much - 
needed `downtown' exposure to a host 
of acts, most of them tied up with 
other firms. Purpose of the showcase 
is to give TV talent people (and oth- 
ers) an opportunity to see these acts 
in a professional setting, and the re- 
sults may well mean increased ex- 
posure for many black artists. 
Opening night show (18) featured 
Barbara Mason, Herb Ward, Honey 
and the Bees, and the Ambassadors. 
Latter group made the most impres- 
sive showing (according to our usually 
reliable source). Turnout for the 
weather, and included reps from the 
event was heavy, despite miserable 
Ed Sullivan, Johnny Carson, Mery 
Griffin, Kraft Music Hall shows, along 
with major TV packaging and adver- 
tising agencies. Eddie O'Jay, WLIB 
deejay, was a top notch M.C. 
Down Town 
Tonight's (25) show will feature 
Eddie Floyd, Dee Dee Sharpe, the 
Exciters and the Pazant Brothers. 
Here's well wishes to all concerned.

HOLLYWOOD 
Arnold Maxin President of MGM Records-and Egypt? 
Some of us get so caught up with 
events in our industry that we tend 
to equate an Omega acquisition, for 
example, with a famine in Biafra- 
or a nuclear nonproliferation treaty. 
We fell into that trap ourselves the 
other day when we spied a Herald - 
Examiner headline "Nixon Planning to 
Go Middle of the Road." Our first 
reaction was that the president-elect 
was undoubtedly planning to program 
nothing but Ray Conniff and Eydie 
Gorme records at the white house. 
A few days after the Arab-Israeli 
conflict last year, we caught a news 
item to the effect that Gamal Abdel 
Nasser had offered to resign as ruler 
of his nation. We mentioned the Nas- 
ser resignation to an east coast rec- 
ord exec who happened to phone us 
that morning. He appeared bowled 
over by the news. 
"What's your guess," he asked, "will 
Arnie Maxin be taking over?"

Krasnow credited Blue Thumb's suc-

proach. Instead of the normal album 
blowups 
and 
die -cut jacket "ap- 
proach," Blue Thumb introduced its 
product with a light show in the win-

Vine, created such a stir that the store 
kept it in an extra week. As a result 
of the traffic and sales created by the 
light show, E. J. Korvette will put 26 
special W. C. Fields windows in its 
stores. 
To further help merchandise the 
Fields' LP, Blue Thumb this week 
will ship 500 deluxe W. C. Fields in- 
store merchandisers at a cost of nearly 
$13,000. Each is five -and -a -half feet 
high, and in the shape of W. C. Fields 
himself. There is a browser box (com- 
ing out of Fields stomach) that holds 
25 LPs. The W. C. Fields nose on the 
display is in dayglo. 
Two weeks ago, Blue Thumb held 
a "Halloween Seance" for W. C. Fields 
in an effort to bring the comedian 
"back" so that he could listen to his 
LP. "It sounds whacky," Krasnow ex- 
plained, "but what it did was get us 
exposure for both Blue Thumb and the 
album on both the ABC and CBS tele- 
vision networks." 
Krasnow is now readying two new 
LPs. One by an English group, Ains- 
ley-Dunbar (release around Jan. 1). 
Release plans call for TV exposure 
of the product. "We'll buy commer- 
cial time on TV with the act. That's 
the kind of act they are-visual-and 
that's the best way for us to expose the 
product. In this case, displays aren't 
needed." 
Krasnow has also signed Berkely 
guitarist/singer Robbie Basho. First 
LP from Basho is set for early Jan- 
uary. 
Leonard To 
Famous Music 
LOS ANGELES - Famous Music 
has appointed Jack Leonard as a pro- 
fessional man, as the firm continues 
its expansion activities. Leonard will 
be based at the company's Hollywood 
headquarters 
in 
the 
Sunset -Vine 
Tower Building. 
His appointment 
closely follows the publishing firm's 
recent acquisition of the services of 
George Sherlock, who joined the west 
coast professional staff several months 
ago. Both men report directly to Jay 
Lowy, general professional manager, 
who is stationed in New York. 
Unlike most music business execu- 
tives, Jack Leonard gained recognition 
initially as a performer. A New York- 
er by birth, Leonard was one of the 
late Tommy Dorsey's first bandsing- 
ers and gained widespread popularity 
as the voice on such Dorsey hits as 
"Marie," "Once In A While" and 
many others. After a five-year asso- 
ciation with the band, Leonard was 
replaced by another well-known sing- 
er, Frank Sinatra. 
Leonard segued into the business 
end of the music scene when he moved 
to the west coast to assume the posi- 
tion of Nat Cole's music coordinator, 
a station he held for fifteen years until 
Cole's death. 
In 1966, following Cole's demise, 
Leonard joined Percy Faith's publish- 
ing operation as professional manager 
of Marpet Music, which position he 
held till now. 
From Z. to r., Famous Music West 
Coast professional man George Sher- 
lock, newly added professional man 
Jack Leonard and William R. Stin- 
son, executive V.P. and general man- 
ager of Paramount Pictures Music 
Publishing companies.

Pop Best Bets 
THE WOZARD OF IZ-A&M SP 4156 
One of the most unusual albums released 
this year, "The Wozard of Iz-An Electronic 
Odyssey," uses the plot of the children's 
classic, "The Wizard Of Oz," to spin an adult 
fable of modern society. Jacques Wilson con- 
ceived the odyssey and wrote the script and 
the lyrics. He also narrates the LP. The 
electronic music was composed and realized 
(on the Moog Synthesizer) by Mort Garson. 
Suzie Jane Hokum is Dorothy; Barney Phil- 
lips is the Scared Crow; Jay Jasin is the In - 
Man; Barney Phillips is the Lyin' Coward. 
This set could become a popular left field 
item. 
STRICTLY PERSONAL-Capt. Beefheart & 
His Magic Band-Blue Thumb S1 
Capt. Beefheart and company, a west coast 
group, have already built a strong. rep 
through personal appearances and a previous 
LP on another label. The group is into 
effect as much as it is into music, and this 
album holds surprises and should qualify 
for good underground airplay. Tunes include 
"Safe As Milk," "Beatle Bones 'N' Smokin 
Stones," and "Kandy Korn." 
SOONER OR LATER-John Hammond- 
Atlantic SD 8206 
John Hammond is one of the most respected 
of the current crop of white blues singers, 
and certainly one of the most authentic and 
proficient. His earlier sides have built him 
a devoted following, and that, coupled with 
the recent blues resurgence, should help make 
this second set for Atlantic a success. Tunes, 
all old blues numbers, include "Shake Your 
Money Maker," "Sugar Mama," "Evil Is 
Going On," and "Don't Start Me Talking." 
FALLING OFF THE EDGE OF THE 
WORLD-Easybeats-United Artists UAS 
6667 
Although hitless for a while, the Easy - 
beats still have plenty of good, commercial 
music in them, more than enough to power 
their second album to strong sales. The 
Australian quintet relies mostly on original 
material, but their versions of "Hit The 
Road Jack" and "Can't Take My Eyes Off 
Of You" have strong impact. "Falling Off 
The Edge Of The World" (a recent single) 
and "Gonna Have A Good Time" (a good bet 
for their next single) are highlights. 
TALK TO 
ME, BABY!-Michael Dees- 
Capitol ST 104 
Singer Michael Dees' new LP is a musical 
delight. Drawing on a wide variety of sources, 
Dees, with the help of arrangers Bob Bain, 
Billy May, and Jimmy Jones, shows up 
strongly on such tunes as "Eleanor Rigby," 
"For Once In My Life," "The Windmills Of 
Your Mind," "The Gentle Rain," "Nice 
'N' Easy," and "Somewhere." Set has excel- 
lent middle-of-the-road potential. 
ISLAND IN THE SKY-Tuneful Trolley- 
Capitol ST 110 
Produced by Jay and the Americans, this 
LP could gain the attention of a wide 
listenership. The Tuneful Trolley, in eleven 
rock ditties, delivers lots of bright, sunny 
sounds. Particularly piquant are "Hello Love," 
"Sunny Days," "Lovely Day," and "I Got 
You Around." Give this one a spin; it might 
catch fire. 
Jazz Picks 
CONCERTO FOR HERD-Woody Herman -- 
Verve V6 8764 
Woody Herman brought the latest edition 
of his Thundering Herd to Monterey for the 
Tenth Annual Jazz Festival, and Verve was 
there to capture the action. Parts of Her- 
man's performance were aired on an NET 
TV special, creating a substantial audience 
for this set. Side one is Bill Holman's three - 
movement "Concerto For Herd," the Festival 
closer. Side Two features three new composi- 
tions, "Big Sur Echo," "The Horn Of The 
Fish," and "Woody's Boogaloo." 
NEW YORK IS NOW VOL. 1-Omette Cole- 
man-Blue Note BST 84287 
Omette Coleman, who plays alto sax and 
violin on this set, wrote all five pieces on 
the disk. Supported by Dewey Redman, tenor 
sax; Jimmy Garrison, bass; and Elvin Jones, 
drums, Coleman wends his way through the 
long (14:03), sinuous "The Garden Of Souls;" 
"Tay Dance;" the wild, frenetic "We Now 
Interrupt For A Commercial;" "Broad Way 
Blues;" and "Round Trip." Coleman fanciers 
will want to own this one.

ARTIE SHAW RE-CREATES HIS GREAT 
'38 BAND-Capitol 2992 
The next logical step after electronic re - 
channeling of old favorites, re-recording old 
favorites using today's modern audio facil- 
ities, has been taken by Artie Shaw on his 
first album in some 14 years. Choosing such 
memorables as `Begin The Beguine," "Lover 
Come Back To Me," "What Is This Thing 
Called Love," and "Softly, As In A Morning 
Sunrise," Shaw demonstrates why his brand 
of music captivated so many listeners. 
HEADS UP-Blue Mitchell-Blue Note BST 
84272 
Trumpeter Blue Mitchell should greatly 
enhance his reputation with "Heads Up!" 
His playing on the set is superb all the way 
through. From the first track, "Heads Up! 
Feet Down!" to the last number, Blue's own 
composition, "The People In Nassau," the 
artist is in rare form. He is excellently sup- 
ported by Burt Collins (trumpet), Julian 
Priester (trombone), Jerry Dodgion (alto 
sax, flute), Junior Cook (tenor sax), Pepper 
Adams (baritone sax), McCoy Tyner (piano), 
Gene Taylor (bass), and Al Foster (drums). 
TCHAIKOVSKY: 1812 OVERTURE/RACH- 
MANINOFF: 
SPRING/THREE 
FOLK 
SONGS-Buketoff/Various Ensembles-RCA 
LS`C 3051 
This new recording of the "1812 Overture" 
includes "choruses adding the original famous 
Russian songs and chants which Tchaikovsky 
used as themes for this work." Many re- 
cordings have been made of the "1812," 
and this is one of the most ambitious. On 
the other side of the disk is the first record- 
ing of Rachmaninoff's "Spring" Cantata, Op. 
20, as well as his "Three Russian Folk 
Songs," Op. 41. The Rachmaninoff works are 
particularly lovely. 
HILDE SOMER PLAYS SCRIABIN-Mer- 
cury SR 90500 
Pianist Hilde Somer gives excellent per- 
formances of a dozen pieces by Russian com- 
poser Alexander Scriabin (1872-1915) on this 
album. The artist plays with a combination of 
technical skill and spirit that satisfies the 
listener's desire for both form and freedom. 
From the shortest prelude (51 seconds) to 
the 8 -minute Sonata No. 4, the LP is a de- 
light. Should do well in classical circles.

FOCUS ON JAZZ 
IWI 
Much of today's recorded jazz con- 
cerns itself with the new movement, 
freedom of expression. I would not 
attempt to guess what the percentage 
is, but suffice to say that what started 
out as a movement has now become a 
very valid and acceptable part of the 
state of jazz. As in all matters explor- 
atory, much of what is being attempt- 
ed in this area is highly experimental 
and, as such, often is far from what is 
the finished product. To some this 
might create an unsatisfactory state 
of affairs; to others it might provide 
a form of reference for the develop- 
ment of a particular artist's concep- 
tion. In either case, we should all be 
aware of the fact that jazz is now, 
more than ever, in a state of flux. 
John Handy, an exceptionally gifted 
musician, is one such artist whose 
musical probings are worthy of com- 
ment. Characteristic to this type of 
musical investigation is his latest al- 
bum on Columbia, "Projections." The 
album was recorded in New York in 
April of this year and is symbolic of 
the John Handy approach to jazz. 
What makes it particularly note- 
worthy is the fact that a couple of 
the selections on the album are things 
that Handy had recorded before, in 
the early Sixties when he was affiliat- 
ed with Roulette Records. Listening to 
the original treatments and then com- 
paring them with the 1968 versions 
gives one a very clearly defined ref- 
erence for the change in conception 
that has takn place in his music. 
Handy has chosen to bill his quintet, 
and very aptly, as the Concert Ensem- 
ble. Unlike much of what is accepted 
as jazz today, this is genuinely an 
ensemble endeavor, as opposed to a 
series of connected solos, with rhythm 
accompaniment. At this point it might 
be worth mentioning that the cohe- 
siveness that is attained by the quin- 
tet is one of the most extraordinary 
aspects of this album. However, the 
group feeling never seems to impede 
the freedom that is so much a part 
of this recording. Actually, it's the 
wedding of the two elements, the 
togetherness and the freedom, that 
makes the music very much apart 
from what we're accustomed to hear- 
ing in the new jazz. Knowing John 
Handy's background, it's perfectly 
understandable that he feels a definite 
commitment to his musical roots as 
well as a compelling need to probe and 
expand and build upon his attitudes 
and his experiences. I think it would 
be accurate to state that what makes 
John Handy's music unique is the 
fact that he has not forsaken the past 
in deference to the present. He is one 
of the few who finds the eras com- 
patible. Representative Album 
This is not intended as a review of 
MORT FEGA 
his album, but in view of the fact that 
this new Handy album is so repre 
sentative of the group's sound, 
it 
might be noteworthy to make somE 
observations about the album. Of par- 
amount importance, I think, is the 
vast scope of music that is embracec 
within the eight selections that com- 
prise the album. At different intervals 
The Concert Ensemble is delicate; 
frantic, lyrical, melancholy, in truth, 
a collection of virtually all the musi- 
cal truths. Handy's primary instru- 
ment is the alto saxophone; however, 
for the shadings that he finds neces- 
sary, on occasion he does play the 
reasonably obscure saxello, an instru- 
ment that approximates the sound 
of the soprano sax, and an occasional 
statement on the flute. Michael White, 
the violinist in the group, must be 
hailed as one of the most phenomenal 
players to come to our attention in a 
long time... he's definitely something 
else! Heightening the importance of 
White's contribution is the tremendous 
interplay that goes on between him 
and the leader, Handy. The rhythm 
section of Mike Nock on piano, Bruce 
Cale on bass, and Larry Hancock on 
drums is really much more than a 
rhythm section. Their efforts are so 
much a part of the texture of the 
group that they must be considered 
voices unto themselves. There are 
eight selections on this Columbia al- 
bum; they are all originals, four by 
John Handy, three by Mike Nock, and 
one by Michael White. The aggregate 
sound of this group performing these 
eight selections comes very close to 
being an entire musical experience, 
something that very seldom occurs 
within the framework of one jazz 
group. 
I must confess that I'm at a loss to 
understand why John Handy's name 
is not treated with greater authority 
when the leaders of the new jazz 
movement are being considered. I do 
know that in the California area, par- 
ticularly in The Bay area, Handy is 
virtually lionized. Naturally, I haven't 
heard all the jazz groups that play 
free jazz, but of those that I have 
heard, either in person or on record, 
his is the most sophisticated link be- 
tween the established form and the 
new thing. Handy's music is so to- 
gether! And because it is, he should 
be heard at every possible opportun- 
ity. His group should be booked into 
every college campus, every jazz club, 
concert hall that prides itself on pre- 
senting contemporary music. The John 
Handy Concert Ensemble is made up 
of all the components that constitute 
good music: extraordinary virtuosity, 
an unbelievable group sound, a re- 
flection on yesterday, and an eye 
beyond the horizon. Isn't that what 
music, especially jazz, is all about?

GMA Re -Elects 
Myers President 
NEW YORK-The Gospel Music As- 
sociation has re-elected W. F. "Jim" 
Myers to a second term as president. 
Myers, executive administrator and 
director of international relations for 
SESAC, the music licensing organiza- 
tion, is the first two -term president in 
GMA history. 
Myers, long active in gospel music 
circles, was acclaimed for his leader- 
ship during the past year. Through 
his efforts, the association made tre- 
mendous strides and its membership 
was more than doubled at the conven- 
tion held in Memphis. 
Other officers elected to serve with 
Myers were Hovie Lister, first vice 
president; Paul Marks, second vice 
president; Marvin Norcross, secretary; 
and Bob Benson, who was named to 
serve as treasurer for another year. 
Bob 
MacKenzie 
of Heartwarming 
Records was named chairman of the 
board, succeeding James Blackwood. 
Newly elected board members include 
Buck 
Rambo, 
Larry 
Orrell, 
Bob 
Woltering, Mrs. Lou Wills Hildreth, 
Bernie Zondervan, Mrs. Tillie Lowery, 
J. D. Summer, Ed Shea, Les Beasley 
and Travis 
Wolfe. Continuing to 
serve on the Association's board were 
holdovers Herman Harper, Harvey 
Lester, Bill Williams, Pierce LeFevre, 
Wes Gilmer, Conner Hall, Doug Mc- 
Clure, Bill Gaither, Joel Gentry, Ar- 
mond Morales and SESAC's Norman 
Odlum. 
President Myers announced that 
the new board will meet on January 
13th in Nashville.

This was the week that was for classical music in Germany as the record 
ndustry presented the first gala series in Berlin. The festivities opened on 
he 14th of November with opera. International favorites Sylvia Geszty, 
Gundula Janowitz, Anna Moffo, Kurt Boehme, James King, Rudolf Schock, 
Giuseppe Taddei and the Radio Symphony Orchestra -Berlin directed by 
tobert Heger presented their best. On the following day, chamber music was 
'eatured with Grace Bumbry, Ingrid Haebler, Jacqueline du Pré, Gustav 
Leonhardt, Frans Brueggen, Anner Bylsma and the Trio di Trieste. The third 
mnd final night featured symphony concerts with Martha Argerich, Maurice 
André, Arthur Grumiaux and the New Philharmonia Orchestra -London under 
;he direction of Erich Leinsdorf. 
All concerts were taped in color and will be broadcast here, in Spain, Austria, 
Vorway, Denmark, Finland, Holland, Yugoslavia, Portugal and Switzerland. 
[t was quite an event and should herald a new era in the popularity and 
axposure of excellent classical music the world over. 
The five D.J.'s have been set for the pirate station "Radio Nordsee." Pro- 
gram Director Klaus Quirini has lined up Dester Wilken from Essen, Pascal 
Posee from Moenchengladbach, Udo Klein from Neuwied, Horst Reiner from 
Krefeld and Roy West from Eschweiler. The station which will feature music, 
music, music will start broadcasting soon. 
Louis Armstrong is set to visit Germany covering Stuttgart, Berlin, Hann- 
over, Bonn, Frankfurt and Munich. 
Right now, Jimmy Smith and his trio are touring along with the Supremes. 
Peter Lach from Capriccio Music writes that his big push items are the 
music from the German TV series "Rinaldo Rinaldini" and the LP "Gospel 
Train" from Knut Kiesewetter and the Kay -Kays. 
These are the days for Hans Gerig Music as "Those Were The Days" con- 
tinues to garner top honors. The record from Mary Hopkin is high in the 
charts and two new instrumental versions from Larry Page and Zack Laurence 
add to the growing list of recordings of this important song. Another top 
item for Gerig is "Little Arrows" with the Leapy Lee version moving over 
the 50,000 sales mark and 3 new German versions out by Caterina Valente on 
Decca, Vic Dana on Liberty and newcomer Toni on Philips. Terrific results on 
local recordings as nobody-and we mean nobody-gets more than 3 vocal cover 
versions of a song. 
Peter Kirsten of Global Music has a pair of must items going for him now 
with "Listen To Me" from the Hollies and "A Little Bit Of This" with David 
Garrick getting top action here. 
The second German TV is readying the second "Show -Chance" featuring 
young professional talent. The show, set to discover undiscovered stars, will 
be telecast in April next year in color and will also be carried by Swiss and 
Austrian TV. The first such show was broadcast in October of last year. 
That's it for this week in Germany.

Best selling records in October have been announced by each company as 
follows: Victor -RCA's No. 1 single of the month was "D. W. Washburn" by 
the Monkees followed by "Baby, Come Back" by the Equals and "Elevator" 
by the Grapefruit. As for LP sales, "The Monkees Golden Story" has kept the 
top position concurrent with the group's Japan tour. Victor -World Group has 
made the best sales with two new singles: "Hello I Love You" by the Doors 
and "The Little Bird" by Nancy Sinatra. Philips Records Dept. sold Vicky's 
recording of a Japanese composition, "Watashi-no Sukina Chocolate," and 
"Rain And Tears" by the Aphrodite Child, as well as succeeded in the revival 
of "Sunny" by Bobby Hebb. Columbia's top selling singles are all from the 
Buddah material: two singles by 1910 Fruitgum Co., "1, 2, 3 Red Light" and 
"Simon Says"; "Yummy Yummy Yummy" by the Ohio Express; and "Rice 
Is Nice" by the Lemon Pipers. The only exception is Marie Laforet's record- 
ing of "Sound Of Silence." At King Records the chart remains for these 
months with "Jumpin' Jack Flash" and "Tell Me" by the Rolling Stones, but 
following them recent releases have appeared such as "Twenty Ten" by the 
Tinkabell Fairydust, "0 Meu Corolla" by Claudia and "Be My Baby" by the 
Ronettes. Grammophon is still selling "The Dock of The Bay" by Otis Redding, 
"Purple Haze" by Jimi Hendrix and "Hold On" by Sam & Dave. Toshiba's 
top single was the Beatles' "Hey Jude b/w Revolution." 
Dunhill Records has been distributed here by Victor -RCA since December, 
1965, but in accordance with the recent EMI aquirement of the oversee dis- 
tribution rights on Dunhill Records, the release of the catalog is going to be 
made by Toshiba Records under, its exclusive repertoire contracts with EMI. 
The .Dunhill material will be launched by Toshiba under the Stateside label, 
and the initial release will consist of three singles: "California Earthquake" 
by Mama Cass with the Mamas & Papas, "Magic Carpet Ride b/w Sookie 
Sookie" by the Steppenwolf and "Midnight Confessions" by the Grass Roots, 
and two LPs by Mamas & Papas and the Steppenwolf. Victor -RCA keeps the 
rights of manufacturing the already released records until March, 1969, but the 
move of the Dunhill catalog will be a great loss to the international repertoire 
of Victor -RCA Dept. 
Victor -Philips is launching the second LP record of the Philippine group 
D'Swooners, encouraged by the favorable reaction to their debut album which 
is the label's best selling local LP at present. The second album is entitled 
"Portrait Of D'Swooners" and includes "Dock of the Bay," "Sunshine Love," 
"Light My Fire," etc. This group receives requests especially on the midnight 
radio programs. Aiming at the same success, Victor -World Group has launch- 
ed an American R&B group, the House Rockers. This group, composed of two 
singers and seven instrumentalists, was first founded at a U.S. army camp 
near Tokyo thirteen years ago, has become very popular among the army 
camps. The recent rise of R&B boom in Japan spotlighted the group and 
they started to be booked for a famous discoteque in Tokyo. This public 
appearance made their popularity rapidly increase among the Japanese so as 
to get a chance of cutting their first LP for Victor, "Golden R&B/Memphis 
Sound: The House Rockers" with such standard numbers as "Hold On," 
"Knock On Wood" and "The Dock Of The Bay." 
Trini Lopez arrived at Tokyo on November 6th for a week tour. His first 
tour in Japan in autumn last year was quite successful and the live recording 
of a concert here released in an album entitled "Trini Lopez in Tokyo" has 
been selling well. This time he did three concerts in Tokyo, one TV show and 
four night club performances in a week. He added his new reportoire to the 
concert programs, "Guantanamera" and "Sally Was A Good Old Girl," and 
also some titles included in his latest album "Welcome To Trini's Country."

Decca, Kapp Shift Major Executives 
Goldberg Runs Kapp; Wied'mann Decca VP 
NEW YORK-There has been a major 
switch in executive functions between 
the Decca and Kapp labels. 
The labels are both part of the 
MCA disk operation, yet are in direct 
competition with each other "all the 
way down the line," as termed by 
Berle Adams, exec vp of MCA. 
Adams said that Jack Wiedenmann 
and Tony Martell will move over to 
the Decca label, while three former 
Decca execs will guide the future of 
Kapp. They are Syd Goldberg, 35 - 
year Decca veteran who will serve as 
vp and general manager; Lou ,Sebok, 
who will become director of sales; 
and Jack Kiernan, who will direct 
national sales. 
Adams indicated that Goldberg and 
Sebok would broaden Kapp's activities 
in the area of full catalog growth, a 
concept that both execs instituted at 
Martino Shifts 
Home To W. Coast 
NEW YORK-Singer Al Martino has 
taken up permanent residence in Los 
Angeles. A former homeowner in 
Cherry Hill, N.J., the Capitol song- 
ster has just purchased a home on the 
west coast. Martino said that a lot of 
calls for TV work was a major con- 
sideration in making the move. Cur- 
rently playing the Royal York in 
Toronto, Martino plays his first date 
in four years at the Copacabana in 
New York starting Jan. 30. His cur- 
rent Capitol 
single 
is 
the Hank 
Williams favorite, "I Can't Help It 
If I'm Still in Love with You." 
Stations Get Xmas 
Goodies From Col. 
NEW YORK-Fourteen Christmas 
singles, including four newcomers for 
1968, have been assembled in a special 
"Christmas Goodies from Columbia 
Records" package 
directed at the 
label's subscribing stations. The pack- 
age of 45's, notes Ron Alexenburg, 
the label's national promo head, is 
mailed as well as being hand delivered 
by branch managers to the stations 
in their markets. 
The new singles are by Corky Hale, 
Andy Williams, Robert Goulet and 
Burl Ives. Previous years' release 
include Anita Bryant, Patti Page, 
Barbra Streisand, Aretha Franklin, 
Mahalia Jackson, Jim Nabors, Ray 
Conniff, the New Christy Minstrels, 
Carl Grant. Winifred Atwell.

the label to its biggest year in history.

Pockeldiscs To 
TORONTO: Harvey Kalef, general 
manager Park Lane Recordings, has 
just returned from New York after a 
round of talks involving marketing 
features 
etc. for the 
bowing of 
American new pocketdisc, which is set 
for the premium market January 1. 
It's not expected to have product for 
the consumer until early Spring. 
Kalef is excited over the prospects 
of this new product for Canada in 
['HE CLINGERS are shown above 
igning an exclusive contract with 
'olumbia 
Records. 
Accompanying 
hem at the launching of their disk 
areer are CBS Records president 
live Davis (center male) and their 
xcutive 
producer 
Bones 
Howe 
right). The girls sessions will be 
produced under supervision of Toxey 
French and Jeff Comanor. Spearhead- 
ing their recording exposures will be 
eight upcoming Smothers Brothers 
Show shots during the current season 
with negotiations now pending for a 
series of added tv performances. 
Canada Jan, 1 
view of the impact Pocketdiscs made 
in the test area of Seattle, Washing- 
ton. During the period of time from 
Oct. 16 to Nov. 18 there have been 
160,000 sales registered, according to 
Kalef. The breaking point for success 
in this market was 100,000 over a 
three week period. Kalef was quoted 
as saying, "Pocketdisc will do to the 
record industry what the transistor 
did to radio." 
The big selling point for Pocket - 
disc is the pilfer -proof vending ma- 
chine. Kalef hopes to have a vending 
machine capable 
of storing 
300 
Pocketdiscs by the time he is ready to 
roll for the consumer in the spring. It 
is also hoped to keep the price of the 
product on a par with the U.S., which 
is 490 per disk. Much emphasis is to 
be placed on de -centralizing the record 
industry, particularly in the Toronto 
area and other large metropolitan 
areas across Canada. The Pocketdisc 
vending machines can be located in 
super markets, variety stores etc. 
Another interesting point of sale is 
the almost non-destructive make-up of 
Pocketdisc, through its chemical base 
of polyvinyl chloride, obtained from 
France. Machines now being installed 
at Park Lane will be capable of pro- 
ducing over 6000 Pocketdiscs per 
hour. Masters are cut locally at Arc 
Sound. 
Kalef is also working on a light- 
weight portable transitor radio and 
Pocketdisc player, to be manufactured 
under the trade name of Symphonic, 
a Japanese product. This is also ex- 
pected to be ready by early spring. 
A mailing of a Pocketdisc, with a 
suitable message and a sampling of 
Tiny Tim, has already been sent out 
to industry people in Canada. Jim 
Webb, who is working closely with 
Kalef on promoting Pocketdisc, has 
found excellent distributor, store and 
record company interest. One down- 
town Toronto record store has ex- 
pressed 
"exceptional" 
interest 
in 
Pocketdisc.

NEW YORK - Columbia Records' 
Andy Williams will be back as a TV 
regular as part of a new long-term 
contract with the National Broadcast- 
ing Company. Beginning next Fall, 
Williams will resume the weekly 
variety show that netted him three 
Emmy Awards in 1963, 1966 and 1967.

at the end of the 1967 season, has 
been doing specials for the network, 
the next of which will be his eighth 
annual Christmas show, skedded for 
Thursday, Dec. 19.

B.B. King Booked For 
Variety Of '69 PA's 
NEW YORK-Veteran blues singer 
B.B. King, an ABC Records artist, 
has been set for a varied series of 
personal appearances in 1969 by Joe 
Glaser, president of Associated Book- 
ing. 
King, who not too long ago was to 
be heard primarily in Negro and 
southern situations, is to be exposed 
in many other types of outlets- 
ranging from underground boites to 
traditional pop night clubs. Sand- 
wiched between will be appearances at 
important jazz festivals and college 
dates. 
During January and February King 
will have engagements at several 
major spots in the east. These include 
stints at The Village Gate and The 
Fillmore East in New York; The Jazz 
Festival and The Boston Tea Party, 
Boston; The Showboat, Philadelphia; 
The Living Room, Cincinnati and Kent 
University. 
King's professional activities are 
co-ordinated by his own Memphis - 
based B. B. Productions and the Sid- 
ney Seidenberg offices in New York. 
Seidenberg is also King's business 
manager.

LOS ANGELES-Senator George 
Murphy (Republican -Calif.) will co- 
sponsor legislation that would pave 
the way for royalty payments to re- 
cording artists and record companies 
for the commercial use of their re- 
corded works. 
Senator Murphy's co-sponsorship of 
the legislation was revealed by Stan 
Kenton, Chairman of the National 
Committee for the Recording Arts. 
The NCRA, comprised of the na- 
tion's recording artists, was organized 
two years ago to gain support for the 
proposed Williams Amendment to the 
new Copyright Legislation currently 
pending before Congress. The amend- 
ment would give artists, musicians, 
arrangers and record companies copy- 
right protection similar to that en- 
joyed by composers and publishers for 
the past 50 years. 
Kenton Cites Need 
In an address prepared for a meet- 
ing of the California Copyright Con- 
ference at the Hollywood Plaza Hotel 
here last Tues. (26), Kenton said 
that "a large portion of the enter- 
tainment industry exists primarily, 
if not solely, by the use of recorded 
music. Yet, these users pay nothing 
to the performers for the commercial 
use of their creations." Kenton said 
that recorded music is used in about 
"75 per cent of all radio air time and 
this time accounts for more than 80 
per cent of radio revenue-about $800 
million." 
Monument Studio Near 
NASHVILLE - Monument Records 
new sound studio, located in the 
former McNairy Street Cumberland 
Presbyterian Church on 17th Ave. 
South and McGavock Sts., is nearing 
completion. 
Following renovation, the studio 
will accommodate: a 19 by 27 foot con- 
trol and re -mix room; a studio 33 by 
39 feet with 23 foot high ceilings; 
a 
16 -foot -square lacquer cubicle; a 
19 by 27 foot recreation room; four 
accoustical echo chambers; four EMT 
echo chambers; a 12 by 14 foot bus- 
iness office; and a large tape storage 
area. The studio console will accommo- 
date 20 mike inputs and eight channel 
outputs, with direct submix to 4, 2, 
or 1, wet or dry. The console also con- 
tains three cue circuits and four echo 
feed and returns on any or all inputs. 
And all stereo has pan pots to give 
dimension and depth to stereo re- 
cordings. The console will include au- 
tomatic control for selsyncing rec- 
ords. According to Mort Thomasson, 
Monument engineer and construction 
coordinator, "The studio is being de- 
signed primarily to accommodate the 
artists and musicians who will be re- 
cording. It is this feature which has 
been ommitted by more recent studio 
construction. We have planned the 
studio with the comfort of the artists 
and musicians in mind." 
Initially, the sound facilities will be 
used exclusively by Monument Record 
Corporation artists. 
Kenton added that radio stations 
pay to composers and publishers about 
$20 million in royalties, or 2.8 per 
cent of total broadcast 
expenses 
annually. 
He added, "Senator Murphy has 
long been an ardent supporter of fair 
and equitable compensation for the 
creative efforts of people throughout 
the entertainment industry. His co- 
sponsorship of the amendment is a 
great start for this legislation in the 
new Congressional year." 
Senator Harrison Williams (Demo-' 
crat-New 
Jersey) 
introduced 
the 
amendment during the 90th Congress 
as part of the Copyright Law Revi- 
sion Legislation under consideration 
by the Senate Judiciary Committee's 
Patents, Trademarks and Copyrights 
Subcommittee. 
'Moonshot' Probe Is 
New Probe Single 
NEW YORK-The most fantastic 
space probe yet-the flight of men 
around the moon-is the subject mat- 
ter of a rush -release single from 
Probe Records. 
In effect the disk, the output of 
writer/producers John Cacavas and 
Charles Wood, is a complete two-part 
musical spectacular based on the Apol- 
lo Moon Program, which reaches new 
heights Dec. 21 in an attempt to 
send three astronauts around the 
moon in Apollo 8. "Moonshot: The 
Fantastic Voyage" depicts a spatial 
trip combining the delicate tones of 
"Twinkle, Twinkle Little Star" with 
the electronic -effect world of space 
control, and finally both segue into 
the sounds of today's rock tempo and 
an original lyrical ballad. Charles 
Osgood Wood is a radio news broad- 
caster, now with WCBS, the ALL 
News CBS flagship station in New 
York. Wood personally covered all 
of the Gemini space flights for the 
ABC Radio Network, mingled with 
many of the astronauts and space 
officials, and when he heard about the 
exciting plans for Apollo 8, had an 
idea for a song. "Hello moon," it 
would say, "My name is man. I've 
been watching you since the world 
began." He broached the idea to his 
partner, 
composer/arranger 
John 
Cacavas, with whom he has produced 
other topical projects such as Senator 
Everett McKinley Dirksen's hit al- 
bum "Gallant Men," and "Black Is 
Beautiful," Nancy Wilson's current 
show stopping single. 
Writing for Chappell & Co. Inc., 
publishers, the team has recently been 
pursuing an intensified program of 
rock and contemporary acquisitions 
and a nurturing of youthful pop com- 
bos. "Moonshot: The Fantastic Voy- 
age" was produced by John Cacavas 
and Charles Wood as part of this 
continuing movement into the con- 
temporary musical scene.

Philips Inks New 
Classical Artists 
BAARN-Philips' Phonographic In- 
dustries has signed contracts with 
several new classical artists. The 
classical catalogue will include the 
names of Irish lyric tenor Frank Pat- 
terson, Swiss pianist Dinorah Varsi, 
Italian pianist Michele Campanella, 
Dutch soprano Christine Deutekom, 
Swiss oboist Heinz 
Holliger, and 
Dutch soprano Elly Ameling. Philips 
also signed a contract with the Dutch 
conductor Edo de Waart. whose first 
recording for Philips-with the Neth- 
erlands Wind Ensemble-was released 
last month. Pianist Stephen Bishop, 
born in America of Yugoslav parents, 
recently made recordings with Philips 
of Beethoven's 
Diabelli Variations 
and Brahms's Variations on a Theme 
of Handel, both due for release. 
Another Big Song 
By Felix Stahl 
STOCKHOLM - Music 
publisher 
Felix Stahl, who is also composer of 
a number of songs, of which "Many 
Times" is the one that gained the big- 
gest international reputation some ten 
years ago (it topped the British 
charts as well as the American), has 
done it again. His "(Take Back Your) 
Souvenirs" has just been recorded in 
Britain by Frankie Vaughan on a 
Columbia EMI recording. There are 
also American recordings of the tune 
available by now, Stahl reports. 
Swedish lyrics of "Souvenirs" have 
been written by Lisbeth Stahl and the 
British lyrics are signed 
Norman 
Newell. Lisbeth Stahl (Mrs. Felix 
Stahl) writes the Swedish lyrics to 
most of her husband's songs. 
W. Berlin Mayor 
Greets Carla 
WEST BERLIN-Carla Thomas cap- 
ped a successful performance at the 
Berlin Jazz Festival on Nov. 10 by 
meeting West Berlin Mayor Heinrich 
Alberty and his wife, who gifted her 
with champagne backstage after the 
concert. 
She was the only solo female vo- 
calist appearing in the festival, which 
is sponsored by the West German 
government. Other artists included 
Horace Silver and Muddy Waters, 
who Carla joined for a chorus of "Got 
My Mojo Workin'." 
"After the concert, guards came 
backstage and a few minutes later the 
mayor of West Berlin and his wife 
came into my dressing room," the Stax 
star said. "We drank champagne, 
which they'd brought, and talked for 
twenty minutes. 
The artist flew to West Berlin es- 
pecially for the concert. After making 
her appearance, she returned to New 
York where she is studying at the 
American Academy of Dramatic Art.

Saturday's Weiss 
Talks With EMI 
LONDON-Larry Weiss of Saturday 
Music recently spent two weeks in 
Britain for talks with L. G. Wood of 
EMI and Fred Marks and Phil Green- 
e') of Ardmore & Beechwood, EMI's 
publishing affiliate. 
Also Famous - 
Chappell, which publishes the Bob 
Crewe penned "Barbarella" film score 
soundtrack of which is issued here on 
Stateside. Solomon King's new Colum- 
bia single is an original Saturday 
copyright by contract writers Larry 
Brown and Raymond Bloodwater pub- 
lished here through Ardmore & Beech - 
wood. Weiss was very enthusiastic 
about new group The Glitterhouse, 
who waxed the title "Barbarella" and 
hopes to bring the boys to Europe 
early next year for a promotion tour. 
Their new album "Color Blind" is is- 
saed in the States on DynoVoice and 
in the U.K. on Stateside. During his 
British visit Weiss met up with John 
Rasmusson of Denmark; Bengt Sund- 
strom of Sweden and Alain de Ricou 
or France. 
According to Sol Rabinowitz, Mi- 
nucci will handle the acquisition of 
copyrights and catalogs of other mu- 
sic -publishing houses for representa- 
tion by CBS International's music - 
publishing subsidiaries. He will also 
negotiate 
for 
CBS 
International 
the manufacturing and distribution 
rights to hit recordings by other rec- 
ord companies. In addition, he will 
produce, with Rabinowitz, foreign - 
language recordings by CBS artists 
in the United States. 
Minucci comes to CBS International 
with background that covers all phas- 
es of the music industry, from pub- 
lishing and recording to composing 
scores for motion -picture and tele- 
vision productions. He is also a noted 
songwriter. As a composer, he was 
responsible for the scores of ABC - 
TV's documentary series "The Saga 
of Western Man," which included 
Emmy Award winner "Leonardo da 
Vinci." He also wrote the music for 
NBC -TV's drama "The Days of Our 
Youth." His songs, 
which include 
`Domani," "Felicia" and "I'll Never 
Know," have been recorded by such 
well-known artists as Julius LaRosa, 
Vic Damone, The Four Lads and Nat 
"King" Cole. 
Minucci holds both a diploma from 
the Conservatory of Music in Paler- 
mo, Italy, and a law degree from the 
University of Palermo. Since 1950, he 
has resided in the United States.

AFA -Noel Gay Deal 
NEW YORK-Ashley Famous Agen- 
cy, Inc. and Noel Gay Artists, Ltd., 
have concluded a formal reciprocal 
agreement for the representation of 
Ashley Famous Agency artists in the 
Variety, Personal Appearances and 
Light Entertainment Television fields 
throughout the United Kingdom and 
Europe, Ted Ashley, president of Ash- 
ley Famous Agency and Richard Arm- 
itage, managing director of Noel Gay 
Artists, said that Ashley Famous 
Agency will also represent clients of 
the Noel Gay Agency throughout the 
U.S. and Canada. Some of the Noel 
Gay artists represented by Ashley 
Famous Agency are: David Frost, 
Paul Jones and The Scaffold. 
The general manager of Noel Gay 
Artists, Ltd., Brian Hutch, will co- 
ordinate and supervise activities from 
their offices in London, with Joe Hig- 
gins as liaison for Ashley Famous 
Agency, based in New York.

TOSHIBA -APPLE DEAL: Toshiba Records and Apple Records have concluded 
a new distribution contract on the Apple label here. Under the terms of the 
new contract, Toshiba will distribute both singles and LP records on Apple 
label throughout Japan. The first singles to be released on Apple here is 
"Those Were The Days" b/w "Turn, Turn, Turn" by Mary Hopkin. The an- 
nouncement was made jointly in Tokyo by Ron Kass, managing director of 
Apple Records, Alex Mardas of Apple Electronics, Noriichiroh Ishizaka, ex- 
ecutive managing director of Toshiba Records, Shintaroh Asawa, director, and 
general manager of A & R division of Toshiba Records, and Makoto Katoh, 
chief of liaison section of Toshiba Records. At the same time, they announced 
that Mary Hopkin will make a promotional tour in Japan probably in February. 
Photo shows (left to right): Ishizaka, Kass, Mardas, Katoh and Asawa.

Patty Pravo Makes 
i st Visit To U.S. 
NEW YORK-Arriving in New 
York recently on her first visit to 
the United States, was Patty Pravo, 
a top Italian recording artist. 
Miss Pravo, an exclusive RCA Vic- 
tor artist, was invited to perform 
at a benefit for the Institute of Inter- 
national 
Education 
in 
Houston, 
Texas, on Thursday, November 21. 
The benefit this year was a salute 
to Italy, and its theme was "Italy 
Re -Discovered." 
Miss Pravo, a 20 -year -old singer, 
is a native of Venice. In addition 
to TV, concert, and club appearances 
in Italy, she has also toured the Con- 
tinent. Her RCA Italiana LP, "Patty 
Pravo," is in release in the United 
States. In Italy, her record of "La 
Bambola" has sold over a million 
copies. Another, "Sentimento," was 
in the Top 5 on the Italian charts. 
A highlight of Miss Pravo's visit 
was a reception -cocktail party on 
Monday evening, November 25, at the 
St. Regis Hotel, hosted by the Rec- 
ord International Department of the 
RCA Record Division. Among those 
in attendance were: 
Anna Moffo; 
Peggy March; Dario Soria, division 
vice president of the Record Inter- 
national Department of the 
RCA 
Record Division; James N. Bailey, 
manager of marketing administra- 
tion of the Record International De- 
partment of the RCA Record Division. 
Egidio Ortona, Italian Ambassador 
to the United States, was the guest 
of honor at the Houston gala. Also 
appearing was the Italian film maker 
Roberto Rosselini, who showed ex- 
cerpts from his soon -to -be released 
tele -film, "Survival." 
The benefit at Jones Hall, held 
annually, is attended by social, in- 
dustrial, and political figures from 
all over the southwest. 
Performers invited to perform in 
previous years were: Marlene Dietrich, 
Bea Lillie, Patachou, and Louis Arm- 
strong. 
The Institute of International Edu- 
cation is an organization devoted to 
the arranging of the exchange of stu- 
cities, there will be a film presenta- 
tion featuring Vista's new Fanta - 
Sound albums. 
These releases are 
packaged with multipage illustrated 
books of outstanding art work. The 
line includes stage and film successes. 
Bob Elliott, national sales manager 
of Walt Disney Music, will partici- 
pate in all the showings with regional 
sales managers in cities of their re- 
spective territories. 
Marty Kadish, eastern sales man- 
ager, will be co -host with Elliott in 
the cities of his territory. Jerry Wein- 
er will participate in cities out of 
his Cincinnati headquarters. Sandy 
Strohbach will be with Elliott in all 
eastern cities.

Crow-Chee Touring 
In College Drive 
NEW YORK-The husband and 
wife team called Crow-Chee is just 
completing a six week tour of on - 
campus coffee houses in a reputation - 
building trip that brought the writer - 
performer pair to some 30 major 
college grounds. 
The trip was launched under the 
creative direction of the team's pro- 
ducers Cashman, Pistilli and West. 
Traveling through the east and mid - 
west, Crow-Chee visited the Univ. of 
Minnesota, Tennessee, Kentucky most 
recently as the tour drew to a close. 
The act has also made a promotional 
film which is to be sent to 122 schools 
on the coffee house circuit as a means

record releases" according to C, P & 
W. The producers are planning to re- 
lease several cuts by Crow-Chee early 
next year.

Jack Tracy Goes Indie 
As Hollywood Producer 
LOS ANGELES-Jack Tracy, who 
has been A&R producer at Liberty 
for the past 21/z years, has resigned 
from the label to enter independent 
production work in Hollywood. 
Formerly with Mercury and the 
Chess -Checker 
group, 
Tracy 
has 
logged ten years of recording experi- 
ence with a variety of artists. His 
range spans work with Mike Nichols 
and Elaine 
May, 
Sarah Vaughn, 
Quincy Jones, Billy Eckstine, Woody 
Herman, Nilsson and the Johnny 
Mann Singers who earned a Grammy 
last year for "Up, Up & Away." 
He will continue to produce for Sue 
Raney, the Four Freshmen, and the 
comedy team of 'Skiles and Henderson 
for Liberty, now as an indie pro- 
ducer. 
Lucas Expansion 
Expands Quarters 
NEW YORK - The David Lucas 
music complex, consisting of two pub- 
lishing divisions, D'Lisa (ASCAPO 
and Pasmorchick (BMI); airecord pro- 
duction firm, Sata Fortas Attractions 
Ltd.; and David Lucas Associates Inc., 
composers and producers of music for 
TV and radio commercials, plus fea- 
ure films and TV scoring, is finalizing 
negotiations for larger quarters to 
house the multi -media complex about 
the first of the year. 
Lucas has recently been totally in- 
volved in the completion of music for 
two motion pictures and two single 
record releases, one a "Bubble Gum" 
single on Kama Sutra, and the other 
a progressive underground rock single, 
and an LP. 
Recently -added new faces in the 
creative wing of Lucas' office include 
United Artists recording artist Mike 
Manieri who is also an arranger/ 
composer/vibist and Downbeat Poll 
winner, formerly with Buddy Rich 
and Tim Hardin; composer -producer 
George Grant who currently has four 
pop records in or scheduled for re- 
lease; Joey Levine, one of the music 
business' most successful composers, 
who has been intimately associated 
with the development of the "Bubble 
Gum" 
sound with 
such 
hits as 
"Yummy Yummy Yummy" and four 
other current chart records; and com- 
poser Don Payne, who has been asso- 
ciated with Astrud Gilberto and Tony 
Bennett, and has had songs recorded 
by Chris Conner and Jackie and Roy. 
Payne has also written commercial 
music, for Halo among others. 
Roberta Cuber, who for the past 
three years has been Lucas' assistant, 
is organizing their first audio-visual 
presentation reel, and she will be 
serving those people who want to be 
kept abreast of what the complex has 
been providing and is able to provide. 
Lucas feels that these talented addi- 
tions to his already enormously tal- 
ented team will enable him to offer 
all of his clients the best of service 
in all of their fields.

WIOD-Miami, Fla., may well be 
able to lay claim to having built 
the 
world's 
smallest broadcasting 
studio, a two -by -two facility in Fort 
Lauderdale. The studio is in a tele- 
phone booth installed just inside the 
doorway of the courthouse press room, 
and provides a direct line for the 
transmission of news broadcasts from 
Fort 
Lauderdale through WIOD's 
news headquarters in Miami. News 
director Fred Mooke explained that 
Krauser, head of the outlet's Bro- 
ward County News Bureau, "wanted 
a live microphone up there so he could 
get good quality on his feeds to our 
office 25 miles away." At the same 
time, he didn't want the microphone 
out in the open on his pressroom desk. 
Space 
throughout the 
courthouse, 
however, was too cramped to supply 
a room for a radio broadcast studio. 
Not even a broom closet or extra jail 
cell was available. So Krauser hit on 
the idea of a phone booth in the press 
room. The mini -studio is completely 
air-conditioned, and has wall-to-wall 
carpeting. Lady visitors to the press 
room are even suggesting the need 
of drapes. And two artists have 
volunteered to paint impressionistic 
views of future mass communications 
for decorations on the walls. "It's 
fantastic the response I'm getting to 
this thing," says Krauser. "There's 
already a long line daily-single file, 
of course-of peole waiting for a 
tour of the studio."The WIOD news- 
man notes that the tiny studio has 
confused visitors to the courthouse, 
who enter the broadcasting booth 
searching for a place to deposit their 
dimes for telephone calls.

mas gift to its listeners. The outlet 
plans to cancel its commercials from 
5 p.m. Christmas Eve through mid-

Last week (6), a new program, 
"The Richter Scale Society," began 
on WRVR-FM-New York. The show, 
which takes its name from the Cali- 
fornia -based system that measures 
earthquakes, blankets everything from 
controversial guests to free -form news 
and weather reports. Conceived and 
directed by youthful host Bill Minkin 
and 20 -year -old producer Steve Prince, 
the program is heard from 12:30 to 
6:30 a.m. nights, Friday through Wed- 
nesday. Programmed in hourly seg- 
ments, the show includes an hour 
of tape -spoken word with rock music; 
new record releases and interviews; 
a spotlight of an artist or group; 
pop and folk music; and an hour of 
straight soul music. Minkin, a comedy 
writer, is a familiar radio commercial 
voice. Prince has managed the Tin 
Angel a Greenwich Village restau- 
rant, worked with the New York 
Shakespeare Festival's mobile theater, 
and served as assistant producer on 
several TV pilots.

Intruders 
The four -man vocal group of the 
Intruders is comprised of Sam (Little 
Sonny) Brown, who sings lead, Eu- 
gene (Bird) Daughtry, Robert (Big 
Sonny) Edwards, and Phillip (Phil) 
Terry. The Intruders are all natives 
of Philadelphia, their ages ranging 
from the teens to the early twenties. 
Little Sonny, who idolizes Chubby 
Checker, is an avid football and bas- 
ketball fan, a good roller skater, and 
a fine ballroom dancer. Bird holds 
several local swimming records, and 
was active in field and track sports. 
He is a self-taught bass player. Big 
Sonny, the descendant of a line of 
gospel 
singers, 
enjoys 
horseback 
riding, and owns two saddle horses. 
A high school football player, Phil 
also participated in dramatics, glee 
club, and choir while in high school. 
The Intruders, Gamble recording ar- 
tists, hit the charts in 1968 with 
"Cowboys To Girls," "Together," and 
"Slow Drag." The group's album, 
"Cowboys To Girls," also made the 
charts. 
Five by Five 
Five by Five consists of Ronnie 
Plants, lead vocals; 
Doug Green, 
drums; Larry Andrew, bass guitar; 
Tim Milam, organ; and Bill Merritt, 
lead guitar. The group members are 
all students at Southern State College 
in Magnolia, Arkansas. Ronnie is a 
sports car enthusiast who spends most 
of his spare time at sports car races 
and reading about his favorite past - 
time. Doug enjoys flying his own 
plane. Larry, a math major, and Tim, 
the youngest member of the group, 
are inveterate girl watchers. Bill is of 
a serious bent; he writes and formu- 
lates new ideas. He also likes to travel 
and meet new fans. "Fire," Five by 
Five's current single on Paula Rec- 
ords, is number 41 on the Top 100 
this week. The fivesome's first album, 
"Next Exit," was released recently.

Magtec Enters Tape Duplication Field 
NORTH HOLLYWOOD, Calif. - 
Magnetic Tape Engineering 
Corp. 
(Magtec), a privately held firm, has 
moved into the field of magnetic tape 
duplicating. Alan Clark, president and 
co-founder, said that "Magtec will 
specialize in the production of all 
standard formats of reel-to-reel, car- 
tridges and cassettes for the enter- 
tainment and educational field." 
Magtec has at its disposal the ex- 
perience of leading business and engi- 
neering personnel in the tape dupli- 
cating field. The combined man-year 
skill experience exceeds 50 years and 
comes from such firms as 3M, Mag- 
netic Tape Duplicators and Alto Fonic 
Programing, Inc. 
"Our company was formed not only 
to fulfill today's most pressing need 
in the entertainment and educational 
fields ... that of providing superior 
quality tape cartridges and cassettes," 
Clark stated, "but to be the added 
operational arm to our customers by 
providing prompt and personalized 
distribution and mailing of their 
products." 
"Demands for quality high speed 
tape duplication have far outsripped 
their supporting technologies. Today 
tape quality is only as good as 
the basic tape and obsolescent pro- 
duction technologies involved in pro- 
ducing the end product . .

Von Felten Joins GRT 
SUNNYVALE, Calif.-Raymond C. 
von Felten has joined General Re- 
corded Tape as tape development man-

magnetic tape products for GRT.

with Memorex Corporation of Santa 
Clara as product engineering man- 
ager.

York University. 
GRT is an independent producer of 
pre-recorded stereo tapes for the en- 
tertainment, educational, government 
and industrial markets.

New Facility 
The new 30,000 sq. ft. facility now 
being outfitted in North Hollywood, 
California, will feature an "electronic 
central" operation control console that 
supervises batteries of fully auto- 
mated high speed duplicators and 
slave production units. Production 
output will be disclosed at a later 
date. 
Key engineering and production per- 
sonnel of the new company were 
formerly associated with Magnetic 
Tape Duplicators of Hollywood. Presi- 
dent and chief executive officer, Clark 
is also president of Alto Fonic Pro- 
graming, Inc., Hollywood. Ken Goates, 
executive vice president and general 
manager, was formerly operations 
manager at MTD. Jack Strayer, vice 
president 
audio 
engineering, 
was 
formerly chief engineer at MTD. Vice 
president, systems engineering, is Roy 
G. Hippie, formerly at MTD as engi- 
nering supervisor. Vice president of 
marketing is James S. Walker, who 
joined Magtec from the 3M company, 
Magnetic Products Division. All of 
these executives are co-founders of 
the new corporation. 
The new facility, scheduled to be 
"on stream" early in 1969, is located 
at 8120 Webb Avenue, North Holly- 
wood, California.

RCA Appoints Len Magnus 
Recorded Tape Producer 
NEW YORK-RCA Records has ap- 
pointed Len Magnus to the position 
of A&R producer of recorded tape, 
according to Elliot Horne, manager 
of recorded tape, product planning. 
Magnus, who reports to Horne, 
joins the recorded tape marketing 
department with wide and varied ex- 
perience in radio production. For the 
past five years, he was associated with 
the ABC Radio Network as its asso- 
ciate director. In this capacity he was 
responsible for producing and direct- 
ing commercials and promotions for 
ABC, as well as various news spe- 
cials, the 1964 Political Conventions, 
space spots from Cape Kennedy and 
documentaries and music shows. 
Magnus has also been associated 
with WNYC, WABC and WINS. At 
WNYC he panned and coordinated 
programming, hired and trained an- 
nouncers, created programs, directed 
station publicity and compiled the 
station's 
Masterwork 
bulletin; at 
WABC he directed News and Music 
Programs and programmed music for 
disc jockey programs; and at WINS 
he programmed music and wrote and 
prepared newscasts as well as di- 
rected the Bill Stern Show, Zeke 
Manners Show, Allen Freed Show and 
the Les Keiter Sports Hour. 
In his new position. Maªnus will be 
responsible along with Julian Ross, 
and Chick Crumpacker for producing 
RCA's recorded tape product which 
includes Stereo 8 Cartridge Tapes 
and reel-to-reel tapes.

Nems Enterprises managing director Vic Lewis has finalized a deal with 
Czech impresario Frantisek Spurny whereby Czech and Anglo-American pop 
talent will be exchanged. Spurny is a top show business entrepreneur in Prague 
with a large artist roster. First fruits of the deal are January appearances in 
Prague by Johnny Mathis, followed by Donovan in February. Czech star Karel 
Gott, who has participated in the Eurovision Song Contest, will visit Britain 
reciprocally during January. Meanwhile, on another front, Lewis has expedited 
a single on the Nems label of "Goodnight" and "Julia," two items from the 
latest Beatles double album, using a forty-one piece orchestra and a choir 
of eight. Cyril Black of Nems has set sub -publishing deals for the company's 
copyrights with Stig Anderson of Sweden Music and Polar Music in Sweden, 
Dr. Mario Cantini of RCA Italiana in Italy, Alain Boublil of Vogue for France, 
and is currently conducting negotiations for Spain and Germany. Roy Guest 
of the Nems staff recently returned from two weeks of American discussions 
to fix transatlantic visits for Nems artists in 1969. Guest hopes to bring Joan 
Baez here next year for engagements. 
Songwriter, musical director and Pye A&R man Tony Hatch has signed 
Mark Murphy to the label. Murphy's first Pye single will be released in 
January and is a song written by Hatch with his wife Jackie Trent called 
"Come Back To Me." Hatch is also working on his next orchestral LP "Latin 
Velvet, Vol. 2" before the arrival of Frank Sinatra in town about the second 
week of January. Sinatra will record an album of Hatch -Trent songs for 
Warner -Reprise with Hatch arrangements and accompaniment. The sessions 
replace the ones originally planned for California earlier this fall. 
United Artists will release an LP of the orchestral score written by Francis 
Lai for the forthcoming movie "Hannibal Brooks," conducted by the composer. 
The film stars Oliver Reed and Michael Pollard, and the album will be available 
in February or March. Lai's other recent film score credits include "Mayerling," 
"Challenge In The Snow," a movie of the Winter Olympics at Grenoble, and 
"House Of Cards," which stars George Peppard and Orson Welles. A current 
UA soundtrack LP is Ken Thorne's score for "Inspector Clouseau" starring 
Alan Arkin. The label will also handle two Michel Legrand movie scores. One 
is "Play Dirty," a war film with Michael Caine, and "The Thomas Crown 
Affair" with Steve McQueen and Fay Dunnaway. Noel Harrison sings "The 
Windmills Of Your Mind" over the credits, and he will be featured in the UA 
soundtrack album and also on a single for Reprise to whom he is contracted 
with the same song. A February UA LP will be "Fantasmagorical" featuring 
veteran movie musical arranger and director Irwin Kostal conducting themes 
arranged by him and a suite by Richard Sherman, one of the "Chitty Chitty 
Bang Bang" composers. 
MGM has scheduled three February and three March releases in their VSP 
double album series. The February fare is "Ella And Louis," "Drummer Man" 
by Gene Krupa, and "Fred Astaire." The March releases will be "Ella 
Fitzgerald Sings The Rodgers And Hart Songbook," "Focus On Stan Getz" 
and "The Exotic Sounds Of Cal Tiader." The last two LPs will be the first 
VSP reissues from the Verve catalog to be available in stereo. MGM group 
the Showstoppers has extended their tour here and appeared at the United 
Nations Ball at Grosvenor House December 11th which was attended by 
Mrs. Mary Wilson, wife of the British premier. The group will be in Ireland 
December 13th -15th. MGM organ star Jimmy Smith has arrived from Germany 
and stars in a concert at the Royal Festival Hall December 14th. 
Keith Howell has been named CBS Records press officer in succession to 
Rodney Burbeck. Howell worked for Decca in its sleeve department, followed 
by a spell in the Nems Enterprises press office. His last post was press officer 
for the Film Producers' Guild. 
Francis Hitching and Bob Leaper are launching a new label to be called Fan 
featuring pop repertoire. It will be distributed through the independent BIRD 
network. 
Bud Logan and the Blue Boys, Jim Reeves' old accompanying group, were 
here for U.S. military base dates and some country and western club appear- 
ances. Mary Reeves travelled with them. RCA has released Logan's "What 
Am I Doing Hanging Round?" Nina Simone, hit parading for RCA with 
"Ain't Got No-I Got Life", arrived December 3rd for promotional dates and 
an appearance in David Frost's TV show. The Spectrum rush -recorded "Obla 
Di Obla Da," a song from the Beatles' double album, in an all-night RCA 
session. They face competition on the song from the Marmalade (CBS), among 
others. RCA has released the soundtrack album from "How Sweet It Is," the 
movie starring Maurice Bonet, Debbie Reynolds, James Garner and Terry - 
Thomas. The score was penned by Pat Williams and the title song was written 
by Jim Webb. Also on release from the label is 'r`t'he Flying Nun" LP, 
coinciding with the TV series here on December 12th, and a Hugo Montenegro 
album collating themes from Clint Eastwood westerns including his smash 
version of "The Good, The Bad And The Ugly." His follow-up single to this 
hit is the "Hang 'Em High" theme. Another RCA soundtrack set on release 
is "Interlude" with a score written by Georges Delerue and the title song 
sung by Timi Yuro. The Columbia movie stars Oskar Werner, Barbara Ferris 
and Virginia Maskell. 
The Bandwagon are here with manager Denny Randell for five weeks of 
TV, ballroom and discotheque dates. CBS hosted a reception in their honor at 
the Revolution Club November 27th. While here the group will be routining 
the follow-up to their "Breaking Down The Walls Of Heartache" hit for 
recording on their return to the States. 
American -born jazz singer Joy Marshall was found dead in her Hammer- 
smith apartment, and a coroner's verdict of misadventure was passed. She 
had succeeded Cleo Laine as singer with Johnny Dankworth's orchestra, and 
latterly had done a lot of club work. A Toast single called "And I'll Find You" 
scheduled for November 22nd release was not cancelled by the express wish 
of her parents. 
Ember managing director Jeff Kruger reports a deal with Ariola in Germany 
creating an Ember-Ariola label in that territory to handle Ember product. 
Kruger states that initial orders for forty thousand LPs have been placed by 
Ariola. 
The Beachboys arrived in Britain last Friday and met the press at a 
reception at the Hilton Hotel hosted by EMI Records. The group is here for 
a ten-day tour kicking off on December 1st at the London Palladium and they 
will record an "In Concert" album for future release on Capitol both in the 
U.K. and U.S.A. The Beachboys brought with them a 20 -channel p.a. system 
costing a quarter million dollars which will give greater clarity of sound in 
all parts of the theatre. After leaving London the boys flew to the continent 
for concerts in Milan, Stockholm, Copenhagen and Amsterdam. Their new U.K. 
release is their current American charter "Bluebirds Over The Mountains." 
With "Harper Valley P.T.A." now in the Top Ten, KPM Music are delighted 
to have Jeannie C. Riley's follow-up "The Girl Most Likely" on Polydor. 
Jeannie returns to Britain in January for promotion.

Enrico Macias returned to Paris on the 2nd of December after touring t 
U.S. The success of the singer -composer (born in North Africa) has go 
beyond the hopes of his managers. Enrico is now working out an important 7 
promotion for his new songs. 
Gilbert Bécaud, who records under his own label Dimensions, returns al 
to Paris after a long tour of Canada. As soon as he arrives, he will cut a Tic 
record under the direction of Jacques Poisson at the Pathé Marconi studios. 
CED (La Compagnie Européenne du Disque) and Barclay make a spec 
effort before the Christmas holidays to promote the rhythm and blues recor 
of the labels they represent in France. CED just released 2 albums, Chess a 
Atco, with various artists. Barclay publishes the 2 volumes of "Electric La 
Land" by the Jimi Hendrix Experience. This company also publishes t 
"Volumes 6 & 7" from the Rhythm and Blues Formidable series which grou 
the best artists presented under Atlantic label. 
Philips launches a campaign "Knowledge Of Classical Music," and to pi 
mote such a campaign publishes 8 LPs with 51 classical masterpieces. TI 
series is titled "Le Grand Concert." 
Considerable campaign by Pathé Marconi for Tamla-Motown. The same d 
4 LPs were launched on the market, the very latest of the 4 Tops, Diana Rc 
and the Supremes, the Temptations and Junior Walker. 
Eddie Barclay again organized a seminar for about thirty authors and co- 
posers. This song seminar took place in a castle down in the country from t 
22nd to the 25th November. 
Barclay's aim is to give the authors and composers who work for t 
artists under contract with his firm the opportunity to meet together and d 
cuss various matters and discover ideas. We would like to point out that t 
song "2'35 de bonheur," which was one of the most successful numbers 
Sylvie Vartan (under contract with RCA), was written last year during 
similar seminar. 
Roger Lanzac, the famous TV presenter, starts a new career. He just sign 
a contract as a vocalist with Henri Marchai who manages the independe 
production firm "Sunny Music."

EASTERN FLASHES 
JINGLE BELLS-Operators about 
town are dusting off their holiday 
singles these days, ready to make 
some hay during the lucrative weeks 
ahead. Of course, the good will give- 
away fever comes at the same time, 
but everything compensates in the end. 
Some of our friends have wallets, 
keychains, etc. made up with the com- 
pany name and phone number which 
they hand out as they visit their 
locations. This is a good idea because 
it's cheap and gets the company name 
out before the public. At any rate, we 
wish high collections to all.

Storino, 
Danny 
Sylvester, 
et
